questions.explanation: `Class.forName("com.example.MyClass")` dynamically loads and initializes the class by name, commonly used by frameworks and JDBC drivers historically to register themselves.

questions.question: In a typical Spring Boot application, a singleton-scoped `@Service` bean handles requests from many concurrent HTTP threads. What's true about mutable instance state on that bean?
options: It's automatically thread-safe with no extra effort
It's NOT inherently thread-safe - concurrent access from multiple request-handling threads to shared mutable service state needs explicit synchronization
Spring makes every bean a singleton copy per thread automatically
Thread safety is irrelevant since Java web servers are single-threaded
questions.answer: It's NOT inherently thread-safe - concurrent access from multiple request-handling threads to shared mutable state needs explicit synchronization
questions.explanation: A default (singleton-scoped) Spring bean is ONE shared instance across the whole application - any mutable instance field on it is genuinely shared across all concurrently-handled requests, so it needs the same thread-safety care as any other shared object accessed by multiple threads.

questions.question: Write a method `isPrime(int n)` that returns whether an integer is a prime number, optimized to check divisors only up to the square root of n.
questions.answer: Check divisibility from 2 up to sqrt(n) only, since any factor larger than sqrt(n) would have a corresponding smaller co-factor already checked.
questions.explanation: Casting to `long` for the `i * i` comparison avoids a potential int overflow for large n near Integer.MAX_VALUE.

questions.question: Why would using `HashMap` (instead of `ConcurrentHashMap`) as a shared cache accessed by multiple threads risk more than just incorrect values - what specific JDK bug class is this famous for?
questions.answer: Concurrent structural modification of a plain `HashMap` (like simultaneous resizes/rehashing from multiple threads) can, in older JDK versions, corrupt its internal linked-list bucket structure into a CYCLE, causing a subsequent `get()` call to loop forever and pin a CPU core at 100% - not just return a wrong value, but hang the thread entirely.
questions.explanation: `ConcurrentHashMap` is specifically designed to be safely used by multiple threads without external synchronization and without this failure mode, using fine-grained locking/CAS internally.

questions.question: Can an abstract class implement an interface without providing bodies for all of the interface's methods?
questions.answer: Yes - an abstract class is allowed to leave some (or all) of an implemented interface's methods unimplemented, since it doesn't need to be a fully concrete, instantiable type itself; the obligation to implement them just passes down to whichever concrete subclass eventually extends it.
questions.explanation: This is a common pattern for a partial/skeletal implementation class (e.g. `AbstractList`) that implements most of an interface's methods generically and leaves only a few core ones abstract for subclasses.

questions.question: What actually happens the moment an object becomes unreachable in Java?
options: It is deallocated immediately and synchronously the moment it becomes unreachable
It becomes ELIGIBLE for collection, but the actual reclaim timing is decided by the JVM's garbage collector, not guaranteed to be immediate
It stays in memory forever until the program exits
questions.answer: It becomes ELIGIBLE for collection, but the actual reclaim timing is decided by the JVM's garbage collector, not guaranteed to be immediate
questions.explanation: Becoming unreachable only makes an object a CANDIDATE for garbage collection - the JVM decides when (and whether, in the case of a program that exits first) to actually run the collection cycle that reclaims it.

questions.question: For a function that takes a T and returns a T (same type in and out), which functional interface is most idiomatic to use?
options: Both UnaryOperator<T> and Function<T,T> describe the same shape, but UnaryOperator is the more specific, idiomatic choice
questions.answer: Both UnaryOperator<T> and Function<T,T> describe the same shape, but UnaryOperator is the more specific, idiomatic choice
questions.explanation: `UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T,T>` and exists specifically to make this common 'same-type transform' case more self-documenting than the more generic Function.

questions.question: Which `java.nio.file` method checks whether a file or directory exists at a given Path?
questions.answer: Files.exists(path)
questions.explanation: `Files.exists(Path)` (and its counterpart `Files.notExists`) are the standard NIO.2 way to check existence; `File.check` isn't a real method.

questions.question: Why does `Object` sit at the very top of every Java class hierarchy, even for classes that don't explicitly extend anything?
questions.answer: Every class that doesn't explicitly `extends` another class implicitly extends `java.lang.Object`, which is why every object automatically has methods like `toString()`, `equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `getClass()` available even without writing any inheritance code.
questions.explanation: This universal common ancestor is what makes things like a generic `Object[]` array or `List<Object>` able to hold literally any type of object.

questions.question: Why does calling an overridden method from within a superclass CONSTRUCTOR risk operating on not-yet-initialized subclass state?
questions.answer: Java runs the superclass constructor BEFORE the subclass's own field initializers and constructor body run; if the superclass constructor calls an overridable method that the subclass has overridden, dynamic dispatch means the SUBCLASS's version runs - but at that point the subclass's own fields haven't been initialized yet, so it may see default values (0/null) instead of the values it expects.
questions.explanation: This is a well-known Java gotcha; the general advice is to avoid calling overridable methods from a constructor, or mark such methods `final`/`private` if they must run during construction.

questions.question: Where can a `protected` member be accessed from, in the general (non-same-package) case?
options: Within the same class and any subclass, regardless of package
Within the same package only, subclasses in other packages are excluded
questions.answer: Within the same class and any subclass, regardless of package
questions.explanation: Protected access explicitly extends visibility to subclasses even across package boundaries (with the caveat that access via a subclass reference must happen through the subclass's own type context per the JLS), on top of same-package access.

questions.question: Which of these best describes 'abstraction' as an OOP concept?
options: Hiding implementation complexity behind a simplified interface
Bundling data with methods and restricting direct access
Reusing code from a parent class
Allowing one interface to represent multiple underlying forms
questions.answer: Hiding implementation complexity behind a simplified interface
questions.explanation: The other three describe encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism respectively.

questions.question: Why does a static field declared in a superclass appear to be 'shared' even by all of its subclasses, unlike instance fields which each subclass instance gets its own copy of?
questions.answer: A static field belongs to the class it's declared in, and that single copy is shared by the entire class hierarchy rooted there - subclasses don't get their own separate copy of an inherited static field, they all read/write the SAME one belonging to the superclass (accessed via either the super or sub class name, it's the same memory location).
questions.explanation: This is why using static fields for anything meant to be per-subclass-distinct is a common design mistake - if you need a per-subclass constant that's genuinely different, an instance field (or an abstract method returning it) is usually more appropriate.

questions.question: Write a method `reverseString(String s)` that returns the reverse of a string.
questions.answer: Use `StringBuilder`'s built-in `.reverse()` method rather than manually looping and building a reversed string.
questions.explanation: StringBuilder.reverse() is implemented efficiently in-place on its internal char buffer, which is simpler and less error-prone than a manual loop.

questions.question: What is the correct generic bound syntax to require that a type parameter T is Comparable to itself (e.g. for a generic `max(T a, T b)` method)?
questions.answer: T extends Comparable<T>
questions.explanation: Even though Comparable is an interface, generic bounds always use the keyword `extends` (not `implements`), regardless of whether the bound is a class or an interface.

questions.question: Why does deserializing an object whose class has since had a field ADDED (compared to when it was serialized) generally still work without error?
questions.answer: Java's default deserialization matches fields by name against the CURRENT class definition - any field present in the current class but absent from the serialized stream simply gets its default value (0/false/null), rather than causing a failure, as long as the class's `serialVersionUID` still matches (or is compatible).
questions.explanation: Removing or fundamentally changing an EXISTING field's type is riskier and more likely to cause `InvalidClassException` or silently wrong data, which is why serialization is considered a fragile mechanism for long-term data persistence across evolving class versions.

questions.question: What does SQL stand for and what is it used for?
questions.answer: SQL stands for Structured Query Language; it is used to create, query, update, and manage data in relational databases.
questions.explanation: SQL is a declarative language for relational database management systems (RDBMS) — you describe what data you want, not how to fetch it.

questions.question: Which of the following is a Relational Database Management System (RDBMS)?
questions.answer: PostgreSQL
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL is a relational database that stores data in tables with rows/columns and enforces a schema; the others are NoSQL stores.

questions.question: What is the difference between a database and a table?
questions.answer: A database is a container that holds one or more tables (plus views, indexes, etc.); a table is a structured collection of rows and columns storing actual data.
questions.explanation: Tables are the concrete storage unit inside a database; a database is the organizational unit grouping related tables together.

questions.question: What is the difference between a primary key and a unique key?
questions.answer: Both enforce uniqueness, but a table can have only one primary key (which also disallows NULLs) while it can have multiple unique keys (which allow one NULL per column, in most databases).
questions.explanation: The primary key is the canonical identifier for a row and is implicitly NOT NULL; unique keys are additional uniqueness constraints that may permit NULLs.

questions.question: Which command is used to remove all rows from a table but keep its structure, resetting identity columns, and cannot be rolled back in most databases?
questions.answer: TRUNCATE
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE quickly deallocates all rows and typically resets auto-increment counters; DELETE removes rows individually (and can be rolled back and filtered with WHERE), while DROP removes the whole table.

questions.question: Write a query to select the `name` and `email` columns from a table called `users`.
questions.answer: SELECT name, email FROM users;
questions.explanation: Listing specific columns instead of `SELECT *` avoids pulling unnecessary data and is more resilient to schema changes.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), email VARCHAR(100));

questions.question: Write a query to select all distinct values of `city` from a `customers` table.
questions.answer: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers;
questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result set based on the selected column(s).
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, city VARCHAR(50));

questions.question: Write a query that returns the top 5 highest-paid employees from an `employees` table (columns: id, name, salary), ordered by salary descending.
questions.answer: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5;
questions.explanation: ORDER BY salary DESC sorts highest first, and LIMIT 5 restricts the result to the first 5 rows (use TOP 5 / FETCH FIRST in SQL Server/Oracle syntax instead).
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), salary DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: What does `SELECT *` do?
questions.answer: Selects every column of every matching row
questions.explanation: The asterisk is a wildcard meaning 'all columns' in the table(s) referenced by the FROM clause.
options: Selects every column of every matching row

questions.question: Why is using `SELECT *` in production application code generally discouraged?
questions.answer: It fetches unnecessary columns (wasting bandwidth/memory), breaks if columns are added/removed/reordered, and can silently include sensitive columns.
questions.explanation: Explicit column lists make queries self-documenting and resilient to schema evolution, and only transfer the data actually needed.

questions.question: Write a query to find all products in a `products` table with a price greater than 100.
questions.answer: SELECT * FROM products WHERE price > 100;
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before they are returned, evaluated per row against the given condition.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE products (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), price DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: Which operator checks whether a value falls within a given range, inclusive of both ends?
questions.answer: BETWEEN
questions.explanation: BETWEEN a AND b is shorthand for `col >= a AND col <= b`, inclusive on both bounds.

questions.question: Write a query to find customers whose `email` ends with '@gmail.com'.
questions.answer: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com';
questions.explanation: LIKE with a leading `%` wildcard matches any characters before the fixed suffix.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(100));

questions.question: Why does `WHERE column = NULL` never return any rows, even for rows where the column is actually NULL?
questions.answer: In SQL, NULL represents an unknown value, so any comparison with `=` against NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN rather than TRUE — you must use `IS NULL` instead.
questions.explanation: SQL's three-valued logic (TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN) treats NULL as 'unknown', and `x = NULL` is always UNKNOWN regardless of x, which WHERE treats as a non-match.

questions.question: Which clause is used to filter groups AFTER aggregation, as opposed to filtering individual rows before aggregation?
questions.answer: HAVING
questions.explanation: HAVING filters on aggregate results (e.g. COUNT(*) > 5) after GROUP BY has produced the groups; WHERE cannot reference aggregate functions.

questions.question: Write a query to list all employees ordered by `last_name` alphabetically.
questions.answer: SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY last_name ASC;
questions.explanation: ASC (ascending) is the default sort direction; it can be omitted but is shown here for clarity.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT PRIMARY KEY, last_name VARCHAR(50));

questions.question: What is the default sort order of ORDER BY if no direction is specified?
questions.answer: Ascending
questions.explanation: ASC is the SQL standard default when neither ASC nor DESC is written.

questions.question: Write a query to sort a `students` table first by `grade` descending, and for students in the same grade, by `name` ascending.
questions.answer: SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY grade DESC, name ASC;
questions.explanation: Multiple ORDER BY columns are applied left to right — later columns only break ties among rows equal on the earlier columns.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE students (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), grade INT);

questions.question: How do most databases order NULL values by default when sorting a column ascending?
questions.answer: In most databases (e.g. PostgreSQL, Oracle) NULLs sort last by default in ASC order and first in DESC order, but this default varies by database (MySQL sorts NULLs first in ASC).
questions.explanation: There is no single SQL-standard default for NULL ordering; `NULLS FIRST`/`NULLS LAST` (where supported) makes the behavior explicit and portable.

questions.question: Write a query to count the total number of rows in an `orders` table.
questions.answer: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts all rows regardless of NULLs; COUNT(column) would only count non-NULL values of that column.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, amount DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: Which aggregate function returns the average of a numeric column?
questions.answer: AVG
questions.explanation: AVG computes the arithmetic mean of the non-NULL values in the column.

questions.question: Does COUNT(column_name) count NULL values in that column?
questions.answer: No — COUNT(column_name) only counts rows where that column is NOT NULL. Only COUNT(*) counts every row regardless of NULLs.
questions.explanation: Aggregate functions other than COUNT(*) generally ignore NULLs entirely (SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX skip NULL values in their computation).

questions.question: Write a query to find the total `amount` of all orders in the `orders` table, along with the highest and lowest single order amount.
questions.answer: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, MAX(amount) AS highest, MIN(amount) AS lowest FROM orders;
questions.explanation: SUM, MAX, and MIN can be computed together in one SELECT since they all aggregate over the same row set.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, amount DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: Write a query to find the number of orders placed by each customer in an `orders` table (columns: id, customer_id, amount).
questions.answer: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows sharing the same customer_id into one group per customer, and COUNT(*) counts rows within each group.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, amount DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: Write a query to find customers who have placed more than 3 orders.
questions.answer: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups after aggregation — you cannot write `WHERE COUNT(*) > 3` because WHERE runs before grouping/aggregation happens.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, amount DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: In a query with GROUP BY, which columns are allowed in the SELECT list (in standard SQL)?
questions.answer: Only columns in the GROUP BY clause, or aggregate functions
questions.explanation: Standard SQL requires every non-aggregated selected column to appear in the GROUP BY clause, since each group must reduce to one row per output column.
options: Only columns in the GROUP BY clause, or aggregate functions

questions.question: What is the logical order of execution among FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, and ORDER BY in a SQL query?
questions.answer: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY (with LIMIT/OFFSET typically last).
questions.explanation: SQL is declarative and written in a different order than it is logically evaluated: rows are sourced and filtered before grouping, groups are filtered by HAVING, then the SELECT list (including aliases) is computed, and finally the result is sorted.

questions.question: What is the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN?
questions.answer: INNER JOIN returns only rows that have matching values in both tables; LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matched rows from the right table, with NULLs where there is no match.
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves unmatched left-side rows (filled with NULL for right-side columns), which INNER JOIN would simply exclude.

questions.question: Write a query to list each order along with the customer's name, given `orders(id, customer_id, amount)` and `customers(id, name)`, including orders whose customer somehow no longer exists.
questions.answer: SELECT o.id, o.amount, c.name FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from `orders` (the left table) even if there's no matching customer, returning NULL for `c.name` in that case.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100)); CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, amount DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: What does a CROSS JOIN produce between two tables of size M and N rows?
questions.answer: M * N rows (the Cartesian product)
questions.explanation: CROSS JOIN pairs every row of the first table with every row of the second, with no join condition, producing the full Cartesian product.

questions.question: Write a query using a self-join to find pairs of employees who work in the same department, given `employees(id, name, department_id)`.
questions.answer: SELECT e1.name AS employee1, e2.name AS employee2 FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.department_id = e2.department_id AND e1.id < e2.id;
questions.explanation: A self-join joins a table to itself using two aliases; `e1.id < e2.id` avoids pairing an employee with themself and avoids duplicate mirrored pairs.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), department_id INT);

questions.question: What is the difference between a RIGHT JOIN and rewriting the same query as a LEFT JOIN?
questions.answer: A `A RIGHT JOIN B` is equivalent to `B LEFT JOIN A` (with columns reordered) — RIGHT JOIN keeps all rows from the right table and NULL-fills unmatched left-table columns.
questions.explanation: RIGHT JOIN is rarely used in practice because swapping the table order and using LEFT JOIN expresses the same result more conventionally/readably.

questions.question: Write a query to find all employees whose salary is above the company average, given `employees(id, name, salary)`.
questions.answer: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);
questions.explanation: The subquery computes a single scalar value (the average), which the outer query then compares each row's salary against.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), salary DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: What is a 'correlated subquery'?
questions.answer: A subquery that references a column from the outer query and is re-evaluated per outer row
questions.explanation: Correlated subqueries depend on the current row of the outer query, so conceptually they execute once per outer row (though optimizers may rewrite this).
options: A subquery that runs once before the outer query
A subquery that references a column from the outer query and is re-evaluated per outer row
A subquery inside a WHERE clause only
A subquery that always returns multiple rows

questions.question: Write a query to find customers who have placed at least one order, given `customers(id, name)` and `orders(id, customer_id)`, using EXISTS.
questions.answer: SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
questions.explanation: EXISTS returns true as soon as the correlated subquery finds at least one matching row, and is typically efficient because it can short-circuit.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100)); CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT);

questions.question: Why can EXISTS often outperform IN when checking membership against a subquery that returns many rows?
questions.answer: EXISTS can stop scanning as soon as it finds one matching row, whereas IN historically required materializing the full subquery result to compare against; modern optimizers narrow this gap but EXISTS remains a safe, semantically clear choice, especially with NULLs.
questions.explanation: Additionally, NOT IN has a well-known pitfall: if the subquery result contains a NULL, `NOT IN` can unexpectedly return no rows at all, while `NOT EXISTS` does not have this problem.

questions.question: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
questions.answer: UNION combines the results of two queries and removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL combines them and keeps all duplicates.
questions.explanation: Because UNION must de-duplicate, it typically performs an implicit sort/hash step and is slower than UNION ALL when duplicates aren't a concern.

questions.question: What must be true about the two SELECT statements combined with UNION?
questions.answer: They must return the same number of columns with compatible types, in the same order
questions.explanation: UNION/UNION ALL/INTERSECT/EXCEPT all require the participating queries to have the same number of columns with compatible data types positionally.
options: They must query the same table
They must return the same number of columns with compatible types, in the same order
They must have identical column names
They must both use ORDER BY

questions.question: Write a query using INTERSECT to find customer IDs that appear in both a `2023_customers` table and a `2024_customers` table (each with a single `customer_id` column).
questions.answer: SELECT customer_id FROM 2023_customers INTERSECT SELECT customer_id FROM 2024_customers;
questions.explanation: INTERSECT returns only the rows present in both result sets (some databases like MySQL historically lacked INTERSECT and required a JOIN/IN workaround instead).
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE year_2023_customers (customer_id INT); CREATE TABLE year_2024_customers (customer_id INT);

questions.question: What is a SQL view?
questions.answer: A view is a saved, named SELECT query that behaves like a virtual table — querying it re-runs the underlying query without permanently storing its own copy of the data (unless it's a materialized view).
questions.explanation: Views are useful for simplifying complex queries, enforcing row/column-level access control, and presenting a stable interface even if underlying tables change.

questions.question: What is a materialized view?
questions.answer: A view whose result is physically stored and must be refreshed to reflect underlying data changes
questions.explanation: Unlike a regular view (re-executed each time it's queried), a materialized view caches its result set on disk for fast reads, at the cost of needing periodic REFRESH.
options: A view that cannot be queried
A view whose result is physically stored and must be refreshed to reflect underlying data changes
A synonym for a temporary table
A view that only works with joins

questions.question: Can you always INSERT or UPDATE through a view?
questions.answer: No — only 'simple' views (typically a single-table SELECT without aggregates, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, or joins) are usually updatable; views involving joins or aggregation generally are not, unless the database provides INSTEAD OF triggers.
questions.explanation: Because a view is a query, the database must be able to unambiguously map a change back to a single underlying row, which isn't always possible for complex views.

questions.question: What is an index in a database, and why is it used?
questions.answer: An index is a separate data structure (commonly a B-tree) that stores a sorted reference to column values, allowing the database to look up matching rows much faster than scanning the whole table.
questions.explanation: Without an index, a query filtering on a column requires a full table scan; an index lets the database jump directly to relevant rows, similar to a book's index.

questions.question: What is a downside of adding many indexes to a table?
questions.answer: Slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, since indexes must also be maintained, plus extra storage
questions.explanation: Every index must be updated whenever the underlying data changes, so write-heavy tables pay a cost for each additional index, along with the storage it consumes.
options: Slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, since indexes must also be maintained, plus extra storage

questions.question: Why might an index on a column NOT be used by the query optimizer even if the column appears in a WHERE clause?
questions.answer: Common reasons: the column is wrapped in a function or expression (e.g. WHERE LOWER(name) = ...), the query would return a large fraction of the table (making a full scan cheaper), the index is on a different leading column in a composite index, or statistics are stale.
questions.explanation: The optimizer estimates cost for both plans and picks whichever it predicts is cheaper — an index isn't automatically used just because it exists on a filtered column.

questions.question: In a composite (multi-column) index on (a, b, c), which queries can still use the index efficiently?
questions.answer: Queries filtering on a leftmost prefix of the columns can use it efficiently: filtering on `a` alone, `a AND b`, or `a AND b AND c` — but filtering on `b` alone (without `a`) generally cannot use this index efficiently.
questions.explanation: A composite B-tree index is physically sorted by the first column, then the second within each first-column value, and so on — so the index is only directly seekable from its leftmost column.

questions.question: What does a FOREIGN KEY constraint enforce?
questions.answer: It enforces referential integrity by ensuring a column's value must match an existing value in a referenced table's primary/unique key (or be NULL, if allowed).
questions.explanation: This prevents 'orphan' rows — e.g. an order referencing a customer_id that doesn't exist in the customers table.

questions.question: Which constraint ensures a column's value satisfies a custom boolean condition, e.g. `age >= 18`?
questions.answer: CHECK
questions.explanation: CHECK constraints let you define arbitrary conditions that every row must satisfy for that column (or combination of columns).

questions.question: What are the common referential actions available for ON DELETE on a foreign key (e.g. CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT)?
questions.answer: CASCADE deletes dependent rows automatically; SET NULL sets the foreign key column to NULL; RESTRICT/NO ACTION blocks the delete if dependent rows exist; SET DEFAULT sets it to a default value.
questions.explanation: These options control what happens to child rows when the referenced parent row is deleted, letting the schema encode the desired real-world behavior.

questions.question: What problem does database normalization solve?
questions.answer: Normalization organizes tables to reduce data redundancy and avoid update/insert/delete anomalies, by decomposing tables based on functional dependencies.
questions.explanation: For example, storing a customer's address redundantly in every order row risks inconsistency if the address changes; normalization moves it into a separate customers table referenced by foreign key.

questions.question: A table is in Second Normal Form (2NF) when it is in 1NF and additionally:
questions.answer: Every non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole primary key (no partial dependency)
questions.explanation: 2NF eliminates partial dependencies — relevant when a table has a composite primary key and some column depends on only part of that key.
options: Every non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole primary key (no partial dependency)

questions.question: What is a transitive dependency, and how does Third Normal Form (3NF) address it?
questions.answer: A transitive dependency exists when a non-key column depends on another non-key column, which in turn depends on the primary key (A -> B -> C). 3NF requires every non-key attribute to depend directly on the key, not transitively through another non-key attribute.
questions.explanation: For example, if `orders(order_id, customer_id, customer_city)` stores customer_city, and customer_city really depends on customer_id (not order_id), that's a transitive dependency 3NF would remove by moving customer_city to a customers table.

questions.question: When might you intentionally denormalize a database design?
questions.answer: When read performance is critical and the redundant data changes rarely, denormalizing (e.g. storing a computed total or duplicating a lookup value) can avoid expensive joins/aggregations at query time, trading some redundancy risk for speed.
questions.explanation: Denormalization is a deliberate trade-off, common in reporting/analytics schemas (e.g. data warehouses using star schemas), and should be applied selectively, not as a default.

questions.question: What does the 'A' in ACID stand for, and what does it guarantee?
questions.answer: Atomicity — it guarantees that a transaction's operations either all succeed and are committed, or if any part fails, the entire transaction is rolled back as if none of it happened.
questions.explanation: This prevents a transaction from leaving the database in a partially-applied, inconsistent state (e.g. debiting one account without crediting another).

questions.question: What does the Isolation property in ACID primarily concern?
questions.answer: Controlling how concurrently running transactions see each other's uncommitted changes
questions.explanation: Isolation levels (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable) define what anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads) concurrent transactions may observe.
options: Controlling how concurrently running transactions see each other's uncommitted changes

questions.question: What is a 'phantom read', and which isolation level is required to fully prevent it?
questions.answer: A phantom read occurs when a transaction re-runs a query and gets a different SET of rows (new rows appeared or existing ones vanished) because another transaction inserted/deleted matching rows in between. SERIALIZABLE isolation is required to fully prevent it.
questions.explanation: REPEATABLE READ prevents non-repeatable reads (a re-read row changing value) but, in the strict standard definition, does not guarantee against phantom rows appearing/disappearing; SERIALIZABLE effectively orders transactions as if run one at a time.

questions.question: What is a deadlock in the context of database transactions?
questions.answer: A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can proceed — e.g. Transaction A holds a lock on row 1 and waits for row 2, while Transaction B holds row 2 and waits for row 1.
questions.explanation: Most databases detect deadlocks automatically and abort one of the transactions (rolling it back) so the other can proceed.

questions.question: What is a stored procedure?
questions.answer: A stored procedure is a named, precompiled set of SQL statements (often with parameters and control flow) stored in the database and invoked by name.
questions.explanation: Stored procedures can encapsulate business logic close to the data, reduce network round-trips for multi-step operations, and be reused across applications.

questions.question: What is a key difference between a stored procedure and a user-defined function (UDF) in most SQL databases?
questions.answer: A function must return a value and can typically be used inside a SELECT/expression, while a procedure need not return a value and is invoked with CALL/EXEC
questions.explanation: Functions are designed to be composable inside expressions/queries and are usually restricted from side effects like DML in strict-mode databases, whereas procedures are invoked as standalone statements and commonly perform DML.
options: A function must return a value and can typically be used inside a SELECT/expression, while a procedure need not return a value and is invoked with CALL/EXEC
Functions can modify data but procedures cannot

questions.question: What is a database trigger?
questions.answer: A trigger is a piece of stored logic that automatically executes in response to a specific event (INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE) on a table.
questions.explanation: Triggers are useful for enforcing complex business rules, auditing changes, or maintaining derived/denormalized data automatically, without relying on application code to remember to do so.

questions.question: What is the difference between a BEFORE and an AFTER trigger?
questions.answer: BEFORE fires before the triggering operation is applied (can modify/validate the row), AFTER fires once it has been applied
questions.explanation: BEFORE triggers can inspect and even change the incoming row (e.g. via NEW in MySQL/PostgreSQL) before it's written, useful for validation/defaulting; AFTER triggers run once the change is committed to the table, useful for auditing or cascading effects.
options: BEFORE runs on SELECT, AFTER on INSERT
BEFORE fires before the triggering operation is applied (can modify/validate the row), AFTER fires once it has been applied
AFTER triggers cannot access the changed row

questions.question: What risk do triggers introduce for application maintainability, and how can you mitigate it?
questions.answer: Triggers execute 'invisibly' from the application's perspective — a developer looking at application code may not realize extra logic runs on INSERT/UPDATE, making behavior harder to trace and debug. Mitigation: keep triggers minimal, well-documented, and prefer explicit application-level logic for anything business-critical or complex.
questions.explanation: Because triggers are defined in the database rather than version-controlled application code (unless migrations are carefully tracked), they can become a hidden source of bugs and hard-to-reproduce behavior.

questions.question: Write a query that ranks employees by salary (highest first) within each department, given `employees(id, name, department_id, salary)`.
questions.answer: SELECT name, department_id, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS salary_rank FROM employees;
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY restarts the ranking for each department, and ORDER BY salary DESC determines the rank order within each partition; RANK() gives tied values the same rank and skips the next rank number.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), department_id INT, salary DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: What is the difference between RANK() and DENSE_RANK() when there are ties?
questions.answer: RANK() leaves gaps in the ranking sequence after a tie; DENSE_RANK() does not
questions.explanation: If two rows tie for rank 2, RANK() assigns them both 2 and the next row gets rank 4 (skipping 3); DENSE_RANK() assigns them both 2 and the next row gets rank 3 (no gap).
options: RANK() leaves gaps in the ranking sequence after a tie; DENSE_RANK() does not
DENSE_RANK() leaves gaps; RANK() does not
RANK() only works with PARTITION BY

questions.question: How does a window function differ from GROUP BY aggregation?
questions.answer: GROUP BY collapses multiple rows into one row per group, losing row-level detail; a window function computes an aggregate/ranking value PER ROW while still returning every original row, using OVER(...) to define the window of rows it considers.
questions.explanation: This lets you show, e.g., each employee's salary alongside their department's average salary in the same row, which plain GROUP BY cannot do without a self-join or subquery.

questions.question: What does EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN PLAN) show, and why is it useful?
questions.answer: EXPLAIN shows the execution plan the database's query optimizer intends to use for a query — which indexes (if any) it will use, join order, join algorithms, and estimated row counts/cost.
questions.explanation: It's the primary tool for diagnosing why a query is slow, e.g. revealing an unexpected full table scan where an index scan was expected.

questions.question: Which of the following typically hurts query performance the most on a large table?
questions.answer: A full table scan caused by a non-sargable predicate (e.g. wrapping the column in a function)
questions.explanation: Non-sargable predicates (Search ARGument ABLE) — like `WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024` instead of a range comparison — prevent the optimizer from using an index on that column, forcing a full scan.
options: Using an indexed column in WHERE
A full table scan caused by a non-sargable predicate (e.g. wrapping the column in a function)

questions.question: A query joining three large tables is slow. What are three concrete things you would check to speed it up?
questions.answer: Check: (1) EXPLAIN plan for full table scans and confirm join columns are indexed, (2) whether the join order/algorithm chosen makes sense given table sizes and selectivity, (3) whether the query fetches more columns/rows than actually needed (e.g. missing WHERE filters, unnecessary DISTINCT, or SELECT *).
questions.explanation: Systematic diagnosis (plan first, then indexes, then query shape) is more reliable than guessing — the EXPLAIN plan usually points directly at the bottleneck (e.g. a specific unindexed join column).

questions.question: Which category of SQL statements does `CREATE TABLE` belong to?
questions.answer: DDL
questions.explanation: DDL (Data Definition Language) covers statements that define/alter schema objects: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE.

questions.question: Which category do INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE belong to?
questions.answer: DML
questions.explanation: DML (Data Manipulation Language) covers statements that manipulate the actual data rows: SELECT is sometimes classified separately as DQL, but INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE are DML.

questions.question: What is the difference between COMMIT and ROLLBACK, and what category of statement are they?
questions.answer: Both are TCL (Transaction Control Language) statements. COMMIT permanently saves all changes made in the current transaction; ROLLBACK discards them, reverting the database to its state before the transaction began.
questions.explanation: TCL statements manage transaction boundaries; without an explicit COMMIT, changes may only be visible within the current session depending on the database's autocommit setting.

questions.question: GRANT and REVOKE, which control user permissions, belong to which category?
questions.answer: DCL
questions.explanation: DCL (Data Control Language) manages access control/permissions on database objects.

questions.question: What is an Entity-Relationship (ER) diagram used for?
questions.answer: An ER diagram visually models the entities (things) in a system, their attributes, and the relationships between them, before translating that design into actual database tables.
questions.explanation: It's a design tool used during the database design phase to capture requirements and relationships (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many) clearly before implementation.

questions.question: How is a many-to-many relationship typically implemented in a relational database?
questions.answer: Using a junction (bridge/associative) table with foreign keys to both entities
questions.explanation: A junction table (e.g. `student_courses` linking `students` and `courses`) holds one row per association, converting the many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships.
options: By adding a foreign key directly on both tables
By adding a foreign key on the table with fewer rows
Using a junction (bridge/associative) table with foreign keys to both entities
It cannot be implemented in relational databases

questions.question: You are modeling a blog: users write posts, and posts can have multiple tags while tags can apply to multiple posts. Describe the tables and relationships you'd create.
questions.answer: Tables: `users(id, ...)`, `posts(id, user_id FK, title, content, ...)`, `tags(id, name)`, and a junction table `post_tags(post_id FK, tag_id FK)`. users->posts is one-to-many; posts<->tags is many-to-many via post_tags.
questions.explanation: The one-to-many (user to posts) is expressed with a simple foreign key on the 'many' side; the many-to-many (posts to tags) requires the junction table since neither side's foreign key alone can represent multiple associations per row.

questions.question: What is a SQL injection attack?
questions.answer: SQL injection occurs when untrusted user input is concatenated directly into a SQL query string, allowing an attacker to alter the query's logic — e.g. inputting `' OR '1'='1` to bypass a login check.
questions.explanation: Because the database can't distinguish attacker-supplied SQL syntax from the intended query structure once it's concatenated as a string, the attacker effectively gets to write part of the query themselves.

questions.question: What is the most effective defense against SQL injection?
questions.answer: Using parameterized queries / prepared statements
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries send the SQL structure and the user-supplied values separately to the database driver, so user input is always treated as data, never as executable SQL syntax, regardless of its content.
options: Escaping quotes manually in application code

questions.question: A login query is built as: `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + username + "' AND password = '" + password + "'"`. Explain how an attacker could bypass authentication, and how to fix it.
questions.answer: An attacker could set username to `admin' -- ` (or `' OR '1'='1' -- `), which comments out the password check or makes the WHERE clause always true, logging in without a valid password. Fix: use a parameterized query, e.g. `WHERE username = ? AND password = ?` with bound parameters, and never build SQL via string concatenation of user input.
questions.explanation: The `--` starts a SQL comment in most dialects, so everything after it (including the password check) is ignored; parameterization eliminates this entire class of attack because the driver never re-parses user input as SQL syntax.

questions.question: Write a query to find the second-highest salary from an `employees` table (columns: id, salary), without using LIMIT/OFFSET.
questions.answer: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
questions.explanation: The inner subquery finds the overall maximum; the outer query then finds the maximum salary strictly less than that, which is the second-highest (handles ties on the top salary correctly).
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT PRIMARY KEY, salary DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: Write a query to find duplicate email addresses in a `users` table (columns: id, email).
questions.answer: SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
questions.explanation: Grouping by email and filtering groups with more than one row identifies which email values occur more than once.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(100));

questions.question: Write a query to find all departments that have no employees, given `departments(id, name)` and `employees(id, name, department_id)`.
questions.answer: SELECT d.name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.id = e.department_id WHERE e.id IS NULL;
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps every department even without a matching employee; filtering for `e.id IS NULL` isolates departments where no employee row matched.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE departments (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100)); CREATE TABLE employees (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), department_id INT);

questions.question: Write a query to find employees who earn more than their department's average salary, given `employees(id, name, department_id, salary)`.
questions.answer: SELECT e.name FROM employees e WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id);
questions.explanation: This is a correlated subquery: for each outer row, the inner query recomputes the average salary restricted to that employee's own department, then compares.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), department_id INT, salary DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: Write a query to update the `status` column to 'inactive' for all users in a `users` table who haven't logged in (`last_login` is NULL).
questions.answer: UPDATE users SET status = 'inactive' WHERE last_login IS NULL;
questions.explanation: UPDATE with a WHERE clause modifies only the matching rows; omitting WHERE would update every row in the table.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, status VARCHAR(20), last_login DATE);

questions.question: Write a query to delete customers from a `customers` table who have never placed an order, given `orders(id, customer_id)`.
questions.answer: DELETE FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL);
questions.explanation: Filtering `customer_id IS NOT NULL` in the subquery avoids the classic NOT IN + NULL pitfall, where a single NULL in the subquery result would make NOT IN match no rows at all.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT);

questions.question: Which of these best describes a schema in a relational database?
questions.answer: The structural definition of tables, columns, types, and constraints
questions.explanation: A schema is the blueprint describing what tables exist, their columns/types, and the constraints/relationships between them — distinct from the actual data (rows) stored in it.
options: The structural definition of tables, columns, types, and constraints

questions.question: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
questions.answer: A clustered index determines the physical storage order of the table's rows (a table can have only one), while a non-clustered index is a separate structure pointing back to the row's location, and a table can have many.
questions.explanation: Because a clustered index dictates physical row order, lookups by that key are especially fast, but only one clustering order can exist per table.

questions.question: Write a query to get the 3 most recently placed orders from an `orders` table (columns: id, order_date, amount).
questions.answer: SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT 3;
questions.explanation: Sorting by order_date descending puts the newest first, and LIMIT 3 restricts the result to just those three rows.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, order_date DATE, amount DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: Can you ORDER BY a column that isn't in the SELECT list?
questions.answer: Yes, in most databases, as long as it's from a table referenced in the FROM clause
questions.explanation: ORDER BY is evaluated after the row set is formed and generally can reference any column available from the FROM clause, not just ones in the final SELECT list (some restrictions apply with DISTINCT/UNION).
options: Yes, in most databases, as long as it's from a table referenced in the FROM clause

questions.question: Write a query to find how many distinct customers have placed at least one order, given `orders(id, customer_id)`.
questions.answer: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders;
questions.explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts unique non-NULL values rather than every row, so a customer with 5 orders is only counted once.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT);

questions.question: Why can't you write `SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders` without a GROUP BY, if `customer_id` isn't unique per row?
questions.answer: Standard SQL rejects mixing a non-aggregated column with an aggregate function in the same SELECT without GROUP BY, because it's ambiguous which customer_id value should represent the single aggregated SUM row.
questions.explanation: Some databases (like older MySQL in non-strict mode) silently allow this and pick an arbitrary row's value, which is why relying on it is considered a bug-prone anti-pattern; GROUP BY customer_id resolves the ambiguity explicitly.

questions.question: What happens if you try to insert a row that violates a UNIQUE constraint?
questions.answer: The INSERT fails with a constraint violation error
questions.explanation: Constraint violations cause the statement to fail and roll back (in the context of that statement/transaction), protecting data integrity rather than silently corrupting or skipping data.
options: The row is inserted with a warning
The database silently ignores the duplicate value
The INSERT fails with a constraint violation error
The old row is automatically deleted

questions.question: Can a column with a FOREIGN KEY constraint contain NULL values?
questions.answer: Yes, by default, unless the column also has a NOT NULL constraint — a NULL foreign key simply means 'no relationship for this row', and referential integrity checks don't apply to NULLs.
questions.explanation: This is commonly used for optional relationships, e.g. an `orders.assigned_agent_id` that's NULL until an agent is assigned.

questions.question: Write a query to create a view named `high_value_customers` showing customers (from `customers(id, name)`) with total order amount over 10000, given `orders(id, customer_id, amount)`.
questions.answer: CREATE VIEW high_value_customers AS SELECT c.id, c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total_spent FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id, c.name HAVING SUM(o.amount) > 10000;
questions.explanation: The view encapsulates the join + aggregation + HAVING filter logic behind a simple name that can be queried like `SELECT * FROM high_value_customers` going forward.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100)); CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, amount DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: What is the difference between EXCEPT (or MINUS in Oracle) and a NOT IN subquery for finding rows in one set but not another?
questions.answer: EXCEPT/MINUS is a set operation comparing whole rows between two same-shaped queries and handles NULLs predictably, while a NOT IN subquery has the well-known pitfall of returning zero rows entirely if the subquery contains any NULL value.
questions.explanation: For excluding rows based on a subquery, EXCEPT or a NOT EXISTS correlated subquery are generally safer choices than NOT IN when NULLs might be present.

questions.question: Does UNION ALL guarantee any particular row order in its result?
questions.answer: No — row order is undefined unless an explicit ORDER BY is added at the end
questions.explanation: Like any SQL query without an ORDER BY, the result order of UNION/UNION ALL is not guaranteed by the standard — an explicit ORDER BY on the combined result is required for a reliable order.
options: Yes, always ascending by first column
No — row order is undefined unless an explicit ORDER BY is added at the end
Yes, insertion order is always preserved

questions.question: What is a key security/performance benefit of stored procedures when handling user input?
questions.answer: Stored procedures naturally use parameters rather than string concatenation, which helps prevent SQL injection, and because they are precompiled, the database can cache and reuse their execution plan across calls.
questions.explanation: Application code calling a procedure with bound parameters (e.g. `CALL update_balance(?, ?)`) never builds SQL from raw user input, closing off the injection vector entirely for that operation.

questions.question: You want to automatically log every change to a `salary` column in an `employees` table into an `audit_log` table. What kind of trigger would you use, and why?
questions.answer: An AFTER UPDATE trigger on `employees`, which inserts a row into `audit_log` (old value, new value, timestamp, user) once the update has actually been applied.
questions.explanation: AFTER is appropriate here because the goal is recording what happened, not validating/blocking the change beforehand, and using AFTER avoids re-triggering validation logic that might belong in a BEFORE trigger.

questions.question: Write a query using a window function to show each order's amount alongside a running total of amounts ordered by order_date, given `orders(id, order_date, amount)`.
questions.answer: SELECT id, order_date, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total FROM orders;
questions.explanation: SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) with no PARTITION BY computes a cumulative sum across all rows up to and including the current row's position in the specified order, without collapsing rows like GROUP BY would.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, order_date DATE, amount DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem, and how does it typically arise?
questions.answer: It occurs when code fetches a list of N parent records with one query, then issues a separate query for each parent's related data (N additional queries) instead of fetching everything in one join or batched query, resulting in N+1 total round-trips.
questions.explanation: This is a common ORM pitfall; fixing it usually means eager-loading the related data with a JOIN or a single `WHERE parent_id IN (...)` query instead of looping and querying per row.

questions.question: What is the goal of First Normal Form (1NF)?
questions.answer: 1NF requires each column to hold atomic (indivisible) values and each row to be uniquely identifiable, with no repeating groups or multi-valued columns (e.g. no storing a comma-separated list of phone numbers in one column).
questions.explanation: Splitting a multi-valued column into a separate related table (or separate rows) is the typical fix to bring a table into 1NF.

questions.question: What is the difference between a weak entity and a strong entity in ER modeling?
questions.answer: A strong entity has its own primary key and can exist independently; a weak entity cannot be uniquely identified by its own attributes alone and depends on a relationship with an 'owner' strong entity (using a partial key plus the owner's key).
questions.explanation: A classic example: `order_items` might be a weak entity — an item only makes sense in the context of a specific order, identified by (order_id, item_number).

questions.question: Which practice most directly reduces the blast radius of a successful SQL injection, independent of preventing the injection itself?
questions.answer: Running the application's database user with the minimum privileges it actually needs (least privilege)
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits what an attacker can do even if injection succeeds — e.g. a reporting app's DB user shouldn't have DROP TABLE or write access it never needs.
options: Running the application's database user with the minimum privileges it actually needs (least privilege)

questions.question: Write a query to find the department with the highest average salary, given `employees(id, department_id, salary)`.
questions.answer: SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department_id ORDER BY avg_salary DESC LIMIT 1;
questions.explanation: Grouping by department and averaging salary per group, then sorting descending and taking the top row, isolates the single highest-average department.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT PRIMARY KEY, department_id INT, salary DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: Write a query to find customers who placed orders in every month of 2024, given `orders(id, customer_id, order_date)`.
questions.answer: SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2024 GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)) = 12;
questions.explanation: Counting the distinct months (1-12) present per customer within 2024 and requiring that count to equal 12 identifies customers with at least one order in every month.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, order_date DATE);

questions.question: What does the acronym SQL stand for?
questions.answer: Structured Query Language
questions.explanation: SQL is the standard language for storing, manipulating, and retrieving data in relational database systems.

questions.question: Which SQL clause is used to filter groups after aggregation, as opposed to filtering rows before aggregation?
questions.answer: HAVING
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY runs; HAVING filters the aggregated groups produced by GROUP BY, so it can reference aggregate functions like COUNT() or SUM().

questions.question: Is SQL case-sensitive for its keywords (e.g. SELECT vs select)?
questions.answer: No, SQL keywords are case-insensitive in virtually all major RDBMSs
questions.explanation: `SELECT`, `select`, and `Select` are all treated identically by the parser; however, identifier (table/column name) case sensitivity DOES vary by database and platform (e.g. quoted identifiers on PostgreSQL are case-sensitive), so conventions like uppercase keywords are a readability choice, not a requirement.

questions.question: Write a query to select all columns from a table named `employees`.
questions.answer: SELECT * FROM employees;
questions.explanation: The `*` wildcard selects every column; while convenient for ad-hoc queries, explicitly naming columns is generally preferred in application code to avoid breaking when the schema changes.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR(100), department VARCHAR(50), salary DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: How do you rename a selected column's output name using an alias?
questions.answer: SELECT column_name AS alias_name
questions.explanation: The `AS` keyword (optional in most dialects) renames a column or expression in the result set only - it does not change the underlying column name in the table.

questions.question: Write a query to select distinct department names from the `employees` table.
questions.answer: SELECT DISTINCT department FROM employees;
questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result set based on the selected column(s), so each department name appears only once even if many employees share it.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR(100), department VARCHAR(50), salary DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: What is the difference between `IS NULL` and `= NULL` in a WHERE clause?
questions.answer: `= NULL` never matches anything (always evaluates to UNKNOWN); `IS NULL` is the correct way to test for NULL
questions.explanation: NULL represents an unknown value, so any comparison using `=` against NULL yields UNKNOWN rather than TRUE, even comparing NULL to NULL - SQL requires the special `IS NULL`/`IS NOT NULL` predicates to test nullness.

questions.question: Write a query to find employees whose name starts with 'A' using LIKE.
questions.answer: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name LIKE 'A%';
questions.explanation: The `%` wildcard in LIKE matches zero or more of any character, so `'A%'` matches any string starting with 'A'.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR(100), department VARCHAR(50));

questions.question: What is the default sort direction of ORDER BY if none is specified?
questions.answer: Ascending (ASC)
questions.explanation: SQL defaults to ascending order; DESC must be explicitly specified for descending order.

questions.question: Write a query to sort employees by department ascending, then by salary descending within each department.
questions.answer: SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY department ASC, salary DESC;
questions.explanation: ORDER BY can take multiple columns; the first is the primary sort key, and subsequent columns break ties within groups that share the same value for the earlier columns.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR(100), department VARCHAR(50), salary DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: If a query uses ORDER BY on a column not in the SELECT list, but also uses DISTINCT, what problem can occur?
questions.answer: Some databases require every ORDER BY column to appear in the SELECT list when DISTINCT is used, and will raise an error otherwise
questions.explanation: Because DISTINCT deduplicates rows based only on the SELECT list's columns, sorting by a column that was never part of that deduplication is ambiguous - which of several 'duplicate' original rows' value for that column should be used? Some engines reject it outright rather than guess.

questions.question: Which aggregate function returns the number of rows in a group, including rows with NULL values (when used as COUNT(*))?
questions.answer: COUNT(*)
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts every row regardless of NULLs; COUNT(column_name) only counts rows where that specific column is non-NULL - a common source of confusion.

questions.question: What does AVG() do when a column being averaged contains NULL values?
questions.answer: NULLs are excluded from both the sum and the count used to compute the average
questions.explanation: AVG ignores NULL rows entirely rather than treating them as 0, so averaging [10, NULL, 20] gives 15, not 10.

questions.question: Write a query to find the total salary paid per department.
questions.answer: SELECT department, SUM(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department;
questions.explanation: SUM aggregates the salary column, and GROUP BY department ensures the sum is computed separately for each department rather than across the whole table.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR(100), department VARCHAR(50), salary DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: Write a query to find departments with more than 5 employees.
questions.answer: SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
questions.explanation: HAVING filters on the aggregated COUNT(*) result per group, which WHERE cannot do since WHERE runs before grouping/aggregation occurs.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR(100), department VARCHAR(50));

questions.question: Can a column appear in SELECT without being in GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate function?
questions.answer: In standard SQL, no - it causes an error; MySQL historically allowed it (returning an arbitrary row's value) unless ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY mode is enabled
questions.explanation: Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT list must be functionally dependent on the GROUP BY columns, otherwise the database cannot determine which row's value to report for that column within a group - most databases (PostgreSQL, SQL Server) enforce this strictly.

questions.question: Which JOIN type returns only rows that have matching values in both tables?
questions.answer: INNER JOIN
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN excludes any row from either table that doesn't have a corresponding match in the other table, based on the join condition.

questions.question: What does a LEFT JOIN return for rows in the left table that have no match in the right table?
questions.answer: The left table's columns with their actual values, and NULL for every column from the right table
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves every row from the left table regardless of match, filling in NULLs for the unmatched right-side columns - this is the key difference from INNER JOIN.

questions.question: What does a CROSS JOIN between a table with 3 rows and a table with 4 rows produce?
questions.answer: 12 rows (the Cartesian product: 3 x 4)
questions.explanation: CROSS JOIN pairs every row of the first table with every row of the second table with no join condition, so the result size is the product of both table sizes - it's rarely intentional in production queries outside generating combinations.
questions.code_snippet: SELECT * FROM table_a CROSS JOIN table_b; -- table_a has 3 rows, table_b has 4 rows

questions.question: Write a query to list each employee's name along with their department's name, given a separate departments table.
questions.answer: SELECT e.name, d.department_name FROM employees e INNER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id;
questions.explanation: The join condition `e.department_id = d.id` connects each employee row to its matching department row via the foreign key relationship.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR(100), department_id INT); CREATE TABLE departments (id INT, department_name VARCHAR(50));

questions.question: Write a query to find employees who earn more than the average salary, using a subquery.
questions.answer: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);
questions.explanation: The subquery computes a single scalar value (the average), which the outer query then compares each employee's salary against.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR(100), salary DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: What is a correlated subquery, and how does it differ from a regular (non-correlated) subquery?
questions.answer: A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, so it must be re-evaluated once per outer row, unlike a non-correlated subquery which runs once independently
questions.explanation: Because a correlated subquery depends on the current outer row's values, the database conceptually executes it repeatedly (though optimizers often rewrite it as a join for performance) - this makes correlated subqueries potentially much slower on large tables if not optimized.

questions.question: Does UNION ALL guarantee the rows keep the same relative order as the two original SELECT statements?
questions.answer: Not unless an explicit ORDER BY is added to the overall UNION ALL statement - without one, row order is not guaranteed by the SQL standard
questions.explanation: Many databases happen to preserve the order rows were produced in practice, but relying on that is not portable or guaranteed - if a specific order matters, always add an explicit ORDER BY at the end of the combined query.

questions.question: For a UNION to work between two SELECT statements, what must be true about their result sets?
questions.answer: Both must have the same number of columns, with compatible data types in the same column positions
questions.explanation: UNION combines rows positionally, not by column name, so column count and type-compatibility (not necessarily identical names) between the two queries is required, or the database raises an error.

questions.question: Can a view be built on top of another view?
questions.answer: Yes, views can be nested (a view's defining query can select from another view)
questions.explanation: This is convenient for layering abstractions, but deeply nested views can hurt query performance and readability, since the database must effectively inline/expand every layer when the outer view is queried.

questions.question: Under what circumstances can you INSERT/UPDATE data through a view?
questions.answer: Only when the view is 'simple' enough - typically based on a single table with no aggregates, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, or set operations - so the database can unambiguously map the change back to the base table
questions.explanation: A view that joins multiple tables or aggregates data usually cannot be directly updated because there's no unambiguous way to translate a change in the view's output back into a change on the underlying rows.

questions.question: Why can adding too many indexes to a table slow down write performance?
questions.answer: Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE must also update every index defined on the affected columns, so more indexes mean more work per write
questions.explanation: Indexes trade write speed and storage space for read speed - this is why indexing strategy typically targets columns that are frequently searched/joined/sorted on, not every column.

questions.question: What is a composite (multi-column) index, and why does column order within it matter?
questions.answer: An index built on multiple columns together; it can efficiently satisfy queries that filter on a leading prefix of those columns, but not queries that only filter on a non-leading column
questions.explanation: A composite index on (a, b) is structured like a sorted list first by `a`, then by `b` within each `a` value - a query filtering only on `b` cannot use it efficiently, similar to how a phone book sorted by last-then-first name can't quickly find people by first name alone.

questions.question: Which constraint ensures a column's value must be unique across all rows but still allows NULL values (in most databases)?
questions.answer: UNIQUE
questions.explanation: Unlike PRIMARY KEY (which forbids NULL), a UNIQUE constraint allows NULLs, and most databases even allow multiple NULLs since NULL is never considered equal to another NULL for uniqueness purposes.

questions.question: What happens if you try to delete a row that is referenced by a FOREIGN KEY in another table, with no ON DELETE clause specified?
questions.answer: The delete is rejected with a foreign key constraint violation error
questions.explanation: The default foreign key behavior (RESTRICT/NO ACTION) prevents deleting a parent row while child rows still reference it, protecting referential integrity - ON DELETE CASCADE or SET NULL must be explicitly configured for different behavior.

questions.question: What problem does Second Normal Form (2NF) address that First Normal Form (1NF) does not?
questions.answer: Partial dependency - where a non-key column depends on only PART of a composite primary key rather than the whole key
questions.explanation: 2NF requires 1NF plus the elimination of partial dependencies, which typically only matters for tables with composite (multi-column) primary keys; tables with a single-column key are automatically in 2NF once they satisfy 1NF.

questions.question: What is a transitive dependency, and which normal form eliminates it?
questions.answer: A transitive dependency is when a non-key column depends on another non-key column, which in turn depends on the primary key (A -> B -> C); Third Normal Form (3NF) eliminates it
questions.explanation: For example, storing both `department_id` and `department_name` in an employees table creates a transitive dependency (department_name depends on department_id, not directly on employee id) - 3NF requires moving department_name to its own departments table.

questions.question: What does the 'I' in ACID stand for, and what does it guarantee?
questions.answer: Isolation - concurrent transactions produce the same result as if they had executed one after another (serially), even though they may actually run concurrently
questions.explanation: Isolation is enforced via locking or multi-version concurrency control (MVCC); the exact strength of the guarantee depends on the configured isolation level (Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable, etc.).

questions.question: What is a 'phantom read' and which isolation level is specifically designed to prevent it?
questions.answer: A phantom read occurs when a transaction re-runs a query and sees NEW rows that satisfy the condition, inserted by another committed transaction in between; SERIALIZABLE isolation prevents it
questions.explanation: Unlike a non-repeatable read (an existing row's value changing between reads), a phantom read is about the ROW SET changing size - REPEATABLE READ prevents changes to already-read rows but doesn't guarantee against new matching rows appearing, which is why SERIALIZABLE is the level that fully closes this gap.

questions.question: What is one key advantage of using a stored procedure over sending the equivalent raw SQL from application code each time?
questions.answer: The execution plan can be pre-compiled/cached and reused, and it reduces the amount of data sent over the network (just the procedure call + parameters, not the full SQL text)
questions.explanation: Stored procedures also help centralize business logic in the database and can reduce SQL injection risk if parameters are used correctly, though modern parameterized queries from application code achieve similar security.

questions.question: How does NTILE() differ from RANK() and DENSE_RANK()?
questions.answer: NTILE(n) divides the ordered rows into n roughly equal-sized buckets and returns the bucket number for each row, rather than a rank based on value comparisons
questions.explanation: NTILE is used for percentile/quartile-style bucketing (e.g. NTILE(4) for quartiles), while RANK/DENSE_RANK reflect a row's position relative to ties in the ordering - the two solve different problems even though both are ranking-style window functions.

questions.question: Write a query using a window function to show each employee's salary alongside the average salary of their department, without collapsing rows via GROUP BY.
questions.answer: SELECT name, department, salary, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg FROM employees;
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY splits rows into groups (like GROUP BY) but OVER() keeps every individual row in the output, just annotated with the aggregate computed over its partition - unlike GROUP BY, which reduces each group to one row.
questions.schema_context: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR(100), department VARCHAR(50), salary DECIMAL(10,2));

questions.question: Why does `SELECT *` often perform worse than selecting only the needed columns, even beyond just network transfer size?
questions.answer: It can prevent the database from using a 'covering index' (an index that already contains all needed columns), forcing an extra lookup into the full table for columns not in the index
questions.explanation: When a query only needs columns that are all present in an index, the database can answer the query directly from the index without touching the table at all - selecting extra unneeded columns defeats this optimization.

questions.question: What does EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN PLAN) show, and why is it the primary tool for diagnosing a slow query?
questions.answer: It shows the execution plan the database's query optimizer chose - which indexes (if any) are used, the join algorithm, the estimated/actual row counts, and the order operations happen in
questions.explanation: Without EXPLAIN, you're guessing why a query is slow; with it, you can see concretely whether the optimizer is doing a full table scan instead of using an available index, doing an inefficient join order, etc.
