questions.explanation: `realloc` may resize in place (same address) or allocate a new block and copy the data over (freeing the old block) - the caller must always use the returned pointer, not assume the original pointer is still valid.

questions.question: What does the expression `x & (x - 1)` compute when `x` is a power of two?
questions.answer: Always equals 0
questions.explanation: A power of two has exactly one bit set; subtracting 1 flips that bit to 0 and sets all lower bits to 1, so ANDing with the original leaves no bits in common, giving 0. This trick is commonly used to check `if ((x & (x-1)) == 0)` to test whether x is a power of two.

questions.question: What does the `register` storage class keyword suggest to the compiler?
options: Store the variable in a CPU register for faster access (a hint, not a guarantee)
Store the variable in a database register
Prevent the variable from ever changing
questions.answer: Store the variable in a CPU register for faster access (a hint, not a guarantee)
questions.explanation: Modern compilers largely ignore `register` as a hint since their own register-allocation optimizers are better at this decision than programmer hints; you also cannot take the address of a `register` variable in the older interpretation.

questions.question: Why is it important to treat `argv[]` strings as read-only in most portable code?
questions.answer: While the C standard technically allows modifying the characters `argv` points to, some environments store them in memory shared with environment variables or other OS structures, so modifying them can have unintended side effects; treating them as effectively `const char*` is the safer, portable convention.
questions.explanation: This is why well-written code that needs a modifiable copy of an argument makes an explicit copy (e.g. with `strdup`) rather than mutating `argv` directly.

questions.question: Why is a doubly linked list's node typically larger than a singly linked list's node, and what capability does that extra field buy?
questions.answer: A doubly linked list node stores both a `next` and a `prev` pointer (versus just `next` for a singly linked list), which costs one extra pointer's worth of memory per node but allows O(1) traversal backward and O(1) removal of a node given only a pointer to it (no need to walk from the head to find its predecessor).
questions.explanation: This tradeoff (more memory per node, but cheaper removal/backward traversal) is why doubly linked lists are preferred when frequent arbitrary-position deletion is needed, like in LRU cache implementations.

questions.question: Write a function that returns the largest element in an integer array of size n.
questions.answer: Track a running maximum, initialized to the first element, updating it whenever a larger element is found.
questions.explanation: Starting `max` at `arr[0]` (rather than 0 or INT_MIN) correctly handles arrays of all-negative numbers.

questions.question: Why is checking the return value of `malloc()` for `NULL` considered essential in robust C code?
questions.answer: `malloc` returns `NULL` if the allocation fails (e.g. the system is out of memory); proceeding to dereference the returned pointer without checking leads to undefined behavior (typically a crash) instead of a controlled error path.
questions.explanation: In long-running or resource-constrained systems (embedded devices, servers under memory pressure), allocation failure is a real, recoverable scenario that well-written C code should handle gracefully rather than assume never happens.

questions.question: What is 'undefined behavior' in the C standard's technical sense, and how does it differ from 'implementation-defined behavior'?
questions.answer: Undefined behavior means the standard imposes NO requirements at all on what happens - the program could crash, produce garbage, or even appear to work; the compiler is free to assume it never occurs and optimize accordingly. Implementation-defined behavior means the standard requires each implementation to choose a behavior and DOCUMENT it consistently (e.g. the size of `int`), so it's unspecified between compilers but consistent and predictable within one.
questions.explanation: This distinction matters a lot in practice: relying on implementation-defined behavior is merely non-portable, while relying on undefined behavior is a genuine bug that can break unpredictably, even on the same compiler after a version/optimization-level change.

questions.question: Why does the C standard guarantee `sizeof(char)` is always exactly 1, regardless of how many actual bits a byte has on that platform?
questions.answer: `sizeof` measures size in units of `char` by definition - `sizeof(char)` is defined to be 1 by the standard itself, essentially making `char` the base unit `sizeof` counts in, regardless of whether a byte on that platform is 8, 16, or another number of bits.
questions.explanation: This is why `sizeof(int)` being '4' doesn't necessarily mean 4 eight-bit bytes on exotic platforms with non-8-bit chars (like some DSPs) - it means 4 chars' worth of storage, whatever that platform's char width is.

questions.question: What does the ternary conditional operator `cond ? a : b` evaluate to?
options: a if cond is true (non-zero), otherwise b
questions.answer: a if cond is true (non-zero), otherwise b
questions.explanation: It's a compact expression form of if-else - `max = (a > b) ? a : b;` assigns whichever of a/b is larger.

questions.question: What does the `continue` statement do inside a loop?
options: Skips the rest of the current iteration's body and proceeds to the loop's next iteration check
Restarts the loop from the beginning
questions.answer: Skips the rest of the current iteration's body and proceeds to the loop's next iteration check
questions.explanation: In a `for` loop, `continue` still runs the increment expression before re-checking the condition; in a `while` loop, it jumps straight to the condition check.

questions.question: What is a 'pure function' informally, and does C enforce purity in any way?
questions.answer: A pure function's output depends only on its inputs and it has no observable side effects (no modifying global state, no I/O). C does not enforce or track purity at all - any function can freely read/write globals or do I/O, and there's no keyword to declare or check for purity.
questions.explanation: Some compilers offer non-standard attributes (like GCC's `__attribute__((pure))`) as an optimization hint, but this is a compiler extension, not a language guarantee.

questions.question: What is the index of the first element in a C array?
questions.explanation: C arrays are zero-indexed - `arr[0]` is the first element, and `arr[n-1]` is the last element of an n-element array.

questions.question: What is a 'wild pointer', and how does it differ from a null pointer or a dangling pointer?
questions.answer: A wild pointer is one that has never been initialized at all and holds an indeterminate (garbage) value from whatever was previously in that memory - unlike a null pointer (deliberately points to nothing, a known safe sentinel) or a dangling pointer (used to point somewhere valid but no longer does), a wild pointer's value was never meaningful to begin with.
questions.explanation: Dereferencing any of the three is problematic, but a wild pointer is arguably the most dangerous since its garbage value could coincidentally point to valid-looking memory, masking the bug.

questions.question: Why is comparing two pointers with `<`/`>` only well-defined when they point into the same array?
questions.answer: Pointer relational comparisons are meant to express 'which element comes first' within a single array's layout; pointers into unrelated objects have no such meaningful ordering relationship, so the C standard leaves that comparison's result undefined (though it will still 'compile and run', typically comparing raw addresses).
questions.explanation: This is the same underlying restriction as pointer subtraction being defined only within one array - both rely on there being a genuine, defined notion of relative position.

questions.question: Which function compares two C strings and returns 0 if they are equal?
questions.answer: strcmp()
questions.explanation: `strcmp` returns 0 for equal strings, a negative value if the first differs before the second lexicographically, and positive otherwise - it does NOT return a boolean, which is a common beginner mistake (`if (strcmp(a,b))` actually means 'if NOT equal').

questions.question: Can a struct in C contain a pointer to its own type (e.g. `struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; };`), but not an instance of its own type directly? Why?
questions.answer: Yes, a pointer to its own type is fine because a pointer has a fixed, known size regardless of the pointed-to type's size. An instance of its own type directly (`struct Node next;` instead of `struct Node *next;`) is NOT allowed because it would require the struct to contain itself, an infinitely recursive (and thus impossible to compute) size.
questions.explanation: This is exactly why linked data structures (linked lists, trees) in C are built with self-referential pointers, not embedded self-instances.

questions.question: A long-running server process's memory usage grows steadily over days even though every allocated object appears to eventually be freed somewhere in the code. What are two possible explanations besides an outright missed `free()`?
questions.answer: (1) Memory fragmentation - the heap allocator may be unable to reuse freed-but-scattered small blocks for new larger allocation requests, causing the process's total memory footprint (as seen by the OS) to keep growing even though logically 'used' memory is stable. (2) A slow leak in an error/exception path that's rarely hit in testing but does execute occasionally in production (e.g. a `free()` that's skipped only on a specific error branch).
questions.explanation: Diagnosing this usually requires a memory profiler (like Valgrind's massif or a heap profiler) rather than just code review, since fragmentation and rare-path leaks are both hard to spot by reading code alone.

questions.question: Which function reads a line of text from a file, safely bounded by a maximum length?
questions.answer: fgets()
questions.explanation: `fgets(buffer, size, stream)` reads at most `size-1` characters (leaving room for the null terminator), unlike the dangerous, deprecated `gets()` which has no bounds checking at all and was removed from the C11 standard for this reason.

questions.question: What does the `~` operator do in C?
questions.answer: Bitwise complement (flips every bit)
questions.explanation: `~x` flips every bit of x (0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0); this is different from `!x` (logical NOT), which produces 1 if x is 0 and 0 otherwise.

questions.question: Why might a developer explicitly assign power-of-two values to enum constants (e.g. `RED=1, GREEN=2, BLUE=4`)?
questions.answer: To use the enum as a bitmask/set of flags that can be combined with bitwise OR (`RED | BLUE`) and tested with bitwise AND, allowing a single integer variable to represent any combination of the flags simultaneously.
questions.explanation: This pattern only works cleanly when each value occupies a distinct bit position (powers of two), so combining values with OR never causes overlap/ambiguity between which flags are set.

questions.question: A multi-threaded C program without any locks has two threads incrementing the same global `int counter` variable a million times each, but the final value is consistently less than 2 million. Why?
questions.answer: `counter++` is not atomic - it typically compiles to a read, an increment, and a write as three separate steps. If both threads read the same value before either writes back the incremented result, one thread's increment is effectively lost (a data race), so some increments don't count.
questions.explanation: This requires proper synchronization (a mutex, or a C11 `_Atomic` type / GCC atomic builtins) to fix - it's a textbook demonstration of why unsynchronized shared mutable state between threads is unsafe even for something as 'simple' as incrementing a counter.

questions.question: Write a function that returns the sum of all elements in an integer array of size n.
questions.answer: Accumulate a running total by iterating over every element once.
questions.explanation: Initializing `sum` to 0 correctly handles the empty-array case (n=0), since the loop body simply never executes.

questions.question: What is the difference between a syntax error and a logic error in a C program?
questions.answer: A syntax error violates the language's grammar rules and is caught by the compiler before the program can even be built (e.g. a missing semicolon). A logic error produces a program that compiles and runs fine but produces incorrect results, because the algorithm/logic itself is flawed.
questions.explanation: Logic errors are generally harder to find since there's no compiler message pointing to them - they require testing, debugging, or code review to catch.

questions.question: Which of these correctly declares a constant integer in C?
questions.answer: const int x = 5;
questions.explanation: `const` is the C keyword for declaring a variable whose value cannot be changed after initialization; `constant` and `#final` are not valid C syntax.

questions.question: Why is testing floating-point values for exact equality (`if (x == 0.1)`) generally unreliable in C?
questions.answer: Most decimal fractions (like 0.1) cannot be represented exactly in binary floating-point, so `x` might actually hold something like 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827..., and accumulated rounding from prior computations makes exact equality comparisons fragile and often fail even when values are 'mathematically' equal.
questions.explanation: The standard fix is to compare with a small tolerance/epsilon: `if (fabs(x - 0.1) < EPSILON)` instead of exact equality.

questions.question: Write a function that computes the greatest common divisor of two positive integers using the Euclidean algorithm.
questions.answer: Repeatedly replace (a, b) with (b, a mod b) until b becomes 0; a is then the GCD.
questions.explanation: This is the classic Euclidean algorithm, running in O(log(min(a,b))) time, far faster than checking every possible common divisor.

questions.question: Can you compare two struct variables directly with `==` in C (e.g. `if (p1 == p2)` where p1, p2 are struct Point)?
options: Yes, it compares all members automatically
No - C provides no built-in struct comparison; you must compare members individually or use memcmp with caveats
Only if the struct has exactly one member
Yes, but only for structs containing exclusively integers
questions.answer: No - C provides no built-in struct comparison; you must compare members individually or use memcmp with caveats
questions.explanation: Unlike C++ (where you can overload `operator==`), plain C has no mechanism to compare aggregate types directly; `memcmp` can work but is unsafe if the struct has padding bytes with indeterminate values.

questions.question: What does `free(NULL)` do?
options: Nothing - it's explicitly defined as a safe no-op
questions.answer: Nothing - it's explicitly defined as a safe no-op
questions.explanation: The C standard explicitly guarantees `free(NULL)` does nothing and is always safe to call, which is why setting a pointer to NULL after freeing it makes any accidental subsequent free() harmless.

questions.question: Why do C projects often use tools like Valgrind or AddressSanitizer during development and testing?
questions.answer: Because C gives the programmer full manual control over memory with essentially no built-in safety net, these tools detect classes of bugs the language itself won't catch - out-of-bounds reads/writes, use-after-free, memory leaks, and uninitialized memory reads - by instrumenting the program at runtime.
questions.explanation: Many of these bugs are 'silent' (the program appears to work most of the time) without such tooling, which is why they're considered essential parts of a serious C development workflow, not optional extras.

questions.question: Implement iterative binary search on a sorted array, returning the index of `target` or -1 if not found.
questions.answer: Repeatedly halve the search range by comparing the middle element to the target, narrowing to the correct half each time.
questions.explanation: Using `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` instead of `(lo + hi) / 2` avoids a subtle integer overflow bug when lo and hi are both large.

questions.question: What does the semicolon `;` mark at the end of most C statements?
questions.answer: The end of a statement
questions.explanation: C requires a semicolon to terminate most statements (declarations, expression statements); omitting it is a syntax error the compiler reports at the point it expected one.

questions.question: What is operator precedence, and why does `2 + 3 * 4` evaluate to 14, not 20?
questions.answer: Operator precedence determines the order operators are evaluated in when an expression mixes several - `*` has higher precedence than `+`, so `3 * 4` is computed first (giving 12), then `2 + 12` gives 14.
questions.explanation: Parentheses can always override the default precedence explicitly, e.g. `(2 + 3) * 4` forces the addition first, yielding 20 instead.

questions.question: What does HTML stand for?
questions.answer: HyperText Markup Language
questions.explanation: HTML is the standard markup language used to structure content on the web; 'HyperText' refers to linked documents, 'Markup' to the tags that describe structure.

questions.question: Which tag is used to define the largest heading in HTML?
questions.explanation: HTML headings range from <h1> (largest/most important) to <h6> (smallest); <h1> should typically be used once per page for the main title.

questions.question: What is the correct HTML element for inserting a line break?
questions.explanation:
is a void (self-closing) element that forces a line break within text without starting a new paragraph, unlike

which creates a new block.

questions.question: Is HTML case-sensitive for tag names?
questions.answer: No, HTML tag and attribute names are case-insensitive, though lowercase is the conventional and HTML5-recommended style.
questions.explanation: The HTML5 spec explicitly treats tag/attribute names as ASCII case-insensitive during parsing; XHTML (XML-based) does require lowercase, which is likely the source of the common lowercase convention.

questions.question: What is the difference between an HTML element and an HTML tag?
questions.answer:
A tag is the markup itself (e.g.

or

); an element is the complete unit including the opening tag, its content, and the closing tag (e.g.

Hello

).
questions.explanation:
This distinction matters because void elements like or
have only a single tag and no separate closing tag, yet are still complete elements.

questions.question: Which declaration must appear as the very first line of an HTML5 document?
questions.answer: <!DOCTYPE html>
questions.explanation: The DOCTYPE tells the browser to render the page in standards mode using the HTML5 parsing rules; omitting it can trigger quirks mode with inconsistent CSS box-model behavior across browsers.

questions.question: Which two elements are the direct children of the <html> element in a standard document?
questions.answer: <head> and <body>
questions.explanation: <head> contains metadata (title, meta tags, links to stylesheets/scripts) that is not rendered directly, while <body> contains the visible page content.

questions.question: Where should <script> tags generally be placed to avoid blocking initial page rendering, and what attribute offers an alternative?
questions.answer: Either just before the closing </body> tag, or anywhere with the `defer` (or `async`) attribute on the <script> tag.
questions.explanation: By default, script tags block HTML parsing while the script downloads and executes; placing them at the end of <body> (or using `defer`, which downloads in parallel and runs after parsing completes in document order) avoids delaying the first paint.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the <head> element's <title> tag?
questions.answer: It sets the text shown in the browser's title bar/tab and is used as the default heading for the page in search results and bookmarks.
questions.explanation: Unlike headings inside <body>, <title> content is not rendered on the page itself — it is metadata consumed by the browser chrome, search engines, and social sharing previews.

questions.question: A browser renders a page with visibly broken CSS box sizing (elements wider than expected) even though the CSS looks correct. What document-structure issue commonly causes this?
questions.answer: A missing or malformed <!DOCTYPE html> declaration, which puts the browser into 'quirks mode' instead of standards mode.
questions.explanation: In quirks mode, older/legacy box-model rules apply (width includes padding and border by default in some browsers), producing layout differences from what modern standards-mode CSS assumes.
questions.buggy_code:
<html>
<head><title>Page</title></head>
<body>...</body>
</html>
questions.fixed_code:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Page</title></head>
<body>...</body>
</html>

questions.question: Which of these is a void (self-closing) HTML element?
questions.explanation:
,
,
, , and are void elements — they cannot have children or a closing tag because they represent a single, self-contained piece of content.

questions.question: What is the difference between a block-level element and an inline element?
questions.answer:
A block-level element (e.g.
,

) starts on a new line and takes up the full available width by default; an inline element (e.g. , ) only takes up as much width as its content and does not force a line break.
questions.explanation: This default display behavior comes from the browser's default stylesheet (`display: block` vs `display: inline`) and can be overridden with CSS.

questions.question: What is the difference between <div> and <span>?
questions.answer: <div> is a block-level generic container, while <span> is an inline generic container.
questions.explanation: Both carry no semantic meaning on their own and exist purely for grouping content so CSS/JS can target it; the choice between them is driven entirely by whether block or inline layout is needed.

questions.question: What does the <iframe> element do, and name one security consideration when using it?
questions.answer: <iframe> embeds another HTML document inside the current page as a nested browsing context; a key security consideration is that embedding untrusted third-party content can expose clickjacking risks unless mitigated with the `sandbox` attribute or the embedded site's `X-Frame-Options`/CSP frame-ancestors header.
questions.explanation: Because an iframe's content runs as a semi-independent document, it can be abused to overlay invisible malicious UI on top of a legitimate page (clickjacking) unless the site being framed opts out.

questions.question: Why can excessive nesting of generic <div> elements ('div soup') hurt both accessibility and performance?
questions.answer: Deeply nested non-semantic divs give screen readers no structural landmarks to navigate by, and force the browser to build and reflow a much larger, deeper DOM/render tree than semantic markup would require.
questions.explanation: Screen readers rely on semantic elements and ARIA landmarks to let users jump between regions; a page built entirely of unlabeled divs forces linear reading. On the performance side, layout and style recalculation cost scales with DOM depth and node count.

questions.question: Which attribute specifies an alternate text for an image if it cannot be displayed?
questions.answer: alt
questions.explanation: The `alt` attribute is read by screen readers and shown if the image fails to load, making it essential for both accessibility and graceful degradation.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `id` attribute compared to the `class` attribute?
questions.answer: `id` must be unique within a page and identifies a single specific element; `class` can be applied to many elements and groups them for shared styling/behavior.
questions.explanation: Because `id` values must be unique, they're used for CSS ID selectors, JS `getElementById`, and in-page anchor links (`#section`), while `class` is the right tool whenever a style or behavior applies to multiple elements.

questions.question: What does the `data-*` attribute convention allow you to do in HTML?
questions.answer: It lets you store custom, page-specific data directly on an HTML element without any special meaning to the browser, retrievable in JavaScript via the element's `dataset` property.
questions.explanation: For example `<div data-user-id="42">` exposes `element.dataset.userId === '42'` in JS — a standards-compliant alternative to inventing non-standard attributes for custom data.

questions.question: What is the effect of the `disabled` boolean attribute on a form control?
questions.answer: It makes the control non-interactive (cannot be focused, clicked, or edited) and excludes its value from form submission.
questions.explanation: Boolean attributes like `disabled` are 'true' simply by being present, regardless of their value (`disabled="false"` still disables the element); to enable it, the attribute must be removed entirely.

questions.question: Why does `<input disabled="false">` still disable the input, and how would you actually make it conditionally enabled from a template?
questions.answer: Because `disabled` is a boolean attribute, its mere presence — not its string value — controls behavior; any value including "false" still counts as present. To conditionally enable it you must add/remove the attribute entirely, e.g. only render `disabled` when the condition is true.
questions.explanation: This is a common source of bugs when developers assume boolean HTML attributes behave like typed booleans in a programming language; frameworks like React handle this by accepting a JS boolean and adding/omitting the attribute for you.

questions.question: Which HTML input type is specifically designed for entering an email address with built-in format validation?
questions.answer: type="email"
questions.explanation: `<input type="email">` triggers the browser's built-in email-format validation and, on mobile, shows an email-optimized on-screen keyboard.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the <label> element in a form?
questions.answer: It provides a text caption associated with a specific form control, improving usability and accessibility (clicking the label focuses/activates the control, and screen readers announce it).
questions.explanation: Association is done either by wrapping the input inside the label, or by matching the label's `for` attribute to the input's `id`.

questions.question: What is the difference between the `GET` and `POST` values of a <form>'s `method` attribute?
questions.answer: `GET` appends form data as a URL query string (visible, bookmarkable, size-limited, and cacheable), while `POST` sends form data in the request body (not shown in the URL, no practical size limit, and not cached by default).
questions.explanation: GET is appropriate for idempotent operations like search/filtering where the result should be shareable via URL; POST is used for operations that change state or submit sensitive/large data, since it doesn't expose data in the URL or browser history.

questions.question: What does the `<select>` element's `multiple` attribute do?
questions.answer: It allows the user to select more than one <option> at once (typically via ctrl/cmd+click), and the submitted form data includes all selected values.
questions.explanation: When `multiple` is set, the field's submitted name should end in `[]` in many server frameworks (or be read as an array) since more than one value can be sent under the same field name.

questions.question: A form has multiple radio inputs meant to represent one single-choice question, but the user can select more than one at a time. What is the most likely cause?
questions.answer: The radio inputs don't all share the same `name` attribute — only inputs with an identical `name` are grouped as mutually exclusive by the browser.
questions.explanation: The browser enforces single-selection purely based on the `name` attribute grouping radios; if even one radio in the group has a typo'd or missing `name`, it becomes its own independent group, breaking the intended exclusivity.
questions.buggy_code:
<input type="radio" name="plan" value="a"> A
<input type="radio" name="Plan" value="b"> B
questions.fixed_code:
<input type="radio" name="plan" value="a"> A
<input type="radio" name="plan" value="b"> B

questions.question: Which tag defines a table row in HTML?
questions.answer: <tr>
questions.explanation: <table> defines the table, <tr> defines a row within it, and <td>/<th> define individual data/header cells within a row.

questions.question: What is the difference between <td> and <th>?
questions.answer: <td> is a standard data cell; <th> is a header cell, which browsers render bold and centered by default and which carries semantic meaning for screen readers (it labels the column/row it heads).
questions.explanation: Using <th> instead of <td> for header cells isn't just cosmetic — it lets assistive technology associate data cells with their header context.

questions.question: What do the <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> elements group inside a table?
questions.answer: <thead> groups the header row(s), <tbody> groups the main data rows, and <tfoot> groups summary/footer rows (e.g. totals) — purely structural/semantic grouping, not new visual cells.
questions.explanation: Beyond semantics, separating these lets browsers keep <thead>/<tfoot> visible while <tbody> scrolls in some styling setups, and lets print engines repeat the header on every printed page.

questions.question: What does the `colspan` attribute do on a <td> or <th>?
questions.answer: It makes that cell span across multiple columns, merging the space that would otherwise be occupied by that many separate cells in the row.
questions.explanation: When a cell uses `colspan="2"`, the following row(s) effectively have one fewer explicit cell needed at that position to keep the table's column count consistent; the analogous `rowspan` does the same across rows.

questions.question: Why are HTML tables considered a poor choice for overall page layout (as opposed to displaying tabular data)?
questions.answer: Tables force a rigid grid structure that is hard to make responsive, mix layout with content (making the markup non-semantic and harder for screen readers to interpret), and historically caused slow rendering because the browser must calculate the whole table's layout before rendering any of it.
questions.explanation: Modern CSS layout tools (Flexbox, Grid) achieve any visual arrangement without abusing an element whose semantic meaning is 'tabular data', keeping markup meaningful for accessibility and SEO while rendering incrementally.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is intended to represent the main navigation links of a page?
questions.answer: <nav>
questions.explanation: <nav> is a semantic landmark that identifies a block of primarily navigational links, letting assistive technology and browsers offer quick navigation between page regions.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the <article> element?
questions.answer: It represents a self-contained piece of content that could be independently distributed or reused, such as a blog post, news story, or forum post.
questions.explanation: The key test for <article> is independence: if the content would still make sense extracted and syndicated on its own (e.g. via RSS), <article> is appropriate.

questions.question: What is the difference between <section> and <div>?
questions.answer: <section> is a semantic, thematic grouping of content that typically has its own heading and represents a standalone section of a document/application; <div> is a purely generic, non-semantic container used only for styling/scripting hooks.
questions.explanation: Using <section> when there's no meaningful heading/theme (just for styling) is considered a misuse — <div> remains the correct choice whenever no semantic meaning applies.

questions.question: When should the <aside> element be used?
questions.answer: For content that is tangentially related to the surrounding content, such as a sidebar, pull quote, or advertisement — content that could be removed without reducing the meaning of the main content.
questions.explanation: <aside> gives assistive technology a way to distinguish supplementary content from primary content, which matters for users navigating by landmark.

questions.question: A page uses only <div class="header">, <div class="nav">, and <div class="footer">. What are the concrete downsides of not switching to <header>, <nav>, and <footer>, beyond just 'best practice'?
questions.answer: Screen reader users lose the ability to jump directly to landmark regions (header/nav/footer) via assistive technology shortcuts, search engines get weaker structural signals for indexing/snippet generation, and the markup becomes more fragile since meaning now depends entirely on class names that could be renamed or reused inconsistently.
questions.explanation: Semantic elements expose an implicit ARIA landmark role (e.g. <nav> maps to role="navigation") for free, whereas class-named divs convey no such role unless ARIA roles are manually and consistently added — an easy thing to forget or get wrong.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is used to embed video content natively without a plugin?
questions.answer: <video>
questions.explanation: <video> provides native browser video playback with built-in controls, replacing the older need for Flash or other plugins.

questions.question: What does the `controls` attribute do on a <video> or <audio> element?
questions.answer: It displays the browser's default playback UI (play/pause, volume, seek bar) for that media element.
questions.explanation: Without `controls`, the media element renders with no visible UI at all, and playback must be driven entirely via JavaScript (`element.play()`/`pause()`).

questions.question: Why would you provide multiple <source> elements inside a <video> tag?
questions.answer: To offer the same video in multiple formats/codecs (e.g. MP4 and WebM), letting the browser pick the first source it supports, since not every browser supports every codec.
questions.explanation: The browser evaluates <source> elements in order and uses the first one whose `type` it can play, falling back to any fallback content placed directly inside <video> if none are supported.

questions.question: What accessibility feature should accompany a <video> for deaf or hard-of-hearing users, and which element provides it?
questions.answer: Captions/subtitles, provided via the <track> element with `kind="captions"` or `kind="subtitles"` pointing to a WebVTT file.
questions.explanation: <track> lets the browser overlay time-synced text without needing to burn captions into the video itself, and also lets users toggle them on/off.

questions.question: Why might a <video autoplay> tag fail to autoplay in most modern browsers unless another attribute is also present?
questions.answer: Modern browsers block autoplay of video WITH sound as an anti-annoyance measure; autoplay is generally only allowed if the video is also muted (the `muted` attribute must be present alongside `autoplay`).
questions.explanation: This policy exists because unsolicited audio playback was widely considered a poor user experience; browsers permit silent (muted) autoplay since it can't disrupt the user unexpectedly with sound.
questions.buggy_code: <video src="clip.mp4" autoplay></video>
questions.fixed_code: <video src="clip.mp4" autoplay muted></video>

questions.question: Which attribute of the <a> tag specifies the URL of the page the link goes to?
questions.answer: href
questions.explanation: `href` (hypertext reference) holds the destination URL; without it, an <a> tag is not an active link.

questions.question: What does setting `target="_blank"` on an <a> tag do?
questions.answer: It opens the linked document in a new browsing context (typically a new tab).
questions.explanation: Best practice pairs `target="_blank"` with `rel="noopener noreferrer"` to prevent the new page from gaining a reference back to the opening window (a security/performance concern known as tabnabbing).

questions.question: Why is `rel="noopener"` recommended on links that use `target="_blank"`?
questions.answer: Without it, the newly opened page can access the original page via `window.opener` and potentially redirect it to a malicious page (a phishing technique called tabnabbing), and it can also hurt performance since both pages can share the same rendering process.
questions.explanation: `rel="noopener"` (and `noreferrer`, which also strips the referrer) severs that `window.opener` link, isolating the new tab from the originating page.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a fragment identifier like `#section2` in a URL, and how is it targeted in HTML?
questions.answer: It scrolls the browser to the element on the page whose `id` matches the fragment (e.g. `id="section2"`), enabling in-page navigation without a full reload.
questions.explanation: This is how a page's own table-of-contents links typically work, and it also lets JavaScript listen for `hashchange` events to react to in-page navigation.

questions.question: A single-page app changes the URL fragment (`#/profile`) via JavaScript for client-side routing, but a user who bookmarks and reopens that URL directly sees a 404 from the server. Why, and what's a common fix?
questions.answer: The fragment portion of a URL is never sent to the server (only the path before the `#` is), so on a direct load the server only sees the base path and doesn't know which client-side route to render — it just serves (or fails to serve) whatever exists at that base path.
questions.explanation: A common fix is to configure the server to serve the app's single `index.html` for all unknown paths (a 'catch-all' fallback) so the client-side router can then read the URL and render the correct view once JavaScript loads, or to switch to the History API (`pushState`) with matching server-side route handling.

questions.question: Which meta tag ensures a webpage renders properly and scales correctly on mobile devices?
questions.answer: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
questions.explanation: Without this viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render the page at a desktop-width virtual viewport (usually 980px) and then zoom out, making text tiny and layout hard to use.

questions.question: What does the <meta charset="UTF-8"> tag specify?
questions.answer: The character encoding used to interpret the document's bytes as text, ensuring special characters (accents, symbols, non-Latin scripts) render correctly.
questions.explanation: UTF-8 is the de facto standard encoding for the web because it can represent virtually any character while remaining backward-compatible with ASCII for plain English text.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a `<meta name="description" content="...">` tag for SEO?
questions.answer: It provides a short summary of the page's content that search engines often display as the snippet text under the page's title in search results.
questions.explanation: While it doesn't directly boost search ranking, a well-written description can significantly improve click-through rate from search results, which is a real SEO-relevant outcome.

questions.question: What does `<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">` instruct search engine crawlers to do?
questions.answer: `noindex` tells the crawler not to include this page in its search index, and `nofollow` tells it not to follow (or pass ranking credit through) any links found on the page.
questions.explanation: This is commonly used on pages that shouldn't appear in search results, such as internal admin pages, duplicate content, or thank-you pages after a form submission.

questions.question: A site's pages all rank poorly and search result snippets show generic or irrelevant text. Besides missing meta descriptions, what other common meta/head-level issue could cause this?
questions.answer: Every page sharing an identical or auto-generated <title> and <meta name="description"> (rather than unique, page-specific values), which prevents search engines from understanding what distinguishes each page and often results in them ignoring the description in favor of scraping arbitrary page text.
questions.explanation: Search engines treat title/description uniqueness across a site as a signal of content quality and structure; duplicate or missing metadata across many pages is a classic, high-impact technical SEO problem that's easy to overlook when metadata is templated without per-page overrides.

questions.question: What does ARIA stand for?
questions.answer: Accessible Rich Internet Applications
questions.explanation: ARIA is a set of HTML attributes that add extra semantic/accessibility information for assistive technologies, especially for custom widgets that don't have a native HTML equivalent.

questions.question: What does the `aria-label` attribute do?
questions.answer: It provides an accessible name for an element that a screen reader announces, used when there is no visible text (or the visible text isn't descriptive enough) to serve as the label.
questions.explanation: For example, an icon-only button (like a trash icon) has no text content for a screen reader to read, so `aria-label="Delete item"` supplies that missing accessible name.

questions.question: What is the 'first rule of ARIA use'?
questions.answer: If a native HTML element or attribute already has the semantics and behavior you need, use it instead of re-purposing an element and adding ARIA to make it accessible.
questions.explanation: For example, a native <button> already has correct keyboard focus, activation on Enter/Space, and an implicit role of 'button' for free; recreating a button out of a <div> with `role="button"` and `tabindex="0"` requires manually reimplementing all of that behavior correctly.

questions.question: What does `aria-hidden="true"` do, and what is a common mistake when using it?
questions.answer: It hides an element (and its descendants) from the accessibility tree, so screen readers skip it entirely even though it remains visible on screen; a common mistake is applying it to focusable content, which leaves keyboard/screen-reader users able to tab into an element that is announced as if it doesn't exist.
questions.explanation: `aria-hidden` is meant for purely decorative content (like a decorative icon next to a labelled button) — hiding meaningful, interactive, or focusable content with it creates a confusing or broken experience for assistive-technology users.

questions.question: A custom dropdown built from <div>s is fully clickable with a mouse but completely unusable with a keyboard, and a screen reader announces no role or state changes. What's the minimum set of fixes needed to make it accessible?
questions.answer: Add `tabindex="0"` so it's keyboard-focusable, implement keyboard event handlers for Enter/Space (activate) and Escape/arrow keys (navigate options), add an appropriate ARIA role (`role="combobox"`/`role="listbox"` with `role="option"` children as applicable), and toggle `aria-expanded`/`aria-selected` attributes to reflect open/closed and selected state changes.
questions.explanation: Native <select> elements provide all of this behavior automatically; recreating a dropdown with generic divs means every one of these behaviors — focus, keyboard interaction, and state announcement — must be manually implemented and kept in sync with the visual state, which is exactly the tradeoff the 'first rule of ARIA' warns about.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between <canvas> and SVG for graphics?
questions.answer: <canvas> is a raster (pixel-based) drawing surface controlled entirely via JavaScript, with no memory of individual shapes once drawn; SVG is a vector, XML-based markup where each shape is a separate DOM element that can be styled and manipulated individually.
questions.explanation: This means SVG shapes remain accessible/inspectable/stylable via CSS and can be crisp at any zoom level, while canvas content is just pixels — great for performance-heavy, frequently-redrawn graphics like games, but you must track shape state yourself.
options: They are identical, just different syntax
Canvas is vector-based, SVG is raster-based
Canvas is a raster pixel surface drawn via JS; SVG is vector markup with individually addressable DOM elements
SVG can only display static images

questions.question: Why does an SVG shape stay sharp when the page is zoomed in, while a <canvas> drawing can become blurry?
questions.answer: SVG shapes are defined mathematically (vectors) and are re-rendered at the new resolution whenever the browser redraws, so edges remain crisp at any zoom level; <canvas> content is just a fixed grid of pixels that gets scaled like a bitmap image when zoomed, causing blurring/pixelation.
questions.explanation: This is the core vector-vs-raster tradeoff: vectors scale losslessly because they're recalculated, while raster pixel data has a fixed resolution baked in at draw time.

questions.question: Why is it generally easier to add a click handler to one specific shape in SVG than in canvas?
questions.answer: Each SVG shape is its own DOM element, so you can attach an event listener directly to it (e.g. `circle.addEventListener('click', ...)`); a canvas has no per-shape DOM nodes — the whole thing is one element, so you must manually calculate whether a click's coordinates fall within a shape you drew.
questions.explanation: This DOM-per-shape structure is exactly why SVG plays well with CSS and standard DOM event handling, at the cost of scaling worse than canvas when rendering thousands of shapes/frequent redraws.

questions.question: You're building a data visualization with tens of thousands of frequently-updating points (e.g. a live scatter plot). Would SVG or Canvas generally perform better, and why?
questions.answer: Canvas generally performs better for very large numbers of frequently-updating elements, because SVG's per-shape DOM node overhead (style recalculation, layout, and the DOM tree size itself) becomes the bottleneck at high element counts, whereas canvas redraws are just pixel operations on one surface with no DOM overhead per point.
questions.explanation: SVG's advantages (CSS styling, individual event listeners, crisp scaling) come from maintaining a live DOM node per shape — a cost that scales linearly (or worse) with element count and becomes prohibitive well before tens of thousands of elements; canvas trades away those conveniences for raw pixel-drawing throughput.

questions.question: What is the key difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
questions.answer: Data in localStorage persists indefinitely (until explicitly cleared) even after the browser is closed and reopened, while sessionStorage data is cleared when the browser tab is closed.
questions.explanation: Both share the same synchronous key-value string API (`setItem`/`getItem`/`removeItem`) and are scoped per-origin, differing only in lifetime/scope: sessionStorage is also scoped to a single tab, not shared across tabs of the same origin.
options: localStorage persists across browser sessions; sessionStorage clears when the tab closes
sessionStorage persists across browser sessions; localStorage clears when the tab closes
localStorage is server-side; sessionStorage is client-side

questions.question: What data type can be stored directly in localStorage, and what must you do to store an object?
questions.answer: localStorage can only store strings; to store an object (or array), you must serialize it with `JSON.stringify()` before saving, and parse it back with `JSON.parse()` when reading.
questions.explanation: Calling `localStorage.setItem('user', {name: 'A'})` silently stores the string `"[object Object]"` rather than the object, which is a very common beginner bug.

questions.question: Roughly how much storage capacity does localStorage typically offer per origin, and how does that compare to cookies?
questions.answer: Typically around 5-10 MB per origin (browser-dependent), which is far larger than cookies, which are usually limited to about 4 KB total and are also sent with every HTTP request to the server.
questions.explanation: Because localStorage is never automatically transmitted to the server (only accessible via JavaScript), it's suitable for client-only data, while cookies remain the tool of choice when the server itself needs to read the value on every request (e.g. session identifiers).

questions.question: An app stores a JWT auth token in localStorage for convenience. What is the main security risk of this choice compared to storing it in an HttpOnly cookie?
questions.answer: Any JavaScript running on the page — including injected malicious script from an XSS vulnerability — can read localStorage directly and exfiltrate the token, whereas an HttpOnly cookie is inaccessible to JavaScript entirely, so an XSS attack cannot read it (though the cookie approach then needs its own CSRF protections).
questions.explanation: localStorage has no equivalent of the HttpOnly flag; it is deliberately fully accessible to any script in the page's origin, which trades safety against XSS-based token theft for developer convenience.

questions.question: Which HTML5 API allows a web page to request the user's physical location?
questions.answer: The Geolocation API
questions.explanation: `navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition()` prompts the user for permission and, if granted, returns latitude/longitude coordinates.

questions.question: What does the Drag and Drop API's `draggable` attribute enable, and which events fire during a drag operation?
questions.answer: Setting `draggable="true"` on an element allows the user to pick it up and drag it; during the operation, events like `dragstart`, `dragover`, `drop`, and `dragend` fire on the source/target elements so JavaScript can control the interaction.
questions.explanation: `dragover` must have `event.preventDefault()` called in its handler, or the browser will not allow a `drop` event to fire on that target at all — a very common gotcha.

questions.question: What problem does the Web Workers API solve?
questions.answer: It lets JavaScript run computationally expensive code on a separate background thread, off the main UI thread, so long-running scripts don't freeze the page's rendering and user interaction.
questions.explanation: Workers communicate with the main thread only via message passing (`postMessage`/`onmessage`) and cannot directly touch the DOM, which is the tradeoff for true off-main-thread execution in a single-threaded-by-default JS runtime.

questions.question: A page uses the Fetch API to load data and the request appears to succeed (a response object comes back) even for a 404 or 500 server error. Why doesn't `fetch()` reject its promise on HTTP error status codes?
questions.answer: By design, `fetch()` only rejects its promise for network-level failures (e.g. DNS failure, no connectivity, CORS block) — a successfully received HTTP response, even with a 4xx/5xx status, is still considered a 'successful' fetch from the API's point of view, so the promise resolves and you must manually check `response.ok` or `response.status`.
questions.explanation: This differs from many other HTTP client libraries that treat non-2xx statuses as errors automatically, so code that assumes `fetch().then()` only runs on success will silently mishandle server errors unless it explicitly checks `response.ok`.
questions.buggy_code: fetch('/api/data').then(res => res.json()).then(data => render(data));
questions.fixed_code: fetch('/api/data').then(res => { if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status); return res.json(); }).then(data => render(data));

questions.question: Which HTML attribute makes an input field mandatory before the form can be submitted?
questions.answer: required
questions.explanation: The `required` boolean attribute triggers the browser's built-in validation, which blocks submission and shows a native error message if the field is left empty.

questions.question: What does the `pattern` attribute on an <input> do?
questions.answer: It specifies a regular expression that the input's value must match for the field to be considered valid during native HTML form validation.
questions.explanation: For example `pattern="[0-9]{5}"` restricts the field to exactly 5 digits, useful for things like postal codes without needing JavaScript.

questions.question: What is the difference between client-side and server-side form validation, and why are both usually needed?
questions.answer: Client-side validation (HTML attributes or JS) gives immediate feedback in the browser and improves UX, while server-side validation independently re-checks the data on the server before trusting/storing it; both are needed because client-side validation can always be bypassed (disabled JS, direct API calls, browser devtools).
questions.explanation: Relying on client-side validation alone means any attacker can simply send a request directly to the server's endpoint with invalid or malicious data, bypassing the browser entirely — server-side validation is the actual security/data-integrity boundary.

questions.question: What CSS pseudo-classes let you style a form input based on its current native validation state?
questions.answer: `:valid` and `:invalid` (and related ones like `:required`, `:optional`, `:in-range`, `:out-of-range`) let you apply styles based on whether the field currently passes its HTML5 validation constraints.
questions.explanation: These update live as the user types, so `input:invalid { border-color: red; }` will highlight a field the moment its value violates constraints like `required`, `pattern`, `min`/`max`, or `type="email"` format.

questions.question: A form field has `required` and `pattern="\d{10}"` set, but a user submits a value with exactly 10 digits and the browser still blocks submission showing a validation error. What's a likely cause?
questions.answer: Leading/trailing whitespace in the field's value (e.g. from a pasted value with a trailing space) — the `pattern` attribute must match the ENTIRE value, so any extra character not accounted for by the pattern causes a mismatch even if 10 digits are visually present.
questions.explanation: HTML5 pattern matching implicitly anchors the regex to the whole string, so unlike some regex uses elsewhere, a substring match isn't enough; trimming input (or including optional whitespace in the pattern) is the fix.

questions.question: Why should images always include a meaningful `alt` attribute, even for purely decorative images (using `alt=""`)?
questions.answer: Meaningful images need `alt` text so screen reader users understand their content, and even decorative images should have an explicit empty `alt=""` so screen readers skip them silently instead of announcing the image's filename as a fallback.
questions.explanation: Omitting `alt` entirely (rather than setting it empty) can cause some screen readers to read out the raw file path, which is a confusing, meaningless announcement for a purely decorative image.

questions.question: Why is it considered bad practice to use inline `style` attributes extensively across a large site?
questions.answer: Inline styles are harder to maintain and reuse (styling must be repeated on every element rather than defined once), have the highest specificity which makes overriding them from a stylesheet difficult, and prevent separation of concerns between structure (HTML) and presentation (CSS).
questions.explanation: A style defined in an external stylesheet can be cached separately from the HTML, reused across many pages, and overridden predictably via normal CSS specificity/cascade rules — none of which apply cleanly to inline styles.

questions.question: Why should you avoid using the same `id` value on more than one element in a page?
questions.answer: `id` is defined by the spec to be unique per document; when duplicated, `document.getElementById()` and CSS `#id` selectors will only reliably target the first matching element, silently breaking any code/styles meant for the others.
questions.explanation: This is a subtle bug because the HTML will still often render visually as expected, but any behavior relying on unique targeting (form label association via `for`, JS lookups, fragment links) becomes unpredictable.

questions.question: A large legacy site's HTML validates fine but real users on screen readers report the site is very hard to navigate, despite semantic tags like <header>/<nav>/<main> being present. What additional practice is likely missing?
questions.answer: Meaningful heading structure and landmark labelling — e.g. multiple <nav> elements without distinguishing `aria-label`s so a screen reader user can't tell them apart, or headings that skip levels/are used for styling rather than document outline, breaking the ability to navigate by heading hierarchy.
questions.explanation: Valid HTML only guarantees the markup parses correctly, not that it conveys a usable structure; accessibility requires that landmarks be distinguishable (via `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` when there's more than one of the same landmark type) and that headings form a logical, unbroken hierarchy that mirrors the actual content outline.

questions.question: Why is it good practice to specify `width` and `height` attributes on tags even when the image is styled responsively with CSS?
questions.answer: It lets the browser reserve the correct amount of space for the image before it finishes loading, preventing the surrounding layout from visibly shifting once the image arrives (a poor UX metric known as Cumulative Layout Shift).
questions.explanation: The browser computes the image's intrinsic aspect ratio from the `width`/`height` attributes and reserves that ratio of space immediately, even before the CSS or the image itself has loaded, which CSS alone (e.g. `max-width: 100%`) cannot do on its own without also knowing the ratio.

questions.question: Which element is the root element of every HTML document?
questions.answer: <html>
questions.explanation: <html> wraps the entire document and is the single top-level element; <head> and <body> are its two children.

questions.question: What is the correct file extension for a standard HTML5 document?
questions.answer: .html (or the legacy .htm)
questions.explanation: .html is the conventional extension web servers map to the text/html MIME type; .htm is an older DOS-era 3-letter variant that still works but isn't preferred.

questions.question: What does it mean that HTML is a 'markup language' rather than a programming language?
questions.answer: HTML describes the structure and meaning of content using tags/elements; it has no variables, loops, or logic of its own - it just annotates content for the browser to render.
questions.explanation: This distinguishes it from JavaScript (a real programming language) - HTML alone cannot compute or make decisions, only describe document structure.

questions.question:
What does a browser render for the HTML `

Hello World!

`?
questions.code_snippet: Hello World!
questions.answer: Hello World! - with the word 'World' rendered in bold
questions.explanation: <b> is an inline element that bolds its content without starting a new paragraph or line; the surrounding text renders normally in the same line.

questions.question:
Why will most browsers still render `

Text

questions.answer:
HTML5 parsers implement error-recovery rules: opening a new

questions.explanation: This 'implied end tag' behavior is defined in the HTML5 parsing spec precisely so real-world malformed markup still renders predictably instead of failing outright.

questions.question: Which of these correctly writes an HTML comment?
questions.answer: <!-- this is a comment -->
questions.explanation: HTML comments use <!-- ... --> and are never rendered or sent to the user visually, though they remain visible in page source.

questions.starter_code: <!-- build a minimal valid HTML5 document with a title of 'My Page' -->

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>

<body>

test_cases.input: load the document in a browser
test_cases.expected_output: browser tab shows 'My Page' as the title, blank body
no errors - doctype, html, head, title, and body are all present and correctly nested

questions.answer: A doctype declaration, <html>, <head> with <title>My Page</title>, and an empty <body>.
questions.explanation: Every valid HTML5 document needs exactly these elements in this nesting; omitting doctype triggers quirks mode, and omitting <title> fails validation.

questions.question: Which attribute of the <html> tag declares the document's human language for accessibility and SEO?
questions.answer: lang
questions.explanation: `<html lang="en">` tells screen readers which pronunciation rules to use and helps search engines serve the right language to users.

questions.question: What is the practical difference between content placed in <head> versus <body>?
questions.answer: <head> holds metadata (title, charset, linked stylesheets/scripts, meta tags) that is never directly rendered as visible page content; <body> holds everything the user actually sees.
questions.explanation: Browsers process <head> to configure the page (encoding, styles, title) before rendering the visible <body> content.

questions.question: Why does omitting the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration risk triggering 'quirks mode' rendering?
questions.answer: Without a doctype, browsers can't be sure the page intends modern standards-compliant rendering, so they fall back to a legacy compatibility mode that mimics old, non-standard browser box-model and layout behavior.
questions.explanation: Quirks mode changes box-sizing defaults and other layout algorithms to match decades-old browsers, which can make modern CSS behave unpredictably.

questions.question: Which element, if present, must appear inside <head> and sets a base URL for all relative links on the page?
questions.answer: <base>
questions.explanation: `<base href="https://example.com/">` makes every relative URL on the page resolve against that base instead of the current document location.

questions.question: A page includes two <base> tags with different href values in <head>. Which one does the browser actually use?
questions.answer: Only the FIRST <base> element is used; any subsequent <base> tags are ignored by the HTML spec.
questions.explanation: The spec explicitly says a document must have no more than one <base> element with an href, and browsers honor only the first one encountered.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the <noscript> element?
questions.answer: It defines content to display only when the browser doesn't support scripting or has JavaScript disabled.
questions.explanation: This lets a page degrade gracefully - e.g. showing a message asking the user to enable JavaScript - rather than rendering blank content.

questions.question: A stylesheet <link> tag is placed at the very end of <body> instead of in <head>. What visible effect can this have on page load?
questions.code_snippet: <body>...content...<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"></body>
questions.answer: A brief flash of unstyled content (FOUC) - the browser renders the raw HTML before the stylesheet loads and applies, then repaints once the CSS arrives.
questions.explanation: Browsers render progressively as HTML streams in; CSS discovered late means layout/styling is applied only after most content is already painted.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a void (self-closing, no closing tag) element?
questions.answer: <span>
questions.explanation:
is a normal inline container that requires a closing ;
, , and are void elements that never have child content or a closing tag.

questions.question: What is the difference between the <b> and <strong> tags, given both render bold text by default?
questions.answer: <strong> conveys semantic importance (read with more emphasis by screen readers), while <b> is purely presentational bold styling with no implied meaning.
questions.explanation: HTML5 redefined <b>/<i> as stylistic-only, while <strong>/<em> carry semantic weight that assistive technology can act on.

questions.question: What does the <template> element do?
questions.answer: It holds inert HTML markup that is parsed but not rendered or executed until explicitly cloned and inserted into the DOM via JavaScript.
questions.explanation: Content inside <template> doesn't run scripts, load images, or display - it's a reusable, inactive fragment meant for later instantiation.

questions.question: Which element is used to define a hyperlink?
questions.explanation: <a> (anchor) with an href attribute creates a clickable hyperlink; <link> is a <head>-only element for resource references like stylesheets.

questions.explanation:

questions.question: What is the difference between the <ol> and <ul> elements?
questions.answer: <ol> creates an ordered (numbered) list, while <ul> creates an unordered (bulleted) list; both contain <li> items.
questions.explanation: Use <ol> when the sequence/order of items is meaningful (e.g. steps), and <ul> when the items have no inherent order.

questions.question: Which attribute, when present on any element (with no value needed), makes that element non-editable and non-interactive but still visible?
questions.answer: inert
questions.explanation: `inert` (a global boolean attribute) removes an element and its descendants from focus/interaction/selection entirely while keeping them visually rendered - distinct from `hidden` which removes visibility too.

questions.question: What is the difference between the `readonly` and `disabled` attributes on a form input?
questions.answer: `readonly` prevents editing but the value is still submitted with the form and the field can still receive focus; `disabled` prevents editing, focus, AND excludes the value from form submission entirely.
questions.explanation: This distinction matters when you want to show a value the user can't change but still needs to be sent to the server - `readonly` is the correct choice there, not `disabled`.

questions.question: What does the `contenteditable` attribute do when added to any HTML element?
questions.answer: It makes that element's content directly editable by the user in the browser, similar to a rich-text editor, without needing a <textarea> or <input>.
questions.explanation: This is the foundation many rich-text/WYSIWYG editors are built on, since it turns arbitrary HTML (not just plain text fields) into an editable surface.

questions.question: Which attribute prevents a user from selecting/dragging text or images to copy them by default?
options: There is no fully reliable built-in attribute for this - it's mainly done with CSS `user-select: none`
questions.answer: There is no fully reliable built-in attribute; `user-select: none` in CSS is the standard approach.
questions.explanation: HTML has no dedicated 'disable selection' attribute; preventing text selection is a CSS/JS concern, and it can never fully stop determined copying (e.g. via browser devtools).

questions.question: A form has `<input type="text" required minlength="5">` but a user submits exactly 4 characters and the browser blocks submission with a validation message. What built-in mechanism caused this, without any JavaScript?
questions.answer: The HTML5 Constraint Validation API, triggered automatically by the `required` and `minlength` attributes, which the browser enforces natively before allowing form submission.
questions.explanation: Browsers implement a native validation layer that checks these declarative attributes and shows its own UI (a bubble/tooltip) - no JS is needed for basic constraints like this.

questions.question: What does the `tabindex` attribute control, and what does a negative value like `tabindex="-1"` specifically do?
questions.answer: `tabindex` controls an element's position in keyboard Tab-key navigation order; a negative value removes it from the natural Tab order while still allowing it to be focused programmatically (e.g. via JS `.focus()`).
questions.explanation: This is commonly used for elements like modal dialogs that should be focusable when opened but not reachable by simply tabbing through the page.

questions.question: Which input type restricts the on-screen keyboard on mobile and provides a numeric spinner on desktop?
questions.answer: type="number"
questions.explanation: `type="number"` signals numeric intent to the browser, which adjusts the mobile keyboard and adds increment/decrement controls on desktop.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `<fieldset>` and `<legend>` elements in a form?
questions.answer: <fieldset> groups a set of related form controls together, and <legend> provides a caption/label for that whole group.
questions.explanation: This is both a visual grouping tool (a border/box around related fields) and a semantic/accessibility one, since screen readers announce the legend when a control inside the fieldset receives focus.

questions.question: What does the `placeholder` attribute do, and why is it not a substitute for a <label>?
questions.answer: `placeholder` shows hint text inside an empty input that disappears once the user types; it is not a substitute for <label> because it vanishes on input, isn't reliably announced by all screen readers, and provides no persistent visible context.
questions.explanation: Accessibility guidance is explicit: placeholders should supplement, never replace, a real associated <label>.

questions.question: Which attribute links a <label> to a specific form control by id?
questions.answer: for
questions.explanation: `<label for="email">` associates the label with `<input id="email">`, so clicking the label focuses/activates that input.

questions.question: A checkbox group is meant to let users select multiple options, but only one checkbox can ever be checked at a time. What's the likely bug?
questions.buggy_code:
<input type="checkbox" name="option" value="a">
<input type="checkbox" name="option" value="b">
questions.fixed_code:
<input type="checkbox" name="option[]" value="a">
<input type="checkbox" name="option[]" value="b">
questions.answer: The bug is elsewhere (likely JS treating them as a radio group), not the shared `name` itself - checkboxes with the same `name` CAN all be checked simultaneously, unlike radio buttons.
questions.explanation: This is a common misconception: shared `name` only forces mutual exclusivity for `type="radio"`, not `type="checkbox"` - multiple checkboxes with the same name submit as an array/list.

questions.question: What is the difference between the `value` attribute on a submit button versus on a text input?
questions.answer: On a text input, `value` sets the initial/current text content; on a submit button, `value` sets the button's visible label text.
questions.explanation: The same attribute name serves different roles depending on the input `type` - this is a common source of confusion for beginners.

questions.question: Which attribute on a <th> or <td> makes a single cell span multiple rows?
questions.answer: rowspan
questions.explanation: `rowspan` extends a cell downward across multiple rows, while `colspan` extends it across multiple columns.

questions.question: What does the `scope` attribute on a <th> element do, and why does it matter for accessibility?
questions.answer: `scope="col"` or `scope="row"` tells assistive technology whether a header cell applies to its column or its row, so screen readers can announce the correct header when a user navigates to a data cell.
questions.explanation: Without `scope`, screen readers have to guess table structure, which becomes ambiguous in tables with headers on both axes.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the <caption> element in a table?
questions.answer: It provides a title/description for the table, displayed by default above the table and announced by screen readers as the table's name.
questions.explanation: <caption> must be the first child of <table> and gives both sighted and non-sighted users context about what the table represents.

questions.question: A table renders with all columns oddly sized because one row has far more content in one cell than others, distorting the whole table's layout. What CSS property/value is commonly used to fix this?
questions.answer: `table-layout: fixed` on the <table>, combined with explicit column widths - this makes column widths independent of content length instead of the default auto-sizing behavior.
questions.explanation: The default `table-layout: auto` measures all cell content before deciding column widths, so one oversized cell can distort the entire table; `fixed` layout ignores content size after the first row.

questions.question: Which element is used to group and label a set of columns in a table for styling purposes?
questions.answer: <colgroup>
questions.explanation: <colgroup> (with nested <col> elements) lets you apply shared styling like width to entire columns without touching every cell in that column.

questions.question: Which semantic element represents a self-contained composition that could be distributed independently, like a blog post?
questions.answer: <article>
questions.explanation: <article> is meant for content that makes sense on its own outside the page's context, unlike <section> which groups thematically related content within a larger document.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the <figure> and <figcaption> elements?
questions.answer: <figure> wraps self-contained content (typically an image, diagram, or code listing) that could be moved elsewhere without breaking the flow of the main content, and <figcaption> provides its caption.
questions.explanation: Unlike a plain with surrounding text,

questions.question: Why is using semantic elements like <nav>, <main>, and <footer> considered better practice than an all-<div> layout?
questions.answer: Semantic elements convey meaning to browsers, search engines, and assistive technologies (screen readers can jump directly to <main> or <nav>), whereas generic <div>s carry no inherent meaning without extra ARIA roles.
questions.explanation: This improves accessibility, SEO, and code readability simultaneously, essentially for free, compared to a purely presentational div-based structure.

questions.question: Which element should be used exactly once per page to wrap the dominant, unique content of that page?
questions.answer: <main>
questions.explanation: <main> identifies the primary content, excluding repeated elements like headers/nav/sidebars/footers, and a page should have at most one visible <main>.

questions.question: A page nests <article> elements inside a <section>, expecting each article to be treated as a standalone item, but a screen reader user reports confusing navigation. Looking at the markup, each <article> itself has no heading. What's missing?
questions.buggy_code: Some post content...
questions.fixed_code:
Post Title

Some post content...
questions.answer: Each <article> is missing its own heading (e.g. <h2>), which screen readers rely on to label and let users jump between distinct pieces of content.
questions.explanation: Semantic sectioning elements like <article>/<section> are far more useful to assistive technology when each one starts with a heading that names it - without one, screen reader users hear generic 'article' landmarks with no way to tell them apart.

questions.question: Which attribute on <video> makes the video start over automatically when it finishes?
questions.answer: loop
questions.explanation: `loop` is a boolean attribute that restarts playback from the beginning once the media ends; `autoplay` only controls whether it starts playing on load.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the <track> element inside a <video> tag?
questions.answer: It supplies timed text tracks - like subtitles, captions, or chapter markers - synced to the video's playback time, typically as a WebVTT file via the `src` attribute.
questions.explanation: This is the standard, accessible way to add captions without baking them into the video file itself, letting users toggle them independently.

questions.question: Why does the element exist alongside plain ?
questions.answer: lets the browser choose among multiple candidate image sources based on conditions like screen size, pixel density, or supported image format, whereas a plain always loads one fixed source.
questions.explanation: This enables responsive images (serving a smaller image to mobile) and modern-format fallbacks (serving WebP where supported, JPEG otherwise) without any JavaScript.

questions.question: A <video> element plays fine in Chrome but shows a broken/empty player in Safari. The developer only provided one <source> with an .mp4 file using the H.264 codec. What's the likely issue and general fix?
questions.answer: This particular case usually isn't a codec problem (H.264 mp4 is broadly supported including Safari) - more likely the video file itself is malformed, served with a wrong MIME type, or blocked by autoplay/CORS policy; the general fix for real codec gaps is to provide multiple <source> elements in different formats/codecs so the browser picks one it supports.
questions.explanation: Providing multiple <source> children (e.g. WebM and MP4) is the standard defensive pattern precisely because no single format has universal, guaranteed browser support.

questions.question: Which attribute mutes a <video> or <audio> element by default?
questions.answer: muted
questions.explanation: `muted` is a boolean attribute; note browsers generally require it (alongside `autoplay`) for videos to autoplay without a user gesture.

questions.question: Which value of the <a> tag's `target` attribute opens the link in the same browsing context (the default)?
questions.answer: _self
questions.explanation: `_self` is the default target - the link loads in the current tab/frame, replacing the current document.

questions.question: What is the difference between an absolute URL and a relative URL in an <a href>?
questions.answer: An absolute URL includes the full scheme and domain (e.g. https://example.com/page), while a relative URL is resolved against the current page's location (e.g. /page or ../page).
questions.explanation: Relative URLs make a site portable across domains/environments (dev, staging, production) without hardcoding a host.

questions.question: What does the `download` attribute on an <a> tag do?
questions.answer: It tells the browser to download the linked resource as a file instead of navigating to/displaying it, optionally with a suggested filename as the attribute's value.
