questions.explanation: This only works reliably for same-origin (or CORS-permitting) resources - cross-origin links without proper headers may still just navigate instead of downloading.

questions.question: A navigation menu built from <a href="#"> links (used purely to trigger JavaScript, no real navigation) causes the page to jump to the top every time a link is clicked. What's the fix?
questions.buggy_code: Click me
questions.fixed_code: Click me
questions.answer: `href="#"` is a real navigation target (the top of the page / empty fragment), so the browser jumps there unless the click's default action is prevented; a cleaner fix is to use a <button> instead of a fake link.
questions.explanation: Using `event.preventDefault()` stops the jump, but semantically a control that doesn't navigate anywhere shouldn't be an <a> at all - a <button> is the correct element for JS-only actions.

questions.question: What does `rel="nofollow"` on a link communicate to search engines?
questions.answer: It tells search engine crawlers not to pass ranking credit/authority through that particular link to the linked page.
questions.explanation: This is commonly used for user-generated content links (comments, forum posts) or paid/sponsored links, to avoid implicitly endorsing or boosting the linked site's SEO.

questions.question: Which meta tag property is part of the Open Graph protocol used to control how a link preview appears when shared on social media?
questions.answer: og:title
questions.explanation: Open Graph meta tags (`og:title`, `og:image`, `og:description`, etc.) are read by platforms like Facebook and LinkedIn to build rich link preview cards.

questions.question: What does the `<link rel="canonical" href="...">` tag do, and why is it important for SEO?
questions.answer: It tells search engines which URL is the 'master' version of a page when the same or near-duplicate content is reachable via multiple URLs, preventing duplicate-content ranking penalties.
questions.explanation: Without a canonical tag, search engines might index several URL variants of the same content as separate pages, diluting SEO ranking signals across them.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a `<meta name="viewport">` tag, and what happens on mobile if it's omitted?
questions.answer: It controls how a page's dimensions and scaling are handled on mobile devices; without it, mobile browsers assume a wide desktop-like virtual viewport and render a tiny, zoomed-out version of the page.
questions.explanation: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` is the standard tag that makes a page actually responsive on phones.

questions.question: A site's important pages are correctly built and linked, but Google Search Console shows they were never indexed. The team confirms no `noindex` tag exists on the pages. What other meta-level cause is commonly responsible?
questions.answer: A `robots.txt` file at the site root disallowing crawler access to those paths - this blocks crawling entirely before any per-page meta tag is even read.
questions.explanation: `noindex` (a per-page directive) and `robots.txt` (a site-wide crawl directive) are two separate, often-confused mechanisms; robots.txt can block indexing even with no noindex tag anywhere.

questions.question: Which meta tag value tells a browser to automatically refresh/redirect the page after a delay?
questions.answer: <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="5;url=...">
questions.explanation: This legacy technique refreshes or redirects after N seconds, though a server-side redirect (301/302) is now considered better practice for SEO and UX.

questions.question: Which ARIA attribute announces dynamically updating content (like a live chat message) to screen readers without moving focus?
questions.answer: aria-live
questions.explanation: `aria-live="polite"` (or `"assertive"`) marks a region so screen readers announce changes inside it as they happen, which is essential for chat widgets, notifications, and live status updates.

questions.question: What is the difference between `aria-labelledby` and `aria-label`?
questions.answer: `aria-label` provides an inline text string as the accessible name directly; `aria-labelledby` instead references the `id` of another element on the page whose text content becomes the accessible name.
questions.explanation: `aria-labelledby` is preferred when a visible label already exists elsewhere in the DOM, avoiding duplicated text; `aria-label` is used when there's no visible text to reference.

questions.question: What does the `role` attribute do in ARIA, and give an example of when it's necessary?
questions.answer: `role` overrides or supplies the semantic purpose of an element for assistive technology - e.g. `role="button"` on a <div> that's been styled and scripted to behave like a button, since a plain <div> has no inherent semantic role.
questions.explanation: Native elements (like a real <button>) already have the correct implicit role; `role` is a patch needed only when you've built interactive behavior on top of a non-semantic element.

questions.question: A modal dialog implemented with a plain <div> traps keyboard focus correctly, but screen reader users report they can still 'hear' and interact with background page content while the modal is open. What ARIA attribute is likely missing?
questions.answer: `aria-modal="true"` on the dialog container (paired with `role="dialog"`), and/or `aria-hidden="true"` applied to the rest of the page content while the modal is open.
questions.explanation: Visually trapping focus with JS isn't enough - screen readers need explicit signals that everything outside the dialog is temporarily inert, which `aria-modal`/`aria-hidden` on background content provides.

questions.question: What is the 'accessibility tree', and how does it relate to the regular DOM tree?
questions.answer: The accessibility tree is a parallel structure the browser builds from the DOM, containing only the information assistive technologies need (roles, names, states, properties) - some DOM nodes are omitted or transformed based on their computed accessibility semantics.
questions.explanation: Screen readers and other AT don't read the raw DOM directly; they consume this derived accessibility tree, which is why ARIA attributes (which shape this tree) matter so much.

questions.question: Which technology represents its graphics as a tree of XML elements that can be individually styled with CSS?
questions.answer: SVG
questions.explanation: SVG shapes are actual DOM elements (<circle>, <rect>, <path>, etc.), so CSS selectors and JS DOM APIs can target them individually, unlike <canvas>'s single flat pixel buffer.

questions.question: What does the 2D rendering context obtained via `canvas.getContext('2d')` provide access to?
questions.answer: A set of imperative drawing methods (fillRect, arc, moveTo/lineTo, drawImage, etc.) used to paint pixels directly onto the canvas's bitmap.
questions.explanation: Unlike SVG's declarative element tree, canvas drawing is purely procedural - once something is drawn, the canvas has no memory of it as a distinct shape, only as pixels.

questions.question: What does it mean that an SVG image is 'resolution independent'?
questions.answer: Because SVG shapes are defined mathematically (paths, coordinates) rather than as a fixed pixel grid, they can be scaled to any size and re-rendered sharply at that new size with no blurring or pixelation.
questions.explanation: A raster image (or a canvas snapshot) is a fixed grid of pixels, so scaling it up beyond its native resolution necessarily blurs or pixelates it.

questions.question: An SVG icon renders correctly in isolation but appears the wrong color when embedded via and the developer wants to control its color with CSS `fill`. Why doesn't `fill` work in this case, and what's the fix?
questions.answer: An SVG loaded via is treated as an opaque external resource, isolated from the parent page's CSS - so external stylesheets can't reach inside it; the fix is to inline the SVG markup directly into the HTML (or use it as a CSS `mask`/background with `currentColor` tricks) so the page's CSS can target its internal elements.
questions.explanation: Only SVG that is part of the actual page DOM (inlined -embedded SVG is sandboxed like any other image file.

questions.question: Why does redrawing frequently-changing content on <canvas> generally scale better performance-wise than animating thousands of SVG DOM elements?
questions.answer: Canvas has no per-shape DOM overhead - the browser just repaints pixels - while each SVG shape is a real DOM node whose creation, style recalculation, and layout the browser must track individually, which becomes expensive at very high element counts.
questions.explanation: This is why canvas (or WebGL) is typically preferred for particle systems, real-time charts with huge datasets, or games, while SVG excels at smaller numbers of interactive, stylable shapes.

questions.question: Which Web Storage API method removes a single key from localStorage?
questions.answer: localStorage.removeItem(key)
questions.explanation: `removeItem(key)` is the standard API method; `delete localStorage[key]` also technically works since localStorage is proxy-like, but `removeItem` is the documented, intended method.

questions.question: What triggers the `storage` event, and in which browsing context does it fire?
questions.answer: It fires when localStorage (or sessionStorage) is modified from ANOTHER tab/window on the same origin - not in the tab that made the change itself.
questions.explanation: This lets multiple open tabs of the same site stay in sync (e.g. logging out in one tab can trigger the same effect in others) by listening for cross-tab storage changes.

questions.question: Why is Web Storage (localStorage/sessionStorage) considered synchronous and blocking, and why does this matter?
questions.answer: Every read/write to Web Storage runs synchronously on the main thread, so storing or retrieving large values can briefly block UI rendering and script execution.
questions.explanation: This is a key reason IndexedDB (an asynchronous API) is recommended over Web Storage for larger amounts of data or performance-sensitive code paths.

questions.question: A site stores user preferences in localStorage, but after the browser is set to 'Clear cookies and site data on exit,' the preferences disappear too, even though localStorage isn't a cookie. Why?
questions.answer: Browsers commonly group localStorage under the same 'site data' clearing category as cookies, since both are origin-scoped persistent client-side storage - clearing 'site data' wipes localStorage, IndexedDB, and cookies together, not just cookies specifically.
questions.explanation: This is a common misconception: localStorage avoids cookie-specific issues (like being sent with every HTTP request) but is not exempt from browser privacy/data-clearing settings aimed at 'site data' broadly.

questions.question: What data type does `localStorage.getItem()` always return, even if you stored a number or boolean?
questions.answer: A string, or `null` if the key doesn't exist - localStorage stores and returns everything as strings regardless of what type was originally passed to `setItem`.
questions.explanation: Storing `localStorage.setItem('count', 5)` and later reading it back gives you the string `"5"`, not the number 5, so callers must explicitly parse it back (e.g. `Number(...)`) if a non-string type is needed.

questions.question: Which API lets a web page copy text to the user's system clipboard programmatically?
questions.answer: Clipboard API
questions.explanation: `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` is the modern, promise-based way to write to the clipboard, generally requiring a secure context (HTTPS) and often a user gesture.

questions.question: What problem does the Intersection Observer API solve, compared to manually checking element positions on every scroll event?
questions.answer: It lets a page efficiently detect when an element enters or leaves the viewport (or another container) asynchronously, without the performance cost of repeatedly running layout-reading code inside a scroll event handler.
questions.explanation: This underlies common patterns like lazy-loading images and infinite-scroll, and is far cheaper than polling `getBoundingClientRect()` on every scroll tick.

questions.question: What is the Page Visibility API used for?
questions.answer: It exposes whether the current document/tab is visible to the user or hidden (backgrounded, minimized, switched away from), via `document.visibilityState` and the `visibilitychange` event.
questions.explanation: Common uses include pausing videos/animations, reducing polling frequency, or - relevant to proctored tests - detecting when a user switches away from a tab.

questions.question: A page uses the History API's `pushState()` to change the URL for client-side routing without a full page reload, but clicking the browser's Back button doesn't seem to do anything. What is likely missing?
questions.answer: A `popstate` event listener - `pushState` alone only changes the URL/history entry, it does NOT automatically re-render the page; the app must listen for `popstate` and manually update the UI to match the new/previous URL.
questions.explanation: This is a very common single-page-app routing bug: developers wire up forward navigation (pushState on link clicks) but forget backward navigation needs its own explicit handler.

questions.question: What does the Fetch API's `AbortController` allow you to do?
questions.answer: It lets you cancel an in-flight `fetch()` request before it completes, by calling `controller.abort()` after passing `controller.signal` as the fetch's `signal` option.
questions.explanation: This is essential for scenarios like a user typing a new search query before the previous search's fetch has resolved - the stale request can be cancelled instead of racing with the new one.

questions.question: Which of these attributes is a 'global attribute' usable on virtually any HTML element?
questions.answer: class
questions.explanation:
`class`, `id`, `style`, `title`, and `data-*` are global attributes valid on nearly every element; `href`/`src`/`action` are specific to particular elements like , , and
.

questions.question: Why is HTML described as being parsed with 'error tolerance' compared to strict formats like XML?
questions.answer: Browsers are required by the HTML5 parsing spec to recover from malformed markup (unclosed tags, misordered elements) using well-defined repair rules, rendering something reasonable instead of stopping with a fatal error the way an XML parser would.
questions.explanation: This is a deliberate, standardized design choice (not just historical laxness) - the WHATWG HTML spec defines exact algorithms for how a parser must handle broken markup, ensuring consistent rendering across browsers even for invalid documents.

questions.question: Which meta tag, when placed early in <head>, should generally come before other meta tags for correct character decoding?
questions.answer: <meta charset="UTF-8">
questions.explanation: The charset declaration should appear within the first 1024 bytes of the document so the browser decodes the rest of the page's text correctly before encountering any non-ASCII characters.

questions.question: What is the difference between placing a <script> tag with the `defer` attribute versus the `async` attribute?
questions.answer: `defer` scripts download in parallel but execute only after HTML parsing completes, in original document order; `async` scripts download in parallel and execute as soon as they're ready, potentially out of order and before parsing finishes.
questions.explanation: `defer` is generally safer for scripts that depend on the full DOM being parsed and on running in a specific order relative to other scripts.

questions.question: Which element represents a thematic break between paragraph-level content, typically rendered as a horizontal line?
questions.answer: <hr>
questions.explanation: <hr> is a void element with semantic meaning (a shift in topic), not just a decorative line - purely visual dividers should use CSS borders instead.

questions.question: What is the difference between the <details>/<summary> elements and a JavaScript-built custom accordion widget?
questions.answer: <details>/<summary> provide a native, disclosure widget (expand/collapse) with built-in keyboard accessibility, no JavaScript, and a default open/closed toggle state managed entirely by the browser - a custom JS accordion must reimplement all of that behavior and accessibility manually.
questions.explanation: This is a good example of 'use the platform' - many interactive UI patterns now have native HTML equivalents that are more accessible by default than hand-rolled JS/CSS versions.

questions.question: Which attribute, when added to a <script> tag, marks it as an ES module rather than a classic script?
questions.answer: type="module"
questions.explanation: `<script type="module">` enables `import`/`export` syntax and runs the script in strict mode with deferred execution by default.

questions.question: What does the `crossorigin` attribute on a
questions.answer: It configures whether the resource request is made with CORS credentials, which affects both whether cross-origin errors can be caught in detail (e.g. full script error messages) and whether the browser applies the Same-Origin Policy to reading the resource's data.
questions.explanation: Without `crossorigin`, cross-origin script errors are reported generically as 'Script error' with no stack trace, for security reasons.

questions.question: Which input type provides a native color-picker UI in supporting browsers?
questions.answer: type="color"
questions.explanation: `<input type="color">` opens a native color-selection UI and its value is always a lowercase 7-character hex string like `#ff0000`.

questions.question: What is the difference between the `formaction` attribute on a submit button and the `action` attribute on the enclosing <form>?
questions.answer: `action` on <form> sets the default submission URL for the whole form; `formaction` on an individual submit button OVERRIDES that URL just for that specific button, letting one form submit to different endpoints depending on which button was clicked.
questions.explanation: This is useful for forms with multiple actions (e.g. 'Save Draft' vs 'Publish') without needing separate <form> elements or JavaScript to change the action dynamically.

questions.question: Which attribute historically specified spacing between table cells, now handled by CSS `border-spacing` instead?
questions.answer: cellspacing
questions.explanation: `cellspacing`/`cellpadding` are deprecated presentational HTML attributes; modern code uses CSS (`border-spacing`, `padding`) on the table/cells instead.

questions.question: Why does `border-collapse: collapse` change how borders between adjacent table cells render compared to the default `separate`?
questions.answer: With `collapse`, adjacent cells share a single border line (adjacent cell borders merge into one), while `separate` (the default) gives each cell its own independent border, potentially creating a visible double-border look between cells.
questions.explanation: `collapse` is almost always what's visually intended for a clean grid-style table; `separate` is more useful when `border-spacing` gaps between cells are wanted.

questions.question: Which element is intended specifically to represent a page's or article's introductory content, like a logo and heading group?
questions.answer: <header>
questions.explanation: <header> is a content-sectioning element usable multiple times per page (e.g. once for the whole site, once inside each <article>) unlike <head> which is metadata-only and appears exactly once.

questions.question: Can a page legally contain multiple <header> and <footer> elements, and if so, in what context does this make sense?
questions.answer: Yes - <header>/<footer> are scoped to their nearest sectioning ancestor (like <article> or <section>), not just the page as a whole, so each article in a list of blog posts can have its own <header> (title/date) and the page can still have one overall page-level <header>/<footer> too.
questions.explanation: This is a common point of confusion since the names suggest 'the page header,' but the spec explicitly scopes them to their containing sectioning content.

questions.question: Which attribute on <audio>/<video> hides the browser's default playback controls (play/pause/volume)?
questions.answer: Omitting the `controls` attribute
questions.explanation: Without `controls`, no default UI is shown at all - the media element becomes invisible/non-interactive unless controlled entirely via JavaScript and a custom UI.

questions.question: What does the `preload` attribute on a <video> element control, and what are its three main values?
questions.answer: It hints to the browser how much of the video to load before playback starts: `none` (don't preload anything), `metadata` (load only duration/dimensions), and `auto` (let the browser decide, often preloading substantial data).
questions.explanation: This is a hint, not a guarantee - browsers may ignore it based on factors like the user's data-saving settings or connection type.

questions.question: Which value of `rel` on an <a> tag indicates the linked document is an alternate version of the current page, e.g. a different language?
questions.answer: alternate
questions.explanation: `rel="alternate" hreflang="fr"` is the standard way to point search engines to a translated version of a page.

questions.question: What is the difference between `<a href="mailto:someone@example.com">` and a regular link?
questions.answer: Clicking a `mailto:` link opens the user's default email client with a new message pre-addressed to that address, instead of navigating the browser to another page.
questions.explanation: Additional query parameters like `?subject=Hello&body=Hi` can pre-fill the subject/body of the composed email as well.

questions.question: Which HTTP-equivalent meta tag can instruct the browser to enforce a Content Security Policy from within the HTML itself (rather than an HTTP header)?
questions.answer: <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="...">
questions.explanation: This lets a page declare a CSP without needing server-level header configuration access, though a real HTTP header is generally considered more robust since it can't be tampered with by injected HTML.

questions.question: A site adds structured data (JSON-LD) for recipes to its pages hoping for rich search snippets, but Google's rich results test shows no errors yet the rich snippet never appears in search results. What is a common, non-error reason for this?
questions.answer: Valid structured data is necessary but not sufficient for a rich result - Google independently decides whether/when to actually display a rich snippet based on its own quality and eligibility algorithms, and there can be a significant delay after re-crawling before any change appears in live search results.
questions.explanation: Developers often assume 'valid markup = guaranteed rich result,' but search engines treat structured data as a hint, not a directive, and eligibility can change over time even for technically correct markup.

questions.question: Which ARIA attribute indicates whether a collapsible section (like an accordion panel) is currently expanded or collapsed?
questions.answer: aria-expanded
questions.explanation: `aria-expanded="true"`/`"false"` on the toggle control tells assistive technology the current disclosure state, which must be kept in sync with the actual visual state via JavaScript.

questions.question: What is the 'first rule of ARIA use' as stated in the WAI-ARIA authoring practices, and why does it exist?
questions.answer: If a native HTML element or attribute already has the semantics/behavior you need, use it instead of re-purposing a generic element with ARIA roles - because native elements come with built-in keyboard interaction, focus management, and browser/AT support that ARIA-only reimplementations must painstakingly replicate and often get subtly wrong.
questions.explanation: ARIA can describe semantics but never implements behavior itself - adding `role="button"` to a <div> doesn't give it Enter/Space key activation for free, unlike a real <button>.

questions.question: Which SVG element defines a reusable graphic that can be referenced multiple times via <use>?
questions.answer: <symbol>
questions.explanation: <symbol> (often inside a hidden <defs> block) defines a graphic once; `<use href="#iconId">` then instantiates it anywhere without duplicating the markup.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the SVG `viewBox` attribute?
questions.answer: It defines the internal coordinate system and aspect ratio of an SVG's content, decoupled from the element's actual rendered width/height - letting the graphic scale responsively while preserving its internal proportions.
questions.explanation: Without a `viewBox`, an SVG's coordinates map 1:1 to pixels at its declared width/height, making it much harder to scale cleanly.

questions.question: Which Web Storage method returns the total number of key/value pairs currently stored?
questions.answer: localStorage.length
questions.explanation: `length` is a property (not a method call) that reflects the current number of stored items.

questions.question: Why is storing sensitive data like passwords or full credit card numbers in localStorage considered a poor security practice, even on an HTTPS site?
questions.answer: Any JavaScript running on the page - including from a successful XSS (cross-site scripting) attack - has full read access to localStorage, with no way to mark data as HTTP-only or otherwise inaccessible to scripts, unlike HTTP-only cookies which JS cannot read at all.
questions.explanation: HTTPS protects data in transit, but localStorage's exposure to any script on the page is a client-side risk independent of transport security.

questions.question: Which API provides low-level access to a user's camera and microphone streams directly in the browser?
questions.answer: getUserMedia (Media Capture and Streams API)
questions.explanation: `navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({video: true, audio: true})` returns a promise resolving to a MediaStream, after prompting the user for permission.

questions.question: A page calls `navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition()` expecting the success callback to fire, but nothing happens at all - not even the error callback. What's a likely cause, given the page is served over plain HTTP (not HTTPS)?
questions.buggy_code: navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(onSuccess, onError);
questions.fixed_code: // Serve the page over HTTPS - most powerful browser APIs (geolocation, camera, clipboard write, etc.) require a secure context
questions.answer: Modern browsers restrict the Geolocation API (and many other sensitive APIs) to secure contexts (HTTPS, or localhost) - on plain HTTP, some browsers silently refuse to even prompt, calling neither callback, rather than obviously erroring.
questions.explanation: This 'secure context required' restriction applies broadly across newer web APIs and can be a confusing silent-failure trap for developers testing on non-HTTPS origins.

questions.question: What does CSS stand for?
questions.answer: Cascading Style Sheets
questions.explanation: 'Cascading' refers to the algorithm that resolves which of multiple conflicting style rules applies to an element, based on specificity, source order, and origin.

questions.question: What are the three ways to apply CSS to an HTML document?
questions.answer: Inline (a `style` attribute on an element), internal (a <style> block in the document's <head>), and external (a separate .css file linked via <link>).
questions.explanation: External stylesheets are generally preferred for maintainability and caching across pages; inline styles have the highest specificity and are hardest to override or reuse.

questions.question: Which CSS property changes the text color of an element?
questions.answer: color
questions.explanation: `color` sets the foreground/text color; it's easy to confuse with `background-color`, which sets the element's background fill instead.

questions.question: What is the difference between `class` and `id` selectors in terms of specificity?
questions.answer: An `id` selector (`#name`) has higher specificity than a `class` selector (`.name`), meaning a style targeted by ID will override a conflicting style targeted by class, regardless of source order.
questions.explanation: This specificity hierarchy (inline > id > class/attribute/pseudo-class > element/pseudo-element) is why relying heavily on IDs for styling makes overriding styles later much harder.

questions.question: What is a CSS shorthand property? Give an example.
questions.answer: A shorthand property lets you set several related longhand properties in a single declaration; for example `margin: 10px 20px 10px 20px` sets `margin-top`, `margin-right`, `margin-bottom`, and `margin-left` in one line.
questions.explanation: Shorthands follow a defined order (often top-right-bottom-left, clockwise) and can also reset any longhand property not explicitly specified back to its initial value, which is a common source of accidental overrides.

questions.question:
Which CSS selector selects all

elements that are direct children of a

?
questions.answer: div > p
questions.explanation: The `>` combinator selects only direct (immediate) children, unlike the descendant combinator (a plain space), which selects any nested descendant at any depth.

questions.question: What is the difference between the descendant combinator (space) and the child combinator (>)?
questions.answer:
`div p` selects any

nested anywhere inside a

at any depth; `div > p` selects only

elements that are direct children of a

.
questions.explanation: This distinction matters a lot in deeply nested markup, where a descendant selector can unintentionally match elements many levels deep that a child selector would correctly exclude.

questions.question: Given two conflicting rules `.btn { color: blue; }` and `button { color: red; }` applied to the same <button class="btn">, which color wins and why?
questions.answer: Blue wins, because a class selector (`.btn`) has higher specificity than an element/type selector (`button`), regardless of the order the rules appear in the stylesheet.
questions.explanation: CSS specificity is calculated independently of source order for rules of different specificity; source order only acts as the tie-breaker when specificity is EQUAL.

questions.question: What does the `!important` declaration do, and why is it generally discouraged?
questions.answer: It forces that single declaration to override any other conflicting declaration regardless of specificity (except another `!important` of equal/higher priority); it's discouraged because it breaks the normal cascade, making styles unpredictable and hard to override later without resorting to `!important` everywhere.
questions.explanation: Overuse of `!important` creates a specificity arms race where developers must keep adding it to override previous `!important` rules, ultimately defeating the purpose of a predictable cascade.

questions.question: Given `#nav .item { color: black; }` and `.nav-item.active { color: blue; }` applied to the same element that matches both selectors, which wins, and how is specificity actually calculated?
questions.answer: The first rule wins (black), because CSS specificity is calculated as a tuple of (ID count, class/attribute/pseudo-class count, element/pseudo-element count): `#nav .item` scores (1 ID, 1 class, 0 elements) = (1,1,0), while `.nav-item.active` scores (0 IDs, 2 classes, 0 elements) = (0,2,0); comparing left-to-right, 1 ID beats any number of classes.
questions.explanation: Specificity is compared digit-by-digit from the most significant category (IDs) down, not by simply summing 'points' — a single ID always outweighs any number of classes, and a single class always outweighs any number of element selectors.

questions.question: List the four layers of the CSS box model from innermost to outermost.
questions.answer: Content, padding, border, margin.
questions.explanation: Every rendered element is a rectangular box built from these four concentric layers; `width`/`height` by default apply only to the content box unless `box-sizing` changes that.

questions.question: What is the difference between `box-sizing: content-box` (the default) and `box-sizing: border-box`?
questions.answer: With `content-box`, `width`/`height` apply only to the content area, so padding and border are added ON TOP, making the element visually larger than the specified width; with `border-box`, `width`/`height` include padding and border, so the element's total rendered size matches the specified value exactly.
questions.explanation: `border-box` is widely adopted (often applied globally via `*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }`) because it makes sizing math far more predictable when padding/borders are involved.
options: content-box includes padding/border in width; border-box excludes them
border-box includes padding/border in the specified width/height; content-box excludes them

questions.question: Why can two adjacent elements with `margin-bottom: 20px` and `margin-top: 30px` end up with only 30px of vertical gap between them instead of 50px?
questions.answer: This is 'margin collapsing' — adjacent vertical margins between block-level elements in normal flow collapse into a single margin equal to the larger of the two, rather than summing.
questions.explanation: Margin collapsing only applies to vertical margins of block-level elements in normal document flow (not to horizontal margins, and not to elements that are floated, absolutely positioned, flex/grid items, or have padding/border/overflow between them).

questions.question: What CSS property and value prevents an element's background from extending underneath its border (clips it to the padding edge instead)?
questions.answer: `background-clip: padding-box`
questions.explanation: By default `background-clip` is `border-box`, meaning the background paints under a (semi-)transparent or dashed border; setting it to `padding-box` stops the background at the inner edge of the border.

questions.question: An element has `width: 200px`, `padding: 20px`, `border: 5px solid`, and `box-sizing: content-box`. What is its total rendered width, and how would that change if `box-sizing: border-box` were applied instead?
questions.answer: With `content-box`: total width = 200 (content) + 2×20 (padding) + 2×5 (border) = 250px. With `border-box`: the specified 200px already INCLUDES padding and border, so the content area shrinks to 200 − 2×20 − 2×5 = 150px, and the total rendered width stays exactly 200px.
questions.explanation: This is the core practical consequence of the `box-sizing` property: it changes what the `width`/`height` value actually measures, not the presence of padding/border themselves.

questions.question: What is the default value of the CSS `position` property?
questions.answer: static
questions.explanation: `position: static` means the element follows normal document flow and ignores `top`/`left`/`right`/`bottom`/`z-index`; any other position value (relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) is required before those offset properties take effect.

questions.question: What is the difference between `position: relative` and `position: absolute`?
questions.answer: `relative` positions the element relative to its own normal position in the flow (and it still occupies its original space), while `absolute` removes the element from normal flow entirely and positions it relative to its nearest positioned (non-static) ancestor.
questions.explanation: This is why `position: relative` is so often applied to a container with no offset values at all — purely to establish it as the positioning context (containing block) for an absolutely positioned child.

questions.question: What does `position: sticky` do, and what condition must be met for it to work?
questions.answer: It behaves like `position: relative` until the element crosses a specified threshold (e.g. `top: 0`) during scrolling, at which point it 'sticks' and behaves like `position: fixed` relative to its nearest scrolling ancestor for as long as that ancestor is in view.
questions.explanation: A sticky element requires at least one of `top`/`right`/`bottom`/`left` to be set (otherwise it behaves exactly like `relative`), and it will stop sticking once its parent container scrolls out of view — it's not truly viewport-fixed like `position: fixed`.

questions.question: Why does an absolutely positioned element sometimes end up positioned relative to the entire page (viewport) instead of its intended parent container?
questions.answer: Because `position: absolute` positions relative to the nearest ANCESTOR that has a `position` value other than `static`; if no ancestor is positioned, it falls back to the initial containing block, which is effectively the viewport/root element.
questions.explanation: The fix is to add `position: relative` (with no offsets) to the intended containing element, establishing it as the positioning context so the absolutely positioned child is anchored to it instead of the page.
questions.buggy_code:
.card { }
.badge { position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0; }
questions.fixed_code:
.card { position: relative; }
.badge { position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0; }

questions.question: What does the CSS `z-index` property control, and why can a high `z-index` on an element sometimes fail to bring it above another element that has a much lower `z-index`?
questions.answer: `z-index` controls the stacking order of positioned elements along the axis perpendicular to the screen (which overlaps on top of which); a high `z-index` can still lose if the two elements belong to different 'stacking contexts' — z-index values only compete directly against siblings within the SAME stacking context, so an element trapped inside a low/negative-z-index (or otherwise stacking-context-creating) ancestor can never visually escape above content outside that ancestor, no matter how high its own z-index is set.
questions.explanation: Certain CSS properties (a `position` other than static combined with a z-index value, `opacity` less than 1, `transform`, `filter`, and others) each create a NEW stacking context, effectively 'sealing' the z-index comparisons of descendants inside it relative to the outside world.

questions.question: What is the default `display` value of a <div> element?
questions.answer: block
questions.explanation: Block-level elements take the full available width and start on a new line by default, which is exactly the default rendering behavior of a <div> before any CSS is applied.

questions.question: What does `display: none` do, and how is it different from `visibility: hidden`?
questions.answer: `display: none` completely removes the element from the rendered layout (it takes up no space and is unreachable by assistive technology); `visibility: hidden` keeps the element's space reserved in the layout but makes it invisible.
questions.explanation: Because `display: none` removes the box entirely, surrounding elements reflow to fill the gap; `visibility: hidden` leaves a visible gap where the element used to be, since its layout box still exists.

questions.question: What is `display: inline-block`, and why is it useful compared to plain `inline`?
questions.answer: It makes an element flow inline with surrounding content (like `inline`) while still allowing `width`, `height`, and vertical `margin`/`padding` to take effect (like `block`), which plain `inline` elements ignore for width/height.
questions.explanation: This was historically the go-to technique for laying out horizontal navigation items or button-like elements before Flexbox became widely supported.

questions.question: What layout behavior does `display: flex` give to the direct children of the element it's applied to?
questions.answer: It turns the element into a flex container, causing its direct children to become flex items arranged along a single flex line (row or column by default row) that can grow, shrink, and align according to additional flex properties (`justify-content`, `align-items`, `flex-grow`, etc.).
questions.explanation: Unlike float-based layouts, flex items can be evenly distributed, reordered visually, and made to fill or share available space without manual width calculations.

questions.question: Why can setting `display: flex` on a container unexpectedly change the behavior of a child's `float` or `vertical-align` properties?
questions.answer: Once an element becomes a flex container, its direct children become flex items, and flex items ignore `float`, `clear`, and `vertical-align` entirely — the flex layout algorithm takes over their positioning completely, so those older layout properties simply have no effect anymore.
questions.explanation: This is a common source of confusion when migrating older float-based layouts to Flexbox incrementally: leftover `float`/`vertical-align` rules on now-flex-item children become dead code rather than causing an error, silently doing nothing.

questions.question: Which CSS property, applied to a flex container, controls the direction items are laid out (row vs column)?
questions.answer: flex-direction
questions.explanation: `flex-direction: row` (the default) lays items left-to-right, `column` lays them top-to-bottom, and `row-reverse`/`column-reverse` reverse the respective order.

questions.question: What does `justify-content` control in a flex container?
questions.answer: It controls how flex items are distributed and aligned along the main axis (the direction set by `flex-direction`) — options include `flex-start`, `flex-end`, `center`, `space-between`, and `space-around`.
questions.explanation: It's easy to confuse with `align-items`, which does the equivalent alignment but along the perpendicular CROSS axis instead.

questions.question: What is the difference between `align-items` and `align-content` in Flexbox?
questions.answer: `align-items` aligns individual flex items along the cross axis WITHIN their single flex line; `align-content` aligns entire flex LINES relative to each other along the cross axis, and only has a visible effect when the container has multiple wrapped lines (`flex-wrap: wrap`) and extra cross-axis space.
questions.explanation: This is why `align-content` appears to 'do nothing' on a single-line flex container — with only one line, there's no multi-line space distribution for it to affect.

questions.question: What do the three components of the `flex` shorthand property (`flex-grow`, `flex-shrink`, `flex-basis`) each control?
questions.answer: `flex-grow` is a unitless ratio controlling how much of the container's EXTRA free space an item absorbs relative to siblings; `flex-shrink` is a unitless ratio controlling how much an item shrinks relative to siblings when there ISN'T enough space; `flex-basis` sets the item's initial main-axis size before growing/shrinking is applied.
questions.explanation: A very common pattern, `flex: 1`, expands to `flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 0%`, meaning all such items ignore their content size and just split the available space equally.

questions.question: Three flex items have `flex-grow: 1`, `flex-grow: 2`, and `flex-grow: 1` respectively, and the container has 120px of extra free space after accounting for their base sizes. How is that extra space distributed among them?
questions.answer: The extra space is divided proportionally to each item's flex-grow value out of the total (1+2+1=4 parts, so 120px / 4 = 30px per part): the first item gets +30px, the second gets +60px, and the third gets +30px, added on top of each item's flex-basis.
questions.explanation: flex-grow values are RATIOS, not absolute pixel amounts or percentages of the container — only their relative proportion to each other (and to the total across all items) matters for how leftover space is shared.
questions.starter_code: /* container has 3 flex items with flex-grow 1, 2, 1 and 120px extra space */
questions.expected_solution:
.item1 { flex-grow: 1; } /* +30px */
.item2 { flex-grow: 2; } /* +60px */
.item3 { flex-grow: 1; } /* +30px */

questions.question: Which CSS property turns an element into a grid container?
questions.answer: display: grid
questions.explanation: Once an element has `display: grid`, its direct children become grid items placed into the grid tracks defined by properties like `grid-template-columns` and `grid-template-rows`.

questions.question: What does `grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr` define?
questions.answer: Three columns whose widths are distributed proportionally out of the available space in a 1:2:1 ratio (the middle column gets twice the width of each outer column).
questions.explanation: The `fr` (fraction) unit represents a share of the remaining free space in the grid container, similar in spirit to flex-grow ratios but applied directly to track sizing.

questions.question: What is the difference between `grid-gap` (`gap`) and using margins on grid items to create spacing?
questions.answer: `gap` creates spacing ONLY between grid tracks (rows/columns), never adding extra space at the outer edges of the grid; margins on individual items add space around each item, including at the grid's outer boundary, and can cause uneven spacing if not applied consistently to every item.
questions.explanation: Using `gap` is generally preferred for uniform grid spacing because it's declared once on the container and automatically applies consistently between every row/column without per-item margin bookkeeping.

questions.question: What does the `grid-template-areas` property let you do?
questions.answer: It lets you define a visual, named layout for the grid using a text-based ASCII-art-like syntax, then assign each grid item to a named area via `grid-area`, making complex layouts easy to read directly from the CSS.
questions.explanation: For example, defining areas `"header header" "sidebar main" "footer footer"` immediately communicates the page's layout structure without having to mentally map row/column line numbers.

questions.question: Why might `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))` be preferred over `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr))` for a responsive card layout, and what's the actual difference between them?
questions.answer: `auto-fit` collapses any empty (unfilled) tracks to zero width and lets the existing items stretch to fill the leftover space, so a row with fewer items than would fill the row still looks intentionally full-width; `auto-fill` keeps those empty tracks at their minimum size (as invisible placeholders), which can leave visible gaps rather than letting fewer items expand to fill the row.
questions.explanation: Both compute how many columns of at least 200px fit in the available width, but they diverge specifically when there are FEWER actual items than the number of columns that would fit — auto-fit reclaims that leftover track space for the real items, auto-fill does not.

questions.question: What CSS at-rule is used to apply styles conditionally based on device characteristics like viewport width?
questions.answer: @media
questions.explanation: A media query like `@media (max-width: 600px) { ... }` applies its enclosed rules only when the current viewport matches the specified condition, forming the basis of responsive design.

questions.question: What is the difference between `max-width` and `min-width` in a media query?
questions.answer: `(max-width: 600px)` matches when the viewport is 600px or narrower (commonly used for mobile-specific overrides); `(min-width: 600px)` matches when the viewport is 600px or wider (commonly used as the entry point for progressively larger layouts).
questions.explanation: A 'mobile-first' responsive strategy typically writes base styles for small screens, then layers on `min-width` media queries to add complexity as the viewport grows, rather than starting from desktop and using `max-width` to strip things away.

questions.question: Why does a page that looks correctly responsive in desktop browser dev tools sometimes render as a tiny, zoomed-out desktop layout on an actual mobile device?
questions.answer: The page is missing the viewport meta tag (`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`); without it, mobile browsers assume a wide desktop-like virtual viewport (often 980px) and shrink the whole page to fit the screen, which media queries alone cannot fix since they measure that same (wrong) virtual viewport width.
questions.explanation: Media queries evaluate against the CSS viewport width, which the viewport meta tag is what actually sets equal to the device's real width in the first place — without it, `(max-width: 600px)` may simply never match on a phone because the virtual viewport reports a much larger width.

questions.question: What is the difference between fixed units like `px` and relative units like `rem` when building a responsive layout?
questions.answer: `px` is an absolute unit that doesn't change based on any surrounding context, while `rem` is relative to the root (<html>) element's font size, so scaling the root font size (e.g. via a user's browser zoom/accessibility settings, or a media query that changes root font size) proportionally scales every `rem`-based measurement across the page at once.
questions.explanation: Using `rem` for spacing/typography is a common responsive technique because a single media query change to the root font-size can rescale an entire design's spacing/text proportionally, which would require touching many individual `px` values otherwise.

questions.question: What is 'container queries' and how do they differ from traditional media queries for building reusable responsive components?
questions.answer: Container queries (`@container`) let an element's styles respond to the size of its nearest ANCESTOR CONTAINER rather than the entire viewport, which media queries are limited to; this means the same component can adapt its layout differently depending on where it's placed (e.g. a sidebar vs a main content area) rather than only reacting to the overall screen size.
questions.explanation: This solves a long-standing limitation of component-based responsive design: a card component that should look different when it's narrow (in a sidebar) versus wide (in a main grid) couldn't previously know its own rendered width via CSS alone — only the viewport's width via `@media` — forcing that logic into JavaScript instead.

questions.question: Which CSS color function lets you specify a color with an alpha (transparency) channel using RGB values?
questions.answer: rgba()
questions.explanation: `rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5)` specifies red at 50% opacity; the equivalent for HSL-based colors with alpha is `hsla()`, and modern CSS also allows a slash syntax like `rgb(255 0 0 / 50%)`.

questions.question: What is the difference between an absolute length unit like `px` and a relative length unit like `em`?
questions.answer: `px` always represents the same fixed physical-ish size regardless of context; `em` is relative to the FONT SIZE of the current element (or its parent, for some properties), so the same `em` value renders differently depending on the surrounding font size.
questions.explanation: Because `em` compounds with nested elements that each set their own font-size (each `em` is relative to its own element's computed font-size), unexpected multiplicative scaling in deeply nested components is a common `em` pitfall that `rem` (always relative to the root) avoids.

questions.question: What is the difference between the `rem` and `em` units?
questions.answer: `rem` is always relative to the root (<html>) element's font size, regardless of nesting depth; `em` is relative to the font size of the CURRENT element (which itself may be inherited/scaled from its parent), so `em` values can compound unpredictably in deeply nested structures while `rem` values stay consistent and predictable.
questions.explanation: This is why `rem` is generally preferred for global spacing/typography scales, while `em` remains useful specifically when you WANT a value to scale relative to its own element's font size (e.g. padding that should grow/shrink along with a button's own text size).

questions.question: What does the `vw` and `vh` unit each represent?
questions.answer: `1vw` equals 1% of the current viewport's width, and `1vh` equals 1% of the current viewport's height; both update dynamically if the viewport is resized.
questions.explanation: These units are commonly used for full-viewport layouts (e.g. `height: 100vh` for a hero section that always fills the visible screen), though on mobile browsers `vh` can behave unexpectedly due to the address bar showing/hiding and changing the effective viewport height.

questions.question: A component sets `font-size: 1.5em` and is nested three levels deep inside other elements that each also set `font-size: 1.5em`. Why does its rendered text end up much larger than 1.5× the base size, and how would using `rem` instead avoid this?
questions.answer: Because `em` is relative to the immediately enclosing element's font size, each nested `1.5em` COMPOUNDS with the one above it: after three levels the effective scale is 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.5 ≈ 3.375× the root size, not 1.5×; using `rem` instead would make every one of those declarations relative to the fixed root font-size directly, so each would independently render at exactly 1.5× the root regardless of nesting depth.
questions.explanation: This compounding behavior is one of the most common real-world `em` bugs in component-based UIs where the same class/style might get applied at varying nesting depths.

questions.question: Which CSS property controls the space between lines of text within an element?
questions.answer: line-height
questions.explanation: `line-height` sets the height of each line box; a unitless value (e.g. `line-height: 1.5`) is generally recommended because it scales proportionally with the element's own font-size rather than compounding like some other relative units.

questions.question: What does the `font-weight` property control?
questions.answer: The thickness/boldness of the rendered text, using either keywords (`normal`, `bold`) or numeric values from 100 (thin) to 900 (black/heavy) if the font family provides those weights.
questions.explanation: If a numeric weight isn't actually available in the loaded font file, browsers will typically substitute the closest available weight or synthetically embolden the text, which can look different across browsers/OSes.

questions.question: What is the CSS `font-family` fallback stack for, e.g. `font-family: "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif`?
questions.answer: It lists fonts in order of preference; the browser tries each one in sequence and uses the first that is actually available/installed/loaded, falling back to the next if not, ending in a generic family (like `sans-serif`) as a guaranteed final fallback.
questions.explanation: This ensures reasonable typography even if a specific custom or licensed font fails to load (e.g. slow network, blocked request), rather than falling back to an arbitrary, possibly ugly, browser default.

questions.question: What does `@font-face` allow you to do, and what is `font-display: swap` used for alongside it?
questions.answer: `@font-face` lets you load and register a custom web font file so it can be referenced by name in `font-family`; `font-display: swap` tells the browser to render text immediately using a fallback font and then swap in the custom font once it finishes loading, rather than leaving text invisible (a 'flash of invisible text') while waiting.
questions.explanation: Without `font-display: swap` (or similar), many browsers historically hid text for a short timeout while a custom web font downloaded, which hurts perceived performance; `swap` prioritizes showing SOME text immediately over waiting for the exact intended font.

questions.question: Why can setting `line-height: 20px` (an absolute value) on a base/body style cause subtle layout bugs in child elements that use different font sizes, compared to using a unitless `line-height: 1.5`?
questions.answer: An absolute `line-height` is INHERITED as that fixed computed pixel value, so a child with a much larger font-size (e.g. a heading) will inherit the same fixed 20px line-height, which can be too small for its larger text and cause lines to visually overlap; a unitless `line-height` is inherited as the RATIO itself, so each descendant computes its own proportional line-height based on its own font-size.
questions.explanation: This is one of the most cited reasons unitless line-height is the recommended default in CSS style guides — it inherits as a scale factor rather than a fixed cascaded pixel value, correctly adapting to descendants with different font sizes.

questions.question: What is the difference between a pseudo-class (like `:hover`) and a pseudo-element (like `::before`)?
questions.answer: A pseudo-class selects an element based on a special STATE or position it's in (e.g. being hovered, being the first child), while a pseudo-element lets you style/insert a specific SUB-PART of an element that doesn't exist as its own node in the DOM (e.g. the generated content before an element's actual content).
questions.explanation: The modern CSS spec formalizes this by using a single colon for pseudo-classes (`:hover`) and a double colon for pseudo-elements (`::before`), though browsers still accept the older single-colon syntax for the original four pseudo-elements for backward compatibility.
options: They are the same thing with different syntax
Pseudo-classes select element states; pseudo-elements target sub-parts of an element
Pseudo-elements select element states; pseudo-classes target sub-parts

questions.question: What does the `:hover` pseudo-class match?
questions.answer: An element while the user's pointer is positioned over it.
questions.explanation: It's commonly used for interactive feedback like changing a button's background color, but on touch devices without a true pointer, `:hover` behavior can be inconsistent or 'sticky' after a tap.

questions.question: What is the difference between `:nth-child(2)` and `:nth-of-type(2)`?
questions.answer: `:nth-child(2)` matches an element if it is the 2nd child of its parent, counting ALL sibling elements regardless of tag name; `:nth-of-type(2)` matches an element if it is the 2nd sibling of its SPECIFIC tag type, ignoring siblings of other tag names in the count.
questions.explanation:
This distinction matters when siblings of mixed tag types are interleaved — e.g. `p:nth-child(2)` might match nothing if the 2nd child overall happens to be a
, whereas `p:nth-of-type(2)` would still correctly find the 2nd

regardless of what's interspersed between the

elements.

questions.question: What must the `content` property be set to for a `::before` or `::after` pseudo-element to actually render, and why?
questions.answer: The `content` property must be explicitly set (even to an empty string `content: ""`), because `::before`/`::after` generate entirely new, otherwise-nonexistent boxes whose content is undefined until `content` supplies it — without it, the pseudo-element simply doesn't render at all.
questions.explanation: This is a common beginner mistake: adding styles like `background` or `border` to a `::before` selector has no visible effect if `content` was never set, since there's no generated box to apply those styles to yet.

questions.question: What is the practical difference between `:focus` and `:focus-visible`, and why was `:focus-visible` introduced?
questions.answer: `:focus` matches ANY focused element regardless of how it was focused (mouse click, tap, or keyboard); `:focus-visible` only matches when the browser's heuristics determine the focus indicator should be shown — typically for keyboard navigation, not for a mouse click — letting you show a visible focus ring only when it's actually useful (keyboard users) without an unwanted ring appearing every time a mouse user clicks a button.
questions.explanation: `:focus-visible` was introduced specifically to resolve the long-standing tension between accessibility (keyboard users NEED a visible focus indicator to know where they are) and visual design preference (many designers disliked the focus ring appearing on every mouse click), letting both needs be met without JavaScript workarounds that used to be common (like adding a 'user-is-tabbing' class via JS).

questions.question: What CSS property specifies which property changes should animate smoothly over time when their value changes, and how long that should take?
questions.answer: transition
questions.explanation: `transition: background-color 0.3s ease;` means changes to `background-color` (e.g. triggered by `:hover` or a class toggle) animate smoothly over 0.3 seconds instead of changing instantly.

questions.question: What is the main difference between CSS `transition` and CSS `animation`?
questions.answer: `transition` only animates a property between two states (its starting value and an end value triggered by some change, like `:hover`), requiring an external trigger; `animation` (with `@keyframes`) can define multiple intermediate steps and can run automatically, repeat, or reverse without needing a state-change trigger.
questions.explanation: This makes `animation` the right tool for self-running, looping, or multi-step effects (like a loading spinner), while `transition` is simpler and better suited for one-off state-change feedback (like a button's hover color change).

questions.question: Why are `transform` and `opacity` considered the most performance-friendly properties to animate, compared to properties like `width` or `top`?
questions.answer: Animating `transform` and `opacity` can typically be handled entirely by the browser's compositor on the GPU without triggering layout (reflow) or paint recalculation, whereas animating `width`, `height`, `top`, or `left` forces the browser to recompute layout for the element (and often its siblings) on every frame, which is far more expensive.
questions.explanation: This is why smooth 60fps animations (like sliding/scaling a modal in) are typically implemented with `transform: translateX()`/`scale()` rather than animating `left`/`width` directly, even though they can achieve visually similar effects.

questions.question: What do the percentage values inside an `@keyframes` rule represent?
questions.answer: Each percentage represents a point in the animation's total duration (0% = the start, 100% = the end), at which the specified property values should be reached; the browser interpolates smoothly between each defined keyframe.
questions.explanation: You can define any number of intermediate keyframes (e.g. `0%`, `50%`, `100%`) to create multi-step animations, not just a simple start/end transition.

questions.question: A CSS transition is applied via `transition: all 0.3s;` on hover, but the element's size visibly 'jumps' instantly when its `display` changes from `none` to `block` as part of the same hover state change, instead of fading in smoothly. Why can't `display` be transitioned?
questions.answer: `display` is not an animatable/interpolatable property — it has discrete values (`none`, `block`, `flex`, etc.) with no meaningful intermediate state for the browser to interpolate between, so it always changes instantly regardless of any `transition` declaration; to fade an element in/out, you typically transition `opacity` (and sometimes `visibility` with a delay) instead, keeping `display` changes separate or avoided entirely.
questions.explanation: This is a common gotcha: `transition: all` gives the illusion that every property will animate, but only properties with a defined, continuous interpolation path between two values (like numbers, colors, lengths, transforms) can actually be transitioned — discrete/keyword-only properties like `display` cannot.

questions.question: Which CSS `transform` function resizes an element without affecting the document's layout flow?
questions.answer: scale()
questions.explanation: `transform: scale(1.5)` visually enlarges an element by 1.5x, but — like all transform functions — it does so purely visually, without changing the space the element reserves in the surrounding layout, unlike changing `width`/`height` directly.

questions.question: What does `transform: rotate(45deg)` do to an element?
questions.answer: It visually rotates the element 45 degrees clockwise around its transform origin (by default, the element's center).
questions.explanation: Because it's a transform, the rotation is purely visual and doesn't affect how the element participates in layout — surrounding elements are unaffected by the rotation, even if the rotated box now visually overlaps them.

questions.question: What is the `transform-origin` property, and what does changing it affect?
questions.answer: It sets the point around which transform functions like `rotate()` and `scale()` are applied (the default is the center of the element, `50% 50%`); changing it — for example to `top left` — makes rotations/scaling pivot around that corner instead of the center.
questions.explanation: This matters a lot for animations like a 'flip' or 'grow from a button' effect, where the pivot point needs to visually match where the effect should appear to originate from.

questions.question: Why is `transform: translateX(20px)` generally preferred over `margin-left: 20px` for animating an element's horizontal position?
questions.answer: `translateX` is a compositor-only operation the browser can typically run on the GPU without triggering layout recalculation, while animating `margin-left` forces a layout reflow on every frame since it changes the element's actual box position in the flow, which is significantly more expensive for smooth animation performance.
questions.explanation: This is the same category of performance advantage `transform`/`opacity` have over layout-affecting properties in general — `translate` moves the already-painted layer around visually rather than recalculating where the box sits in the document.

questions.question: An element has `transform: translate(20px, 0)` applied. Does this affect the space it occupies in the document layout, and would a sibling element positioned right after it visually shift to accommodate the move?
questions.answer: No — `transform` never affects layout at all; the element's ORIGINAL layout box (the space it reserves among its siblings) stays exactly where it would have been without the transform, and only its painted, visual appearance is shifted. A sibling immediately after it will NOT shift to accommodate the translated position, and the translated element may end up visually overlapping that sibling.
questions.explanation: This is a fundamental and often-misunderstood property of CSS transforms: they operate purely in the paint/compositing stage, after layout has already been calculated, which is exactly what makes them cheap to animate but also means they cannot be used as a substitute for actually repositioning elements within the flow (that's what changing `margin`, `position` offsets, or flex/grid properties is for).

questions.question: What is the correct syntax to define a custom CSS property (CSS variable) named `--main-color`?
questions.answer: --main-color: #3498db;
questions.explanation: Custom properties are declared with a double-hyphen prefix inside a rule (commonly on `:root` for global scope) and are read elsewhere using the `var()` function, e.g. `color: var(--main-color);`.

questions.question: How do you read the value of a CSS custom property named `--spacing`?
questions.answer: var(--spacing)
questions.explanation: `var()` can also take a second argument as a fallback value, e.g. `var(--spacing, 16px)`, which is used if `--spacing` is not defined (or is invalid) in the current scope.

questions.question: Why are CSS custom properties (`--variable`) considered more powerful than Sass/SCSS variables for theming, despite Sass variables predating them?
questions.answer: CSS custom properties are LIVE and resolved at runtime in the browser based on the actual cascade/DOM, meaning they can be reassigned dynamically per-element or per-media-query and read/written from JavaScript (`element.style.setProperty`) without recompiling any stylesheet; Sass variables are compiled away entirely at BUILD time into static values, so changing a theme at runtime (e.g. a dark-mode toggle) requires re-shipping different compiled CSS or JS-driven class swapping instead.
questions.explanation: This runtime nature is exactly why CSS custom properties are the standard modern approach for things like light/dark theme toggles — you can flip a handful of `--variable` values on `:root` (or scope them differently per component) and every rule referencing them updates immediately, live, in the browser.

questions.question: What does it mean that CSS custom properties are inherited and can be overridden at different scopes in the DOM?
questions.answer: A custom property defined on an ancestor (commonly `:root` for a global default) is inherited by descendants and can be redeclared with a different value on any descendant element/selector, and everything further nested under THAT element will then see the new, more specific value instead — following the normal CSS cascade/inheritance rules.
questions.explanation: This lets you build component-scoped theming, e.g. a `.dark-panel { --text-color: white; }` rule that changes `--text-color` only within that panel's subtree, without affecting the rest of the page that still uses the root-level default.

questions.question: A page toggles dark mode by changing a class on the <body>, but a CSS custom property defined inside a deeply nested component's own stylesheet (with a hardcoded fallback) doesn't update. What's the likely cause?
questions.answer: The component is using `var(--theme-color, someHardcodedFallback)` where `--theme-color` is never actually redefined for the dark-mode class selector, so the fallback value is always used regardless of theme; the fix is to ensure the dark-mode class selector (e.g. `body.dark { --theme-color: white; }`) actually redeclares the SAME custom property name that the component consumes.
questions.explanation: The `var()` fallback only activates when the referenced custom property is truly undefined/invalid in that element's scope — if it resolves to SOME value (even an old/default one from `:root`) rather than being undefined, the fallback is never used, so a 'doesn't update' symptom is more likely a missing redeclaration for the dark theme scope than a fallback issue.

questions.question: Which of these properties is typically INHERITED by default from a parent to its children?
questions.answer: color
questions.explanation: Text-related properties like `color`, `font-family`, `font-size`, and `line-height` are inherited by default, while box-model properties like `margin`, `padding`, `border`, and `background` are NOT inherited by default.

questions.question: What CSS keyword value can be used on any property to explicitly force it to inherit its parent's computed value?
questions.answer: inherit
questions.explanation: This is useful for properties that are NOT inherited by default (like `border` or `background-color`), when you specifically want a child to match its parent's value rather than using the property's normal initial value.

questions.question: What are the four main factors CSS uses, in order, to resolve which of several conflicting declarations wins (the 'cascade')?
questions.answer: Origin & importance (e.g. user !important > author !important > author normal > user-agent default), then specificity, then order of appearance (later rules win ties), and inheritance/proximity is considered separately for property resolution when no direct declaration applies at all.
questions.explanation: Understanding this order explains counter-intuitive outcomes like a lower-specificity but `!important` rule beating a higher-specificity normal rule — importance is checked before specificity, not after.

questions.question: What does the `initial` keyword do when used as a CSS property value, and how is it different from `unset`?
questions.answer: `initial` resets a property to its specification-defined default value (ignoring any inheritance or cascade), regardless of whether that property is normally inherited; `unset` resets a property to `inherit` if it's normally an inherited property, or to `initial` if it's normally a non-inherited property — effectively acting as if no rule had ever been applied to it at all.
questions.explanation: `unset` is often more intuitive to reach for because it 'does the right thing' automatically based on the property's own default inheritance behavior, rather than requiring you to remember whether a given property is inherited or not.

questions.question: A deeply nested <span> unexpectedly renders with a `color` the developer never explicitly set on it or any of its direct ancestors up to a certain point. Tracing the cascade, what's the most likely explanation?
questions.answer: `color` is an inherited property, so the <span> is inheriting its computed value from the nearest ANCESTOR that DOES explicitly declare (or itself inherits) a non-default `color` — the actual source of the value could be several levels up the DOM tree, not necessarily the immediate parent, since inheritance passes the computed value down through every intermediate level that doesn't override it.
questions.explanation: This is a common debugging trap: because inheritance silently passes values down through any number of intermediate elements that don't redeclare the property, the actual 'culprit' rule can be far removed from the element exhibiting the unexpected style, requiring you to walk up the DOM in devtools to find where `color` was actually set.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a vendor prefix like `-webkit-` or `-moz-` on a CSS property?
questions.answer: It lets a browser engine ship an experimental or not-yet-standardized implementation of a CSS feature under a prefixed name, so it doesn't conflict with a potentially different final standardized behavior once the feature is finalized under its unprefixed name.
questions.explanation: For example `-webkit-transform` historically had to be used alongside the standard `transform` for older WebKit-based browsers before the unprefixed property was universally supported.
options: To let browsers ship experimental feature implementations without conflicting with the final standard

questions.question: What tool/service is commonly used to check which browsers support a given CSS feature before using it in production?
questions.answer: caniuse.com
questions.explanation: It provides up-to-date compatibility tables (including partial-support caveats) for CSS, HTML, and JS features across current and historical browser versions, which is essential for deciding whether a feature needs a fallback or prefix.

questions.question: What does the tool Autoprefixer do, and why is it usually preferred over manually writing vendor-prefixed CSS?
questions.answer: It's a build tool (often run via PostCSS) that automatically adds the necessary vendor-prefixed versions of CSS rules based on a configured browser support target (e.g. via a browserslist config), so developers write plain standard CSS and let tooling handle prefix maintenance.
questions.explanation: Manually maintaining prefixes is error-prone and becomes outdated as browser support changes over time; automating it via a build step keeps the source CSS clean and ensures prefixes are added/removed consistently as support requirements evolve.

questions.question: What is a CSS `@supports` rule used for?
questions.answer: It lets you conditionally apply a block of CSS only if the browser supports a specified property/value pair, allowing you to provide a fallback for browsers that don't support a newer feature (progressive enhancement) without relying on JavaScript feature detection.
questions.explanation: For example `@supports (display: grid) { ... }` lets you write Grid-based layout rules that only activate in Grid-supporting browsers, while a simpler fallback layout (e.g. using floats or flexbox) can be defined outside the `@supports` block for older browsers.

questions.question: A CSS feature works in Chrome and Edge during development but silently fails in Safari, with no console error at all. What is the most likely category of cause, and how would you diagnose it?
questions.answer: The feature (or a specific value/syntax variant of it) simply isn't supported in the version of Safari being tested, and CSS doesn't throw errors for unsupported/invalid declarations — the browser just silently ignores that one declaration and falls back to whatever value the property already had; diagnosing it means checking the feature's support table (e.g. on caniuse.com) for Safari specifically, and inspecting the computed styles in Safari's devtools to see the property was never applied at all.
questions.explanation: This 'silent failure' behavior is a deliberate part of CSS's error-recovery design — unrecognized declarations are simply skipped rather than breaking the rest of the stylesheet — which is exactly why cross-browser CSS bugs are so often invisible in the console and require checking computed styles per-browser instead.

questions.question: Which of these is the correct CSS syntax to set an element's text to red?
questions.answer: color: red;
questions.explanation: The `color` property controls text color in CSS; there is no `text-color` or `font-color` property.

questions.question: What is the difference between an inline style, an internal <style> block, and an external stylesheet?
questions.answer: An inline style is set via the `style` attribute directly on one element; an internal <style> block lives in the document's <head> and applies to that one page; an external stylesheet is a separate .css file linked via <link> and reusable across many pages.
questions.explanation: External stylesheets are generally preferred for maintainability and caching; inline styles have the highest specificity and are hardest to override or reuse.

questions.question: What does 'Cascading' in Cascading Style Sheets actually refer to?
questions.answer: It refers to the algorithm the browser uses to resolve conflicting style declarations for the same element/property, based on origin, specificity, and source order.
questions.explanation: Multiple stylesheets (browser default, user, author) and multiple rules can all target the same element; the cascade is the deterministic process that decides which one wins.

questions.question: Which CSS at-rule is used to import one stylesheet into another?
questions.answer: @import
questions.explanation: `@import url("other.css");` pulls in another stylesheet, though it's generally discouraged for performance since it blocks parallel downloading.
