questions.question: Why is `@import` at the top of a CSS file generally discouraged for production performance compared to multiple <link> tags in HTML?
questions.answer: `@import`-ed stylesheets are only discovered and requested after the importing stylesheet itself has been downloaded and parsed, creating a request waterfall, whereas multiple <link> tags in HTML can all be discovered and downloaded in parallel by the browser's preload scanner.
questions.explanation: This sequential-versus-parallel loading difference can meaningfully delay first paint on pages with several imported stylesheets.

questions.question: Which selector targets an element with a specific attribute value, e.g. all <input> elements with type="text"?
questions.answer: input[type="text"]
questions.explanation: Square-bracket attribute selectors match elements by the presence or exact/partial value of an HTML attribute.

questions.question: What is the difference between the CSS selectors `.item ~ .item` and `.item + .item`?
questions.answer: `+` (adjacent sibling) matches only an element immediately following another sibling with the given selector; `~` (general sibling) matches ANY later sibling that shares the same parent, not just the immediate next one.
questions.explanation: `.item + .item` would style only the second of two directly adjacent `.item`s, while `.item ~ .item` styles every `.item` after the first one, regardless of what's in between.

questions.question: What is the CSS specificity value (in the a-b-c-d model) of the selector `#header .nav a:hover`?
questions.answer: 0 ID (1), 2 classes/pseudo-classes (.nav and :hover), 1 element (a) - specificity (0,1,2,1).
questions.explanation: ID selectors count in the second-highest tier, classes/attribute-selectors/pseudo-classes in the third tier, and element/pseudo-element selectors in the lowest tier; specificity is compared tier by tier, not added as one number.

questions.question: Given `a { color: blue; }` and `a:visited { color: purple; }` both applying to a visited link, which color wins and why?
questions.code_snippet:
a { color: blue; }
a:visited { color: purple; }
questions.answer: Purple - `a:visited` has equal specificity to `a` plus one pseudo-class, making it MORE specific, so it wins regardless of source order here.
questions.explanation: Both rules target the same element type, but `:visited` adds a pseudo-class to the specificity count, giving it precedence over the bare `a` selector.

questions.question: What does the `:not()` pseudo-class do, and does it add to a selector's specificity?
questions.answer: `:not(selector)` matches elements that do NOT match the given inner selector; its own specificity contribution equals the specificity of whatever selector is passed inside it (not a flat pseudo-class weight).
questions.explanation: For example, `:not(.active)` contributes the specificity of a class selector, while `:not(#main)` contributes the specificity of an ID selector.

questions.question: Which CSS box-model layer sits directly outside the border and creates space between an element and its siblings?
questions.answer: margin
questions.explanation: Order from inside out is: content, padding, border, margin - margin is the outermost layer, controlling spacing to neighboring elements.

questions.question: What does `margin: 0 auto;` commonly accomplish on a block-level element with a fixed width?
questions.answer: It horizontally centers the element within its parent, by setting top/bottom margin to 0 and letting the browser distribute the remaining horizontal space equally on the left and right.
questions.explanation: This only centers horizontally (not vertically) and only works because the element has a defined width smaller than its parent's - a full-width block has no space left to distribute.

questions.question: What is 'margin collapsing' and which margins are affected by it?
questions.answer: When two block-level elements' vertical margins meet (e.g. one element's bottom margin touches the next element's top margin, or a parent and its first/last child's margins), the browser collapses them into a single margin equal to the LARGER of the two, rather than adding them.
questions.explanation: This applies only to vertical margins in normal flow, not horizontal margins, and not to elements using flexbox/grid layout or with padding/borders separating the margins.

questions.question: A parent <div> with only floated children inside it collapses to zero height, even though the floated children clearly have visible content. What CSS technique fixes this?
questions.buggy_code:
.parent { border: 1px solid black; }
.child { float: left; width: 100px; height: 100px; }
questions.fixed_code:
.parent { border: 1px solid black; overflow: auto; } /* or use a clearfix / display: flow-root */
.child { float: left; width: 100px; height: 100px; }
questions.answer: Floated elements are removed from normal document flow, so their parent doesn't automatically expand to contain their height; adding `overflow: auto` (or `display: flow-root`, or a clearfix) to the parent forces it to include floated content in its height calculation.
questions.explanation: This is the classic 'collapsing parent' problem that predates flexbox/grid, and `display: flow-root` is the modern, side-effect-free fix purpose-built for it.

questions.question: Can padding have a negative value in CSS?
questions.answer: No - unlike margin, `padding` values must be zero or positive; negative padding is invalid and ignored by browsers.
questions.explanation: Margin can be negative (to pull elements closer together or overlap them), but padding conceptually represents space inside the border, which can't be negative.

questions.question: Which `position` value removes an element from normal document flow and positions it relative to the browser viewport, staying fixed even when the page scrolls?
questions.answer: fixed
questions.explanation: `position: fixed` anchors to the viewport (not the document), so the element stays in the same screen position during scrolling, unlike `absolute` which is anchored to its positioned ancestor.

questions.question: What CSS property/value combination establishes a 'stacking context' that affects how `z-index` is interpreted for an element's descendants?
questions.answer: Several trigger it, including `position` with a value other than `static` combined with a `z-index` other than `auto`, `opacity` less than 1, and `transform`/`filter` with a non-none value.
questions.explanation: Once a stacking context is created, z-index comparisons for its children are scoped WITHIN that context - a child with `z-index: 9999` still can't visually escape above elements outside a lower-z-index parent stacking context.

questions.question: What is the effect of `position: relative` on an element if no `top`/`left`/`right`/`bottom` offsets are specified?
questions.answer: Visually nothing changes (the element stays in its normal-flow position) but it now establishes a positioning context for any absolutely-positioned descendants and is affected by `z-index`.
questions.explanation: This 'do-nothing-visually but change positioning context' behavior is a very common CSS pattern used specifically to scope a child's `position: absolute` to that container.

questions.question: A `position: sticky` element is supposed to stick to the top of the viewport while scrolling within a container, but it never sticks at all - it just scrolls away like a normal static element. What are two common causes?
questions.answer: (1) An ancestor has `overflow: hidden/scroll/auto` which clips the sticky context, or (2) the sticky element's container isn't tall enough for scrolling within it to ever leave room for the 'stuck' state, or (3) no `top`/`bottom` offset was specified at all.
questions.explanation: `position: sticky` requires an explicit threshold offset (like `top: 0`) and can be silently broken by any ancestor that clips overflow between the sticky element and the actual scrolling container.

questions.question: What does `position: absolute` position an element relative to, if no ancestor has a non-static position?
questions.answer: The initial containing block, which is effectively the viewport/document's root, if no positioned (`relative`/`absolute`/`fixed`/`sticky`) ancestor exists.
questions.explanation: This is why developers often add `position: relative` to a wrapping container - to intentionally scope where an absolutely positioned child anchors, instead of it escaping to the whole page.

questions.question: Which `display` value hides an element completely while still preserving screen-reader-relevant semantics like ARIA live announcements for elements around it (though the hidden element itself is excluded)?
questions.answer: display: none
questions.explanation: `display: none` removes the element from layout AND the accessibility tree entirely; `visibility: hidden` still occupies layout space and is treated slightly differently by some AT; `opacity: 0` keeps it fully interactive and in the accessibility tree.

questions.question: What is the key layout difference between `display: inline` and `display: inline-block`?
questions.answer: `inline-block` allows an element to have an explicit width/height and respects vertical margin/padding for layout purposes, while plain `inline` ignores width/height and doesn't affect vertical layout spacing the same way.
questions.explanation: This is why `inline-block` was historically used for building horizontal navigation items or button-like elements that needed a fixed size while still flowing inline with text.

questions.question: What does `display: contents` do to an element?
questions.answer: It makes the element itself disappear from the box-generation/rendering tree entirely (no box of its own), while its children are 'promoted' to render as if they were direct children of the element's own parent.
questions.explanation: This is useful for wrapper elements needed for JS/semantic reasons that would otherwise interfere with a parent's grid/flex layout of its 'real' children.

questions.question: An element with `display: contents` is expected to still respond to its own `background-color` and `border` styles, but they simply don't appear. Why?
questions.buggy_code: .wrapper { display: contents; background: red; border: 2px solid black; }
questions.fixed_code: /* display: contents removes the box entirely - background/border must go on the children or a different wrapping approach must be used */
questions.answer: `display: contents` removes the element's own box entirely, so properties that only make sense on a box (background, border, padding, size) have no box left to apply to and are simply not rendered.
questions.explanation: Only properties that don't depend on having a box (like `color`, which is inherited) still take effect on the contents; anything requiring an actual rendered box is a no-op.

questions.question: Which flex container property controls whether flex items wrap onto multiple lines when they don't fit?
questions.answer: flex-wrap
questions.explanation: `flex-wrap: wrap` allows items to flow onto new lines; the default `nowrap` forces them to shrink/overflow onto one line.

questions.question: What does `align-self` do on an individual flex item, and how does it relate to the container's `align-items`?
questions.answer: `align-self` overrides the container's `align-items` value for that ONE specific item on the cross axis, letting a single item align differently from its siblings.
questions.explanation: This is the per-item escape hatch for cross-axis alignment, exactly analogous to how `justify-self` works for individual grid items.

questions.question: What is the difference between the 'main axis' and 'cross axis' in Flexbox?
questions.answer: The main axis is the direction items are laid out along (set by `flex-direction`, e.g. horizontal for `row`), and the cross axis is perpendicular to it - `justify-content` aligns along the main axis, `align-items`/`align-content` align along the cross axis.
questions.explanation: Understanding which property controls which axis is the most common source of Flexbox confusion, especially after switching `flex-direction` from row to column (which swaps which axis is which visually).

questions.question: A flex container has `flex-direction: column` and its child has `align-items: center` set incorrectly on the CHILD instead of the container. What visual effect, if any, does this misplaced property have?
questions.code_snippet:
.container { display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
.child { align-items: center; }
questions.answer: None - `align-items` only has an effect when set on a flex CONTAINER (it controls how that container aligns its own children); setting it on a flex item that isn't itself a flex container with children of its own does nothing.
questions.explanation: This is a common beginner mistake: `align-items`/`justify-content` are container-level properties, while `align-self` is the item-level equivalent for cross-axis alignment.

questions.question: What does setting `flex: 1` as shorthand actually expand to?
questions.answer: `flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 0%;` - meaning the item can grow and shrink freely, starting from an effective zero base size before growth is distributed.
questions.explanation: This differs subtly from `flex: auto` (basis: auto, using the item's content size as the starting point before growth/shrink) - `flex: 1` is the common 'take equal available space' pattern.

questions.question: Which CSS Grid property defines the size of the gap between rows and columns simultaneously?
options: Both `gap` and `grid-gap` work (gap is the modern name)
questions.answer: Both `gap` and `grid-gap` work (gap is the modern name)
questions.explanation: `grid-gap` was the original property name; `gap` is now the standardized, unprefixed name that also works for Flexbox, and is preferred in new code.

questions.question: What does the `grid-column: 1 / 3;` shorthand do to a grid item?
questions.answer: It makes the item span from grid column line 1 to grid column line 3, meaning it occupies two column tracks (columns 1 and 2) instead of just one.
questions.explanation: Grid line numbers refer to the lines BETWEEN tracks, not the tracks themselves, so `1 / 3` spans across two tracks, not three.

questions.question: What is the difference between explicit and implicit grid tracks?
questions.answer: Explicit tracks are the rows/columns you define directly with `grid-template-columns`/`grid-template-rows`; implicit tracks are automatically created by the browser to hold extra items that don't fit into the explicitly defined grid, sized by `grid-auto-rows`/`grid-auto-columns`.
questions.explanation: This matters when a grid has more items than defined cells - the browser doesn't discard the overflow, it silently creates new implicit tracks (defaulting to `auto` size unless configured otherwise).

questions.question: Two grid items are given overlapping `grid-area` placements by mistake. What happens visually, and how would you detect this bug using browser devtools?
questions.buggy_code:
.item-a { grid-area: 1 / 1 / 2 / 2; }
.item-b { grid-area: 1 / 1 / 2 / 2; }
questions.fixed_code:
.item-a { grid-area: 1 / 1 / 2 / 2; }
.item-b { grid-area: 1 / 2 / 2 / 3; }
questions.answer: Both items render stacked on top of each other in the same cell (CSS Grid allows overlap by design, unlike a table); this is easiest to spot using the browser's Grid Inspector overlay, which visually outlines each named/numbered track and area.
questions.explanation: Grid doesn't prevent or warn about overlapping placements - it's a valid, sometimes intentional feature (e.g. layering a caption over an image), so accidental overlaps require visual/devtools inspection to catch.

questions.question: What does the `minmax(100px, 1fr)` function do when used inside `grid-template-columns`?
questions.answer: It sets a track's size to be at least 100px but allowed to grow up to take an equal fractional share (`1fr`) of remaining space - never smaller than the minimum, never larger than the flexible maximum allows.
questions.explanation: This is the core building block of the common responsive-grid pattern `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))`, which lets columns reflow automatically at different viewport widths.

questions.question: Which media feature targets styles based on the device's orientation (portrait vs landscape)?
questions.answer: orientation
questions.explanation: `@media (orientation: portrait) { ... }` applies styles only when the viewport is taller than it is wide.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'mobile-first' and 'desktop-first' responsive design approaches, in terms of how media queries are typically written?
questions.answer: Mobile-first writes base styles for small screens, then uses `min-width` media queries to progressively add complexity for larger screens; desktop-first writes base styles for large screens, then uses `max-width` queries to simplify/adjust for smaller ones.
questions.explanation: Mobile-first is generally preferred because it forces prioritizing essential content/layout first and tends to produce leaner CSS for the most constrained devices.

questions.question: What does the CSS `clamp()` function do, and how does it relate to responsive design without media queries?
questions.answer: `clamp(min, preferred, max)` picks a value that scales fluidly with something like viewport width, but never goes below `min` or above `max` - letting a single declaration handle what might otherwise require several media-query breakpoints.
questions.explanation: For example, `font-size: clamp(1rem, 2vw, 1.5rem)` scales fluidly between two bounds instead of jumping abruptly at fixed breakpoints.

questions.question: A responsive layout looks correct at every width when manually resizing the desktop browser window, but breaks on an actual phone even though matching media queries exist. The `<meta viewport>` tag is present and correct. What's another common culprit?
questions.answer: Content wider than the viewport forcing horizontal scroll - most commonly a fixed-width element (an image without `max-width: 100%`, a table, or a hardcoded `width: 600px` box) that doesn't shrink, which stretches the whole layout's effective viewport width beyond the device's actual screen width.
questions.explanation: A single overflowing element can silently widen the entire page's layout viewport, making every media query 'think' it's at a wider breakpoint than the physical screen actually is.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `prefers-color-scheme` as a media feature?
questions.answer: It lets CSS detect and respond to the user's OS-level light/dark mode preference, e.g. `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { ... }`, without any JavaScript.
questions.explanation: This is one of several 'user preference' media features (alongside `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-contrast`) that let sites respect system-level accessibility/comfort settings automatically.

questions.question: Which CSS unit is always relative to the root (<html>) element's font size, regardless of nesting depth?
questions.answer: rem
questions.explanation: `rem` ('root em') always resolves against the <html> element's font-size, unlike `em` which is relative to the current element's own (possibly inherited/compounded) font-size.

questions.question: What does the CSS color keyword `currentColor` refer to when used as a value for another property, e.g. `border-color: currentColor`?
questions.answer: It refers to the computed value of that same element's `color` property, letting properties like `border`, `box-shadow`, or SVG `fill` automatically match the element's text color without repeating a color value.
questions.explanation: This is especially useful for icons/borders that should always match whatever text color is currently in effect, including through hover states or theme changes.

questions.question: What is the difference between an absolute length unit and a relative length unit in CSS, and give one example of each?
questions.answer: An absolute unit (like `px`, `pt`, `cm`) always represents a fixed physical/pixel size regardless of context; a relative unit (like `em`, `rem`, `%`, `vw`) is computed relative to some other value (parent font-size, viewport size, etc.).
questions.explanation: Relative units are generally preferred for responsive/accessible design since they adapt to user zoom settings and different screen sizes automatically.

questions.question: A user increases their browser's default font size for accessibility, but a component styled entirely in `px` for font-size and padding doesn't visually scale at all, unlike the rest of the page. Why, and what's the fix?
questions.answer: `px` values are fixed absolute units that ignore the user's font-size preference entirely; switching the component's font-size/padding/margins to `rem` (or `em`) makes them scale proportionally with the user's chosen base font size.
questions.explanation: This is a real accessibility issue - users who rely on larger default text sizes for readability get an inconsistent, sometimes illegibly small experience in px-styled components.

questions.question: What do the `hsl()` color function's three arguments represent?
questions.answer: Hue (a degree on the color wheel, 0-360), Saturation (a percentage, 0% = gray to 100% = full color), and Lightness (a percentage, 0% = black to 100% = white).
questions.explanation: HSL is often more intuitive for programmatically generating color variations (like a lighter/darker shade) than RGB, since you can just adjust the Lightness value directly.

questions.question: Which CSS property controls whether text is displayed in uppercase, lowercase, or capitalized, without changing the underlying HTML content?
questions.answer: text-transform
questions.explanation: `text-transform: uppercase` (etc.) is purely a visual/display transformation - the actual text content and its case remain unchanged in the DOM/source.

questions.question: What does the `letter-spacing` property control, and what's a common use case for a small negative value?
questions.answer: It controls the extra space added between characters; a small negative value (e.g. `-0.02em`) is commonly used to tighten large display headings, which can otherwise look loosely spaced at big font sizes.
questions.explanation: Positive values are more common for improving legibility in all-caps or small text; negative values are a typographic refinement typically reserved for large headline text.

questions.question: What is a 'web-safe font', and why does it matter less today than it used to?
questions.answer: A web-safe font is one assumed to be pre-installed on most operating systems (like Arial, Times New Roman, Georgia), so it renders consistently without needing to be downloaded; it matters less today because `@font-face` lets any site reliably deliver custom web fonts to virtually all users.
questions.explanation: Before widespread @font-face support, designers were largely limited to a small shared pool of fonts guaranteed to already be on a user's system.

questions.question: A custom web font loaded via `@font-face` causes a noticeable flash where text is invisible for a second before the font appears (FOIT - flash of invisible text). What `font-display` value fixes this by showing a fallback font immediately instead?
questions.buggy_code: @font-face { font-family: 'Custom'; src: url('custom.woff2'); }
questions.fixed_code: @font-face { font-family: 'Custom'; src: url('custom.woff2'); font-display: swap; }
questions.answer: `font-display: swap;` - this tells the browser to render text immediately using a fallback font, then swap to the custom font once it finishes loading, instead of hiding text while waiting.
questions.explanation: Without `font-display`, browsers historically defaulted to a 'block' period where text is invisible until the custom font loads or a timeout is hit - `swap` eliminates that invisible period entirely.

questions.question: What is the difference between `white-space: nowrap` and `overflow-wrap: break-word`?
questions.answer: `white-space: nowrap` prevents text from wrapping onto a new line at all (it overflows or requires scrolling instead); `overflow-wrap: break-word` still allows wrapping but permits breaking in the MIDDLE of an unbreakable long word if needed to avoid overflow.
questions.explanation: They solve different problems: nowrap forces single-line text, while overflow-wrap is a safety net for wrapping text that still contains one very long unbreakable token (like a URL).

questions.question: Which pseudo-class matches an element that is the only child of its parent?
questions.answer: :only-child
questions.explanation: `:only-child` matches an element that has no sibling elements at all, distinct from `:first-child` which matches even when siblings exist.

questions.question: What is the difference between `:first-child` and `:first-of-type`?
questions.answer: `:first-child` matches an element only if it is literally the first child (of any type) of its parent; `:first-of-type` matches the first occurrence of that specific element type among its siblings, regardless of what other element types come before it.
questions.explanation:
E.g. `p:first-of-type` matches the first

even if a

comes before it in the same parent, but `p:first-child` would NOT match in that case since the

isn't literally the first child.

questions.question: What does the `:is()` pseudo-class function do, and how does it simplify writing selectors?
questions.answer: `:is()` lets you group a list of selectors so a shared trailing part of the selector doesn't need to be repeated - e.g. `:is(header, main, footer) a` instead of writing `header a, main a, footer a` separately.
questions.explanation: A key detail: `:is()` takes on the specificity of its MOST specific argument, which can matter when comparing against other rules.

questions.question: A `::before` pseudo-element is added to inject a decorative icon before some text, but the icon never appears even though the CSS rule seems correctly targeted and has no typos in the property names. What single required property/value is most likely missing?
questions.answer: The `content` property - `::before`/`::after` pseudo-elements are not generated at all unless `content` is explicitly set (even `content: "";` for an empty string is enough), regardless of any other styling applied.
questions.explanation: This is the single most common mistake with generated content pseudo-elements: every other style (background, size, position) is irrelevant if `content` is omitted, since the pseudo-element box simply doesn't exist without it.

questions.question: What is the difference between `:target` and `:focus` pseudo-classes?
questions.answer: `:target` matches an element whose `id` matches the current URL fragment (e.g. `#section2`), useful for styling a linked-to section; `:focus` matches whatever element currently has keyboard/programmatic focus, unrelated to the URL.
questions.explanation: `:target` is driven entirely by navigation/URL state, while `:focus` is driven by user interaction or scripted `.focus()` calls.

questions.question: Which property controls the acceleration curve (e.g. ease, linear, ease-in-out) of a CSS transition or animation?
questions.answer: transition-timing-function
questions.explanation: This (or `animation-timing-function` for @keyframes animations) controls the rate of change over the transition's duration, not just its overall speed.

questions.question: What does `animation-fill-mode: forwards` do to an element after a CSS @keyframes animation completes?
questions.answer: It makes the element retain the computed style values from the animation's LAST keyframe, instead of snapping back to its original pre-animation styles once the animation ends.
questions.explanation: Without `forwards` (the default is `none`), an element visually reverts to its original CSS state the instant the animation finishes, which can look like a jarring 'snap back'.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `prefers-reduced-motion` media feature in the context of animations?
questions.answer: It detects a user's OS-level accessibility setting requesting minimal motion, letting a site disable or simplify animations/transitions for users prone to motion sickness or vestibular disorders.
questions.explanation: `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { * { animation: none !important; } }` is a common pattern to respect this preference site-wide.

questions.question: A `transition: width 0.3s;` is added to an element whose width changes via a class toggle, but the transition never visibly animates - the width just jumps instantly. The class toggle logic itself is confirmed working. What's a common cause?
questions.buggy_code:
.box { width: 100px; transition: width 0.3s; }
.box.expanded { width: auto; }
questions.fixed_code:
.box { width: 100px; transition: width 0.3s; }
.box.expanded { width: 300px; }
questions.answer: Transitioning to/from `width: auto` doesn't animate in most browsers, because `auto` isn't a fixed, interpolatable value the browser can compute a smooth intermediate size for - the fix is to transition between two explicit pixel/percentage values instead.
questions.explanation: This is a well-known CSS transition limitation: `auto`, and a handful of other keyword values, can't be smoothly interpolated, so the browser just jumps directly to the final computed value.

questions.question: What is the difference between `animation-iteration-count: infinite` and setting a specific number like `3`?
questions.answer: `infinite` repeats the animation forever with no natural end; a specific number like `3` plays the animation exactly that many times and then stops (applying `animation-fill-mode` rules, if any, after the last iteration).
questions.explanation: This property only controls repetition count - it says nothing about direction (use `animation-direction` for alternating/reverse playback across iterations).

questions.question: Which `transform` function skews an element along the X and/or Y axis?
questions.answer: skew()
questions.explanation: `skew(xAngle, yAngle)` (or `skewX()`/`skewY()` individually) distorts an element's shape along an axis, unlike `rotate()` which turns it rigidly.

questions.question: What is the difference between `transform: scale(2)` and setting `width`/`height` to double an element's original size?
questions.answer: `scale(2)` visually enlarges the rendered element (including its content) without changing its actual layout box size that siblings react to, while changing `width`/`height` genuinely resizes the box and can push/reflow surrounding content.
questions.explanation: This is why `transform` is preferred for animations - it doesn't trigger layout recalculation for the rest of the page, only a compositing-layer visual change.

questions.question: What does `transform-style: preserve-3d` do, and in what context does it matter?
questions.answer: It tells child elements to render in true 3D space relative to their parent (preserving perspective/depth for nested 3D transforms), instead of the default `flat` behavior where children are flattened into the plane of the parent.
questions.explanation: This matters for effects like 3D card flips or cube rotations where multiple nested transformed elements need to maintain real 3D relationships with each other, not just each independently.

questions.question: An element with `transform: translateZ(0)` was added purely as a hack with no other 3D transform needed, and the developer isn't sure why it's there or if it's safe to remove. What was it likely doing?
questions.answer: It was likely forcing the browser to promote the element onto its own GPU-composited layer ('hardware acceleration hack'), historically used to fix janky scrolling/animation performance on that element - removing it may or may not still be necessary depending on current browser optimization heuristics and whether the original performance issue still exists.
questions.explanation: Modern browsers are much better at automatically deciding what to composite, so this once-common trick is less necessary than it used to be, but it can still occasionally help with specific animation jank.

questions.question: Does applying `transform: rotate(45deg)` to an element change the space it occupies in the normal document flow, affecting where sibling elements are positioned?
questions.answer: No - `transform` never affects layout/flow; siblings are positioned exactly as if the transform wasn't applied, even though the element visually now overlaps or extends beyond its original box.
questions.explanation: This is a defining characteristic of the `transform` property (shared with `translate`/`scale`/`rotate`) - it's purely a visual/paint-time effect, computed after layout has already been determined.

questions.question: What is the correct way to provide a fallback value if a CSS custom property is undefined?
questions.answer: var(--color, blue)
questions.explanation: The second argument to `var()` is the fallback value used only if `--color` is not defined (or is an invalid value) in the current cascade.

questions.question: Can a CSS custom property's value be a partial value, like just a number used later inside a `calc()`?
questions.answer: Yes - custom properties can hold arbitrary token sequences, not just full valid CSS values, so `--gap: 8;` used as `margin: calc(var(--gap) * 1px)` is valid.
questions.explanation: This flexibility (custom properties are essentially just substituted text tokens at computed-value time) is part of why they're more powerful than preprocessor variables, which are resolved at compile time into fixed values.

questions.question: Why can CSS custom properties respond to media queries or class toggles at runtime in the browser, unlike Sass/SCSS variables?
questions.answer: CSS custom properties are resolved live by the browser as part of the normal cascade (inheritance, specificity, and being redefined per selector), so redefining `--theme-color` inside a media query or a `.dark-mode` class selector genuinely changes it at runtime; Sass variables are compiled away into fixed literal values before the browser ever sees the CSS.
questions.explanation: This is the single biggest practical advantage of native CSS variables for things like dark-mode theming or responsive value swaps without a build step or JS re-render.

questions.question: A custom property `--main-color` is defined on `:root`, but a deeply nested component redefines it locally for a specific section, and an unrelated sibling component elsewhere on the page unexpectedly also picks up the new color. What CSS mechanism explains this, and what's the fix?
questions.answer: Custom properties are inherited down the DOM tree from wherever they're (re)defined - if `.footer` happens to be a DOM descendant of `.sidebar` (even if not visually 'inside' it in the page design), it inherits the redefined `--main-color`; the fix is to ensure the override is scoped to a selector that only wraps the intended DOM subtree, not a broader ancestor.
questions.explanation: This is a common trap: custom property scoping follows the actual DOM tree structure, which doesn't always match a developer's mental model of 'visually separate' components.

questions.question: What is the difference between the `inherit`, `initial`, and `unset` CSS keyword values?
questions.answer: `inherit` forces a property to take its parent's computed value even if not normally inherited; `initial` resets it to the property's specification-defined default value; `unset` acts like `inherit` for naturally-inherited properties or `initial` for naturally-non-inherited ones.
questions.explanation: `unset` is essentially 'do what would happen if no CSS at all targeted this property,' which is a convenient way to reset without needing to know whether a property is normally inherited.

questions.question: What are the four main tie-breaking factors CSS uses, in priority order, to resolve which of several conflicting declarations applies to an element?
questions.answer: 1) Origin and importance (e.g. author !important beats author normal, which beats user-agent default), 2) specificity of the selector, 3) order of appearance (later wins if specificity ties), and proximity/inheritance distance is considered separately for inherited values vs directly-targeting rules.
questions.explanation: Understanding this ordered list (rather than just 'specificity' alone) explains cases where a seemingly less-specific but `!important` or later-declared rule wins.

questions.question: A component library ships with `* { box-sizing: border-box; }` as a global reset, but a specific third-party widget embedded on the page needs `box-sizing: content-box` and setting it directly on the widget's own class doesn't seem to override the universal selector rule. What's actually going on?
questions.answer: It almost certainly IS overriding correctly by specificity (a class selector beats the universal `*` selector), so the real cause is more likely rule order (a later stylesheet re-applying the universal reset) or the widget's own inline/shadow-DOM styles taking precedence - specificity math itself favors the class selector here.
questions.explanation: This scenario is a common 'my fix isn't working' debugging trap where the assumption about which rule should win is correct, so the actual bug lies in load order, a later overriding rule, or encapsulated styles (e.g. Shadow DOM) rather than specificity itself.

questions.question: Which vendor prefix is historically associated with Internet Explorer/older Microsoft browsers?
questions.answer: -ms-
questions.explanation: -webkit- is Chrome/Safari (WebKit/Blink), -moz- is Firefox (Gecko), -ms- is Internet Explorer/Edge Legacy, and -o- was the old Opera Presto engine.

questions.question: Why do modern build tools typically add vendor prefixes automatically (e.g. via Autoprefixer) rather than developers writing them by hand?
questions.answer: The set of properties needing prefixes, and which browsers/versions need which prefix, changes constantly as browsers implement and later drop prefix requirements - an automated tool driven by a live browser-support database (like caniuse data) stays accurate without manual upkeep.
questions.explanation: Manually maintained prefixes tend to rot: either missing new cases, or shipping unnecessary prefixes for browsers that no longer need them, bloating the CSS.

questions.question: What does progressive enhancement mean in the context of CSS feature support across browsers?
questions.answer: It means building a baseline experience that works everywhere using well-supported features, then layering on enhancements (like a new CSS feature) for browsers that support them, via feature detection (e.g. `@supports`) - rather than requiring the newest feature for the page to work at all.
questions.explanation: This is the opposite of 'graceful degradation,' which starts from the fullest experience and strips features down for older browsers - both are valid strategies with different starting assumptions.

questions.question: A CSS feature is used with a `@supports (display: grid) { ... }` guard, but a very old browser that doesn't understand `@supports` at all (not even to evaluate it as false) still somehow applies the styles inside it. Why, and is this actually a bug?
questions.answer: This isn't really possible for a spec-compliant browser - browsers that don't understand `@supports` are required to simply ignore the entire unknown at-rule block, not apply its contents; if styles seem to 'leak through' anyway, the real cause is more likely a different code path (inline styles, a separate stylesheet without the guard) accidentally styling the same elements.
questions.explanation: CSS's error-handling model is 'ignore what you don't understand' at the rule/block level, so an unsupported at-rule silently disappears rather than executing its contents unconditionally - a genuinely broken feature-detection guard would point to a different bug.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a CSS reset or normalize stylesheet (like normalize.css) at the top of a project's styles?
questions.answer: It neutralizes small, inconsistent default styling differences that browsers apply to elements out of the box (margins on headings, list bullet styles, form element fonts, etc.), giving a more consistent starting point across browsers before a project's own styles are applied.
questions.explanation: A 'reset' aggressively zeroes out almost all default styling, while a 'normalize' approach preserves useful defaults and only fixes inconsistencies - both aim at the same underlying cross-browser consistency problem.

questions.question: Which CSS property is a shorthand that sets font-style, font-weight, font-size, line-height, and font-family all at once?
questions.answer: font
questions.explanation: The `font` shorthand requires at least font-size and font-family to be valid, with the other sub-properties optional in a specific order.

questions.question: Why can using the `font` shorthand property accidentally reset properties you didn't intend to change, like `font-variant` or `line-height`?
questions.answer: CSS shorthand properties reset every sub-property they cover to its initial value if not explicitly specified in the shorthand, even if that sub-property was set by an earlier, more specific rule - so `font: 16px Arial;` silently resets `line-height` to `normal` even if a separate rule had set it.
questions.explanation: This 'shorthand resets everything' behavior is a common source of subtle bugs when shorthand and longhand declarations for the same properties are mixed carelessly.

questions.question: What is the specificity weight of a single class selector like `.button` in the standard specificity model?
questions.explanation: Using the (inline, ID, class/attribute/pseudo-class, element) 4-part model, a single class contributes exactly one point in the third position.

questions.question: What does the universal selector `*` match, and what is its specificity?
questions.answer: `*` matches every element on the page, and it has zero specificity - it's the weakest possible selector, easily overridden by any other selector type.
questions.explanation: This makes `*` useful for broad resets (like `* { box-sizing: border-box; }`) precisely because almost anything else can override it without a fight.

questions.question: With `box-sizing: border-box`, does setting `width: 200px` include or exclude padding and border in that 200px?
questions.answer: Includes padding and border
questions.explanation: `border-box` makes the declared width/height represent the TOTAL rendered box size, with content area shrinking to accommodate padding/border - the opposite of the default `content-box` behavior.

questions.question: An element has `box-sizing: content-box` (default), `width: 100px`, `padding: 10px`, and `border: 2px solid`. What is its total rendered width?
questions.code_snippet: .box { box-sizing: content-box; width: 100px; padding: 10px; border: 2px solid; }
questions.answer: 124px (100px content + 10px left padding + 10px right padding + 2px left border + 2px right border)
questions.explanation: Under `content-box`, padding and border are added ON TOP of the declared width, so the total occupied width is always larger than the `width` value itself.

questions.question: Which `position` value keeps an element positioned relative to its normal position in the document flow, still occupying its original space?
questions.answer: relative
questions.explanation: `relative` positioning offsets an element visually via top/left/etc. but leaves a 'ghost' gap in the layout where it would have been, unlike `absolute`/`fixed` which remove it from flow entirely.

questions.question: Do `top`, `left`, `right`, and `bottom` have any effect on an element with the default `position: static`?
questions.answer: No - offset properties are entirely ignored on statically positioned elements; they only take effect once `position` is set to `relative`, `absolute`, `fixed`, or `sticky`.
questions.explanation: This is a common beginner mistake: adding `top: 10px` to an element expecting it to move, without realizing `position: static` (the default) makes offset properties inert.

questions.question: Which value makes an element behave as a table-like grid without using actual <table> HTML markup?
questions.answer: display: table
questions.explanation: `display: table` (with children set to `display: table-row`/`table-cell`) mimics HTML table layout purely via CSS on any elements, though Grid/Flexbox are generally preferred today.

questions.question: What is the default `display` value of the element?
questions.answer: `inline` - which is why images can have unexpected extra space below them (treated like inline text with descender space) unless changed to `display: block` or `vertical-align` is adjusted.
questions.explanation: This 'phantom gap under images' is a very common beginner CSS puzzle traced directly back to ``'s default inline display type.

questions.question: Which property, applied to flex ITEMS (not the container), controls their order of appearance independent of their order in the HTML source?
questions.answer: order
questions.explanation: `order` accepts any integer; items are laid out from lowest to highest order value, with ties broken by source order - purely a visual reordering, the DOM/source order (and thus tab order) is unaffected.

questions.question: A developer uses the flex `order` property to visually reorder items for a specific layout, but keyboard/tab users navigate through them in a confusing sequence that doesn't match what they see on screen. Why, and what's the takeaway?
questions.answer: `order` only changes VISUAL rendering order, not the underlying DOM order that keyboard Tab navigation follows, so a mismatch between what's seen and what's tabbed through is expected, not a bug; the fix is to either match visual and DOM order, or accept `order` should be used sparingly for accessibility-sensitive layouts.
questions.explanation: This is a well-documented Flexbox accessibility pitfall: visual reordering via CSS can silently create a confusing disconnect from the actual interaction/reading order.

questions.question: Which property on a grid ITEM aligns it horizontally within its own grid cell, analogous to `align-self` for vertical alignment?
questions.answer: justify-self
questions.explanation: `justify-self` controls inline-axis (horizontal, in a standard writing mode) alignment of one item within its cell; `place-self` is shorthand for `align-self justify-self` together.

questions.question: What does naming grid lines (e.g. `grid-template-columns: [start] 1fr [middle] 2fr [end]`) let you do?
questions.answer: It lets you reference those named lines directly in `grid-column`/`grid-row` (e.g. `grid-column: start / middle`) instead of using bare line numbers, making grid placement more self-documenting and resilient to structural changes.
questions.explanation: Named lines are purely a readability/maintainability aid - they don't change layout behavior, just how you refer to the same underlying grid structure.

questions.question: Which logical operator in a media query requires ALL listed conditions to be true?
questions.answer: and
questions.explanation: `@media (min-width: 600px) and (orientation: landscape) { ... }` applies only when both conditions hold; commas between queries act as OR instead.

questions.question: What is the difference between using a comma and using `and` to combine multiple conditions in a media query?
questions.answer: A comma acts as a logical OR (the query matches if ANY listed condition is true); `and` acts as a logical AND (all conditions in that clause must be true simultaneously).
questions.explanation: `@media (max-width: 600px), (orientation: portrait)` matches if either condition holds, while `@media (max-width: 600px) and (orientation: portrait)` requires both.

questions.question: Which CSS function allows mathematical expressions combining different units, like `calc(100% - 50px)`?
questions.answer: calc()
questions.explanation: `calc()` is the only built-in CSS function for mixed-unit arithmetic, and it's valid almost anywhere a length, percentage, or number value is expected.

questions.question: What does the `ch` unit represent in CSS?
questions.answer: The advance width (roughly the width) of the '0' (zero) character in the element's current font - often used to size text-related boxes (like limiting a paragraph to `65ch` for readable line length).
questions.explanation: Since it's tied to the actual rendered font's character width, `ch` scales appropriately if the font size or font family changes, unlike a hardcoded pixel width.

questions.question: Which CSS property controls whether consecutive white-space characters in HTML are collapsed into a single space when rendered?
questions.answer: white-space
questions.explanation: The default `white-space: normal` collapses runs of whitespace into one space and allows wrapping; `pre` preserves whitespace exactly, similar to a <pre> tag.

questions.question: What is the difference between `word-break: break-all` and `overflow-wrap: break-word`?
questions.answer: `break-all` allows breaking between ANY two characters wherever needed to prevent overflow, even in the middle of normally-breakable words; `overflow-wrap: break-word` only breaks a word mid-way as a last resort, when the word alone is too long to fit even on its own line.
questions.explanation: `break-all` produces more aggressive, sometimes awkward mid-word breaks even for short words, while `overflow-wrap` is more conservative and only intervenes for genuinely unbreakable long tokens.

questions.question: Which pseudo-class matches a form input currently failing its HTML5 validation constraints?
questions.answer: :invalid
questions.explanation: `:invalid` (paired with `:valid` for the opposite case) lets you style form fields based on live constraint-validation state, entirely in CSS.

questions.question: What is the difference between `::placeholder` and using the `placeholder` HTML attribute?
questions.answer: `placeholder` (the HTML attribute) sets WHAT hint text appears in an empty input; `::placeholder` (the CSS pseudo-element) styles HOW that hint text looks (color, font, opacity), and has no effect without the attribute actually being set.
questions.explanation: They work together: one supplies the content, the other styles it - `::placeholder` alone with no `placeholder` attribute styles nothing since there's no placeholder text to target.

questions.question: Which property lets you specify a delay before a CSS transition begins after its triggering property change?
questions.answer: transition-delay
questions.explanation: `transition-delay: 0.5s;` postpones the START of the transition; it doesn't affect how long the transition itself takes once it begins (that's `transition-duration`).

questions.question: Can you transition or animate the `display` property directly to fade an element in while also making it participate in layout again?
questions.answer: Not smoothly with `transition` alone (display isn't interpolable), but modern browsers support animating `display` via `@keyframes` combined with `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` (or historically via a `display: none` swap timed with `setTimeout`/`animationend` in JS).
questions.explanation: This has long been a genuine CSS limitation; the newer `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` property is specifically designed to let discrete properties like `display` participate in an otherwise-smooth transition sequence.

questions.question: Which `transform` function moves an element along the X and Y axes without affecting layout flow?
questions.answer: translate()
questions.explanation: `translate(x, y)` shifts the rendered position visually; `translateX()`/`translateY()` do it along a single axis only.

questions.question: Why is animating `transform: translateX()` generally considered more performant than animating the `left` property for the same visual movement?
questions.answer: Changing `left` triggers layout recalculation (reflow) on every frame since it affects the element's box position in the flow model, while `transform` is handled purely at the compositing stage on the GPU, skipping layout and paint entirely for that change.
questions.explanation: This is why `transform`/`opacity` are often called the 'cheap' properties to animate, while properties affecting box geometry (`width`, `left`, `margin`) are comparatively expensive.

questions.question: What happens if you reference a custom property that was never defined anywhere, with no fallback provided, e.g. `color: var(--undefined-color);`?
options: The declaration is treated as invalid and the property falls back to its inherited or initial value
The browser throws a JavaScript error
It renders as black by default
questions.answer: The declaration is treated as invalid and the property falls back to its inherited or initial value
questions.explanation: An undefined custom property with no fallback makes the whole declaration 'invalid at computed-value time,' which CSS handles by falling back to the property's inherited (or initial) value, not by erroring.

questions.question: Can CSS custom properties be changed dynamically via JavaScript, and if so how?
questions.answer: Yes, via `element.style.setProperty('--my-var', 'newValue')`, which updates the property's value live and triggers the browser to recompute any styles referencing it via `var()`.
questions.explanation: This is a common bridge pattern between JS application state and CSS-driven visuals, avoiding the need to toggle many individual class names for value-based (not just boolean) style changes.

questions.question: Which of these correctly lists CSS's origin priority from LOWEST to HIGHEST precedence (ignoring !important)?
questions.answer: User-agent (browser default) -> User -> Author
questions.explanation: Normally author styles (the website's own CSS) win over user and browser-default styles - though `!important` flips this order specifically for user-origin declarations, which can override even author `!important` in some specs.

questions.question: If two `!important` declarations from the same author origin conflict, how is the tie broken?
questions.answer: The normal cascade rules (specificity, then source order) still apply AMONG declarations marked `!important` - `!important` only elevates a whole tier above non-important declarations, it doesn't remove the need for further tie-breaking within that tier.
questions.explanation: This is a common misconception: `!important` isn't an absolute trump card that ends all further comparison, it just changes which normal-cascade tier the declaration competes within.

questions.question: Which resource is most commonly used by developers to check real-time cross-browser support percentages for a specific CSS feature?
questions.answer: caniuse.com
questions.explanation: caniuse.com aggregates up-to-date browser support data (including specific version numbers and known partial-support caveats) for web platform features, and is the data source many automated tools like Autoprefixer rely on.

questions.question: What does `@supports not (display: grid) { ... }` let you write styles for?
questions.answer: Styles that should apply ONLY to browsers that do NOT support CSS Grid, typically used to provide a fallback layout (e.g. floats or inline-block) for older browsers while the main styles use Grid unconditionally elsewhere.
questions.explanation: This inverts the more common 'if supported, enhance' pattern into an explicit 'if NOT supported, provide fallback' pattern, both built on the same `@supports` feature-detection mechanism.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a primitive type in JavaScript?
questions.answer: object
questions.explanation: object is a reference type; JavaScript's primitives are string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, and null.

questions.question: What is the difference between `null` and `undefined`?
questions.answer: `undefined` means a variable has been declared but not yet assigned a value; `null` is an explicit assignment representing 'no value', deliberately set by the programmer.
questions.explanation: `typeof undefined` is `'undefined'` while `typeof null` is (famously, due to a long-standing bug) `'object'` — they are distinct values with `==` treating them as equal but `===` treating them as different.

questions.question: What does `typeof []` return?
questions.answer: 'object'
questions.explanation: Arrays are a special kind of object in JavaScript, so `typeof` reports `'object'`; use `Array.isArray()` to specifically detect arrays.

questions.question: What is the main scoping difference between `var` and `let`?
questions.answer: `var` is function-scoped (or globally scoped if declared outside a function), while `let` is block-scoped, meaning it only exists within the nearest enclosing `{ }` block.
questions.explanation: This means a `var` declared inside an `if` block leaks out to the surrounding function, while a `let` in the same position does not.

questions.question: Which declaration prevents reassignment of the variable binding itself?
questions.answer: const
questions.explanation: const creates a binding that cannot be reassigned, though if it holds an object/array, the object's contents can still be mutated.

questions.question: Explain why this code throws an error, and how to fix it.
questions.answer: TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
questions.explanation: `total` was declared with `const`, which forbids reassigning the binding; changing to `let total = 0;` fixes it since `let` allows reassignment.

questions.question: What does this loop print, and why does `let` behave differently from `var` here?
questions.explanation: Each loop iteration with `let` creates a fresh binding of `i` scoped to that iteration, so each `setTimeout` callback captures its own `i` value (0, 1, 2) rather than sharing one variable, unlike the classic `var` version of this loop which would print 3, 3, 3.

questions.question: What will `typeof NaN` return?
questions.answer: 'number'
questions.explanation: NaN ('Not a Number') is, ironically, of type number in JavaScript's type system — it represents an invalid numeric result, not the absence of a numeric type.

questions.question: What is the difference between `==` and `===` in JavaScript?
questions.answer: `==` (loose equality) performs type coercion before comparing, while `===` (strict equality) compares both value and type without coercion.
questions.explanation: For example, `1 == '1'` is `true` because the string is coerced to a number first, but `1 === '1'` is `false` since the types differ.

questions.question: What does comparing NaN to itself print here?
questions.answer: false
questions.explanation: `NaN` is the only JavaScript value that is not equal to itself under either `==` or `===`, because IEEE-754 defines NaN comparisons to always be false; use `Number.isNaN()` or `Object.is()` to test for it.
questions.code_snippet: console.log(NaN === NaN);

questions.question: What does the `??` (nullish coalescing) operator do?
questions.answer: Returns the right operand only if the left is null or undefined
questions.explanation: Unlike `||`, which falls through for any falsy value (0, '', false, NaN), `??` only falls through specifically for `null` or `undefined`, preserving legitimate falsy values like 0 or ''.
options: Returns the right operand only if the left is falsy
Returns the right operand only if the left is null or undefined

questions.question: What does this snippet print given the nullish coalescing operator and a falsy-but-not-nullish value?
questions.explanation: `||` treats `0` as falsy and falls through to the right operand (`5`)... wait — actually with `??`, since `0` is neither `null` nor `undefined`, it is returned as-is, so the output is `0`.
questions.code_snippet:
const count = 0;
console.log(count ?? 5);

questions.question: What is the result of `'5' + 3` in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: When either operand of `+` is a string, JavaScript coerces the other operand to a string and concatenates rather than performing numeric addition.

questions.question: What is the result of `'5' - 3`?
questions.explanation: Unlike `+`, the `-` operator has no string-concatenation meaning, so both operands are coerced to numbers: `'5'` becomes `5`, giving `5 - 3 = 2`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `switch` with and without `break` statements?
questions.answer: Without `break`, execution 'falls through' into the next case's code after a match, executing subsequent cases regardless of their own condition, until a `break` or the end of the switch is reached.
questions.explanation: Fall-through can be intentional (grouping multiple case labels to share code) but is a common source of bugs when a `break` is accidentally omitted.

questions.question: What does this switch statement print, given the missing break in the first case?
questions.answer:
one
two
questions.explanation: Case 'a' has no break, so execution falls through into case 'b's code as well, printing both 'one' and 'two' before hitting the break in case 'b'.

questions.question: What is a first-class function, and why does it matter in JavaScript?
questions.answer: A first-class function is one that can be assigned to a variable, passed as an argument, and returned from another function, just like any other value.
questions.explanation: This is foundational to JavaScript's functional-programming features — callbacks, higher-order functions, and closures all rely on functions being treated as ordinary values.

questions.question: What does a function without an explicit `return` statement return?
questions.answer: undefined
questions.explanation: If a function body finishes without hitting a `return`, JavaScript implicitly returns `undefined`.

questions.question: What is the difference between a function declaration and a function expression regarding hoisting?
questions.answer: Function declarations (`function foo() {}`) are fully hoisted — both the name and body are available before their line of code runs. Function expressions (`const foo = function() {}`) only hoist the variable declaration (as undefined, for `var`), not the assignment, so calling it before the assignment throws or fails.
questions.explanation: This is why you can call a function declared later in the file via a declaration, but not one assigned via an expression.

questions.question: What is a key behavioral difference between arrow functions and regular functions?
questions.answer: Arrow functions do not have their own `this` — they inherit it lexically from the enclosing scope
questions.explanation: Regular functions get their own `this` determined by how they're called; arrow functions instead capture `this` from the surrounding lexical scope at definition time, which is why they're popular for callbacks inside methods.
options: Arrow functions do not have their own `this` — they inherit it lexically from the enclosing scope

questions.question: This object method is supposed to log the object's name after a delay, but logs `undefined` instead. Fix it.
questions.answer: TypeError/undefined output because the regular function passed to setTimeout gets its own `this`, which is undefined/global in this context, not the `person` object.
questions.explanation: Changing the callback to an arrow function (`() => console.log(this.name)`) makes it inherit `this` from `greet`'s lexical scope, which correctly refers to `person`.

questions.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
questions.answer: A closure is a function that retains access to variables from its enclosing (lexical) scope even after that outer function has finished executing.
questions.explanation: Closures are what let a function 'remember' the environment it was created in — commonly used to create private state, e.g. a counter function that keeps its own count variable.

questions.question: Write a function `makeCounter()` that returns a function which, each time it is called, returns an incrementing count starting from 1.
questions.explanation: The returned inner function closes over `count`, so each call mutates and reads the same private variable that persists across calls, rather than resetting each time.

questions.question: What does this `var`-based loop print, and why is it different from the `let` version?
questions.explanation: `var` is function-scoped, so all three callbacks close over the SAME `i` variable; by the time the timeouts fire (after the loop has fully finished), `i` has reached 3 for all of them.

questions.question: What is the 'temporal dead zone' (TDZ)?
questions.answer: The TDZ is the period between entering a scope and the point where a `let`/`const` variable is actually declared, during which accessing that variable throws a ReferenceError, even though the variable is technically hoisted.
questions.explanation: Unlike `var` (hoisted and initialized to `undefined`), `let`/`const` are hoisted but not initialized, so referencing them before their declaration line fails fast instead of silently returning `undefined`.

questions.question: What does logging `x` before its `var` declaration print?
questions.answer: undefined
questions.explanation: `var x` is hoisted to the top of the function, so at the point of `console.log(x)` the declaration already exists (with value `undefined`) but the assignment `x = 5` hasn't run yet — this is different from a ReferenceError, which would occur with `let`/`const` in the same position.
questions.code_snippet:
console.log(x);
var x = 5;

questions.question: In a regular (non-arrow) method called as `obj.method()`, what does `this` refer to inside `method`?
questions.answer: `obj`, the object the method was called on
questions.explanation: `this` is determined by the call-site: calling a function as a property of an object (`obj.method()`) binds `this` to that object.
options: `obj`, the object the method was called on

questions.question: Extracting a method into a standalone variable and calling it breaks `this`. Explain why and fix it.
questions.answer: Calling `sayHi` as a bare function loses its connection to `user`, so `this` becomes `undefined` (in strict mode/modules) or the global object, and `this.name` fails or is wrong.
questions.explanation: Fix with `.bind(user)` (`const sayHi = user.sayHi.bind(user);`), or by using an arrow function wrapper (`const sayHi = () => user.sayHi();`), so `this` is explicitly locked to `user` regardless of how `sayHi` is later invoked.

questions.question: How do you check if an object has a property directly on itself (not inherited)?
questions.answer: obj.hasOwnProperty('key')
questions.explanation: `hasOwnProperty` checks only the object's own properties, ignoring anything found further up the prototype chain, unlike the `in` operator which checks inherited properties too.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Object.freeze()` and `Object.seal()`?
questions.answer: `Object.freeze()` prevents adding, removing, AND modifying existing properties (fully immutable, shallowly). `Object.seal()` prevents adding or removing properties, but existing properties can still be modified (just not reconfigured or deleted).
questions.explanation: Both are shallow — a frozen object's nested objects are still mutable unless frozen separately.

questions.question: Write a function `deepClone(obj)` that returns a deep copy of a plain JSON-serializable object (no functions, dates, or circular references).
questions.explanation: For plain JSON-compatible data, serializing to a string and parsing it back creates an entirely independent copy with no shared references at any nesting level; this approach fails for functions, `undefined`, `Date` objects, and circular structures, which is why the constraint is stated.

test_cases.expected_output: {a: 1, b: {c: 2}} (new object, mutating the copy's b.c does not affect the original)

questions.question: Which array method creates a NEW array by applying a function to every element, without mutating the original?
questions.answer: map
questions.explanation: `map` returns a new array of the same length with each element transformed by the callback; `forEach` returns undefined and is used purely for side effects.

questions.question: What is the difference between `map` and `filter`?
questions.answer: `map` transforms every element and returns a new array of the SAME length; `filter` selects a subset of elements (based on a predicate returning true/false) and returns a new array that may be SHORTER.
questions.explanation: Chaining them (`arr.filter(...).map(...)`) is a common pattern for 'select then transform' pipelines.

questions.question: Write a function `sumEvens(numbers)` that returns the sum of all even numbers in an array using `filter` and `reduce`.
questions.explanation: `filter` keeps only even numbers, then `reduce` accumulates them into a single sum starting from an initial accumulator of 0.

questions.question: What does `[1, 2, 3].includes(2)` return?
questions.answer: true
questions.explanation: `includes` performs a value search and returns a boolean indicating whether the array contains the given value (using SameValueZero comparison).

questions.question: What array does mapping `nums` to their squares print here?
questions.explanation: `map` squares each number, producing a brand-new array `[1, 4, 9]`; the original `nums` array is unaffected because `map` never mutates its source.

questions.question: What is the prototype chain in JavaScript?
questions.answer: Every object has an internal link (`[[Prototype]]`, accessible via `Object.getPrototypeOf` or the legacy `__proto__`) to another object; when a property isn't found on the object itself, JavaScript looks it up along this chain of linked objects until it finds it or reaches `null`.
questions.explanation: This is how JavaScript implements inheritance — methods defined on `Array.prototype`, for example, are available on every array instance via the prototype chain, without being copied onto each array.

questions.question: What does the `class` keyword in modern JavaScript primarily provide?
questions.answer: Syntactic sugar over JavaScript's existing prototype-based inheritance
questions.explanation: Under the hood, `class` syntax still creates functions and sets up the prototype chain the same way `Object.create`/constructor-function patterns always did — it's a cleaner syntax, not a different inheritance mechanism.
options: A completely new inheritance model unrelated to prototypes
Syntactic sugar over JavaScript's existing prototype-based inheritance

questions.question: Which ES6 feature allows embedding expressions directly inside string literals using backticks?
questions.answer: Template literals
questions.explanation: Template literals (backtick strings) support `${expression}` interpolation and multi-line strings without concatenation.

questions.question: What problem do JavaScript modules (`import`/`export`) solve compared to plain `<script>` tags?
questions.answer: Modules provide file-scoped variables/functions by default (nothing leaks to global scope unless exported), explicit dependency declarations, and are only executed once even if imported multiple times, avoiding the global-namespace collisions common with multiple plain scripts.
questions.explanation: This makes large codebases more maintainable by making dependencies explicit and preventing accidental global variable clashes between files.

questions.question: Given `const user = { name: 'Ana', age: 30 };`, write a destructuring statement to extract `name` and `age` into standalone variables.
questions.answer: const { name, age } = user;
questions.explanation: Object destructuring pulls out properties by matching variable names to property keys, avoiding repeated `user.name`/`user.age` access.
